title: Uber fined nearly $1B by Dutch regulators over automated suspensions of accounts
summary: Dutch data protection authorities have fined Uber nearly $1 billion, saying the ride-hailing company used automated software to suspend driver accounts, sometimes permanently with no human review to check for mistakes
story: Dutch data protection authorities have fined Uber nearly $1 billion, saying the ride-hailing company used automated software to suspend driver accounts, sometimes permanently with no human review to check for mistakes

Dutch data protection authorities have fined Uber nearly $1 billion, saying the ride-hailing company used automated software to suspend driver accounts, sometimes permanently, with no human review to check for mistakes.

The Dutch Data Protection Authority said Friday it is imposing a fine of 825 million euros ($964 million) because Uber violated the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation. The EU’s data privacy rules prohibit fully automated decision-making.
The authority also said Uber failed inform drivers about its automatic decision-making. The violations took place from 2018 to 2022, the agency said.
Uber said it disagreed with the decision and the fine and will file an appeal.

"The (Data Protection Authority) examined historic policies that were discontinued years ago. We take decisions that affect drivers' ability to earn extremely seriously and we’re fully committed to fair treatment. This includes human reviews, robust safeguards, and the opportunity for drivers to appeal our decisions if they believe we made a mistake,” the company said in a written statement.

This is the fourth time the authority has imposed a fine on Uber. The largest was in 2024, when Uber was hit with a 290 million euro ($324 million) fine for allegedly transferring personal details of European drivers to the United States without adequate protection.

title: Schools are starting to teach AI literacy. For many, that means helping kids see chatbots' flaws
summary: AI chatbots have become the bane of teachers everywhere
story: AI chatbots have become the bane of teachers everywhere

NORTH CHARLESTON, S.C. -- Artificial intelligence chatbots have become the bane of teachers everywhere, but to prepare for the new school year, a group of educators in Charleston, South Carolina, packed into a high school auditorium and talked about inviting AI into the classroom.
The teachers and principals watched as an instructor prompted an AI tool to “create a map of the world.”

The result drew gasps of disbelief and laughter. Projected on a large screen was a map riddled with bizarre errors. Mali was spelled “Mail.” Egypt was identified as “Sopth.” In place of Libya was something simply called “Africa.” Dozens of other countries' names were misspelled or written in pure gibberish.

“If you ever want kids not to over trust these tools, try the map demo,” said the instructor, Amanda Bickerstaff, founder and CEO of AI For Education, an organization that helps schools draft AI policies and train teachers and students in what she calls safe, ethical and effective use of the technology.

After initially trying to ban AI use, a growing number of U.S. public schools are trying a new strategy: encouraging classroom experimentation, partly so students can see its shortcomings, including generative AI’s notorious tendency to “hallucinate,” or fabricate information.

AI literacy has become a buzzword of this back-to-school season as educators try to strike a balance between equipping students with the skills they need for an AI-driven future while preventing them from outsourcing their thinking to chatbots.

There is no single definition of what AI literacy means, or how it should be taught. Tech giants like OpenAI, Google and Anthropic offer schools training sessions in how to use their AI tools. But for educators, there is a growing consensus that AI literacy is about more than learning how to use generative AI and write good prompts.
“Good AI literacy,” said Rebecca Winthrop, director of the Center for Universal Education at the Brookings Institution, “includes knowing when not to use it.”
Thirty-seven states have now published official AI guidance that schools can use as a blueprint. South Carolina is not one of them.

So the state’s second-largest school district set out to do it on its own, said Lucas Clamp, deputy superintendent of the 50,000-student Charleston County School District. “It has been a huge endeavor.”
A year ago, the district contacted AI for Education, which helped draft guidance for Chicago Public Schools, Houston and dozens of other districts.
Phase 1 was laying the foundation. The district developed an AI policy, seeking input from teachers, students and parents.

The district organized student focus groups and learned that student AI use was ubiquitous but unguided. Teachers and students said they were navigating the technology on their own and wanted clear rules and instruction.

Studies show a majority of teenagers and teachers nationwide are using AI for schoolwork, but they're teaching themselves how to use it; very few say they have a technical understanding or have received formal training on how it works.

Schools and parents are eager to avoid mistakes made with social media, where kids were left to explore the online world without learning about addictive algorithms, comparison culture and other downsides that have been linked to a youth mental health crisis and dwindling attention spans.

As the school year begins in Charleston, Phase 2 kicks in: training. Teachers and middle and high schoolers will get a mix of online and in-person instruction on how AI tools work and how to use them effectively.

The student course walks through familiar scenarios — like asking a chatbot to help with a research paper — to show that generative AI might deliver wildly inaccurate information, including made-up studies, with unflinching authority. “Always verify any factual information you get from GenAI, especially for your classwork,” the course advises.
A section on data privacy cautions against sharing personal information with AI tools because conversations can be stored, used for data training and potentially leaked.

High school teacher Ray Knauer attended the summer training and left with “teachable moments” for his AP Research class. He plans to show examples of AI bias and hallucinations to fuel student discussions.

“We’re all trying to figure this out right now: What’s the right balance so we don’t scare students away from AI but don’t encourage them to run to it,” Knauer said. “We have to teach students: You can’t just get an answer and move on. You have to use analytical skills and dig deeper.”
Utah was an early pioneer in taking a statewide approach to AI in education.
In 2024, the board of education named Matt Winters as its AI education specialist, making Utah the first state to create a full-time position overseeing the technology in schools.

Over the past year, Winters led AI training for over 7,000 teachers, almost a third of Utah’s public school instructors. He is helping districts shape AI policies, which they are required by state law to have in place by July 2027.

“There is a clear method from the top in Utah,” said Chris Agnew, director of the Generative AI for Education Hub at Stanford University. “When you’re tackling big change, it’s easier to have coherence if everyone is singing from the same hymn book.”
A handful of other states have since replicated Winters’ post, including Maine, West Virginia and Georgia.

In other states, a patchwork of AI approaches has emerged, with variance from one school district to another. Extensive AI literacy training requires steep investment, raising concerns that kids in under-resourced districts might not get the same attention.

In Utah, training starts with the basics of how AI works to teach an understanding of AI bias, hallucinations, ethical concerns and data privacy needs, Winters said. Teachers can then pursue additional training on specific tools.

“If I had to give advice: Figure out how to make training accessible to everyone,” said Emma Moss, who oversees AI at the Canyons School District and also led an eight-person team that traveled the state doing over 150 AI literacy trainings. The training was funded by a $500,000 AI literacy grant from a local healthcare provider. “We said, ‘We will come to you.’ Whether you are in a rural area or urban, it didn’t matter.”

The state has also played a key role in procuring AI tools, Winters said. He negotiated data privacy agreements along with discounted prices, which has allowed rural and under-resourced districts to get access.

“Everyone needs to understand what this technology is and how it works,” said Winters, who cautions against blanket bans. “AI literacy is much larger than saying: ‘Don’t use AI.’ It’s about how we can prepare kids for the future.”
Changing adult mindsets is also key, said Kristina Yamada, the state Board of Education's digital technology specialist.

“I think teachers need to change their mentality about students using AI to cheat,” Yamada said. There has always been cheating, she said. It’s up to teachers to speak students’ language and convince them they can’t rely on AI for all the answers.

For younger kids it means starting to talk about AI early, with conversations like, “People can lie. A program can lie. A robot can lie,” Yamada said. “For older students it’s different: ‘Sure, you can use ChatGPT to write computer code. But when the program stops working, you need to be able to fix it.’”
Gecker reported from San Francisco.

title: At least 65 Americans missing in Nepal-Tibet floods, officials say amid rescue op
summary: At least 168 people have been confirmed killed by the massive flash flooding that ravaged the Nepal-Tibet border region on Wednesday.
story: The Nepal Tourism Board announced that 65 Americans are among the missing.

LONDON -- At least 168 people have been confirmed killed by the massive flash flooding that ravaged the Nepal-Tibet border region on Wednesday, emergency authorities in Nepal and China said. More than 1,300 people remained missing as of Thursday morning, authorities said.
As search and rescue efforts continued in Nepal on Thursday, authorities there said that at least 165 bodies had been recovered.

At least 826 people -- among them 579 tourists, of whom 476 are foreign nationals and 114 Nepali nationals -- were still out of contact, the Nepal National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said.
Across the border in the Chinese region of Tibet, the state-run Xinhua News Agency reported on Thursday that three people were confirmed killed with 558 others still missing, citing local officials.
The number of those considered missing fluctuated significantly as recovery efforts accelerated. The Nepal Tourism Board announced on Thursday that 65 Americans are among the missing.

The flooding, captured in dramatic video footage, occurred in the northern Rasuwa district, along the border with Tibet, at around 8:40 a.m. local time on Wednesday, authorities said, inundating areas along the Trishuli River, burying some buildings and damaging bridges and roadways.

In a statement, Nepal's office of the prime minister expressed "deep sorrow" over the loss of life. "Offering heartfelt tribute to all those who lost their lives in this natural disaster, it extends its sincere condolences to the bereaved families and relatives," the statement shared on social media said.
The prime minister's office later said search and rescue operations carried out by the Nepali Army would continue through the night.
The State Department said the number of Americans among the missing and otherwise impacted by the floods fluctuated throughout the day on Wednesday.

"The United States extends its deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in the devastating flash floods in the Rasuwa district of Nepal. Our thoughts are with all those affected by this disaster," a department spokesperson said in a statement issued later Wednesday.

The spokesperson said the State Department is "closely monitoring the situation and is deploying a disaster response advisor to the region to support response efforts. The Department will also provide $500,000 in assistance through its global award with Catholic Relief Services, supporting emergency shelter, relief items, and water, sanitation, and hygiene assistance to flood-affected communities."

An Indian spiritual leader and entrepreneur, known as Sadhguru, said in a post to social media that 77 people who were on tours organized by his Isha Foundation were at an immigration center at the Nepal-Tibet border when the floodwaters hit.

The Isha Foundation confirmed to ABC News that 22 of those 77 people were Americans. The organization, which is headquartered in India, also has a base in McMinnville, Tennessee. The group's coordinator told ABC News the organization has been in touch with family members in the U.S.

Three missing Americans were listed as traveling with a Nepali company called Fishtail Tours and Travel. The agency confirmed to ABC News that three American nationals are among the missing tourists traveling with them.
The flood was reportedly triggered by a landslide about 12 miles northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border post along the Nepal-China frontier, according to Nepal Disaster Management.
A 5.2-magnitude landslide was registered in Nepal on Wednesday, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.
The seismic activity from the landslide was initially erroneously reported as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake, the agency said. It is unclear what triggered the landslide.
A geophysicist at New York's Columbia University told ABC News it appeared a landslide in the Himalayas took away a large glacier, or parts of one, in the mountain pass.
ABC News' Desiree Adib, Somayeh Malekian, Charlotte Gardiner, Shannon Kingston, Joseph Simonetti, Dada Jovanovic and Meghan Mistry contributed to this report.

title: CIA director warned Russia not to attack NATO countries during Moscow trip: Sources
summary: CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow earlier this week in part to warn Russia not to attack NATO countries, sources familiar with the trip told ABC News.
story: The CIA director also brought up Iran during the meetings, one source said.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow earlier this week in part to warn Russia not to attack NATO countries, sources familiar with the trip told ABC News.
Ratcliffe also brought up Iran during the meetings in Moscow, one source said.
The Wall Street Journal was first to report the purpose of the trip. The CIA declined to comment on the trip.
President Donald Trump confirmed Ratcliffe's visit earlier Wednesday in an interview with Glenn Beck, but called the visit "semi-routine."
When asked if it had to do with increased Russian aggression against NATO or the increased Iranian economic pressure, Trump claimed it was none of those reasons.
A spokesman for Russian President Vladimir Putin told reporters Ratcliffe was in contact with Russian intelligence agencies but did not meet with Putin.

title: Tate brothers' extradition fight back in Miami court as brothers seek release on bond
summary: A federal judge will consider whether to free Andrew and Tristan Tate from a Miami detention center while they challenge extradition to face rape and sex trafficking charges in the United Kingdom
story: A federal judge will consider whether to free Andrew and Tristan Tate from a Miami detention center while they challenge extradition to face rape and sex trafficking charges in the United Kingdom

MIAMI -- A federal judge will consider Thursday whether social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate should remain in custody as they challenge their extradition to face rape and sex trafficking charges in the United Kingdom.

The Tates have remained in a federal detention center in Miami since making a brief court appearance after their July 18 arrest. Their attorneys have argued that their high profile and active social media presence makes it nearly impossible for them to flee.

U.S. Magistrate Lauren Louis will have a chance to question their defense and prosecutors before determining if the brothers, who have repeatedly denied wrongdoing, should be released during what could be a monthslong extradition process.

The Tates have become among the world’s most polarizing internet personalities by promoting wealth, male dominance and misogyny through their social media empire. The new allegations are the latest in the Tates' long-running international legal saga spanning the U.S., Britain and Romania.
No date for an extradition hearing has been set. The U.K. has until mid-September to provide evidence to the State Department.

Federal prosecutors have urged the court to keep the brothers in custody, citing the strong presumption against bail in international extradition cases. The Tates' claims of having multiple passports and access to wealth and influence in numerous countries demonstrate a heightened risk of flight that no amount of bond could overcome, prosecutors argued.

Attorneys for the Tates say they largely exaggerated their claims of wealth to boost their social media personas, their claims of multiple passports were satirical and a “$50-million-dollar superyacht” featured in one of the brothers' videos does not actually belong to them. The expensive luxury cars, including a $2.1 million Aston Martin, that were featured in other videos were rented, the defense says.

The Tates' attorneys also argued in court filings that the brothers proved they won't flee by complying with pretrial restrictions over a separate case in Romania, where they are accused of luring women for sexual exploitation.
The brothers have long claimed that their violent and misogynistic statements have been taken out of context or were intended as jokes.

The former professional kickboxers, who have dual U.S. and U.K. citizenship, have millions of social media followers and are vocal supporters of President Donald Trump. The White House has said the brothers shouldn’t expect any help from the president.

Andrew Tate, 39, became famous a decade ago when he was a contestant on the U.K. reality television show “Big Brother.” He was ejected from the show when a video appeared to show him assaulting a woman.

He has amassed over 10 million followers on X but has been banned from other platforms, including YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, for violating hate speech guidelines. He has made widely condemned comments, such as saying women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for the attacks and sharing graphic descriptions of how he might attack women.
Tristan Tate, 38, has worked with his brother on multiple businesses, including the production of online webcam pornography.

title: Dolly Parton never forgot Tennessee, now the state pays tribute
summary: The death of country music legend Dolly Parton sent shockwaves around the world, but most notably in her beloved home state of Tennessee.
story: The death of country music legend Dolly Parton sent shockwaves around the world, but most notably in her beloved home state of Tennessee.
Parton died at the age of 80 on Tuesday in Nashville after a "brief battle" with cancer, according to her publicist.
The "Jolene" singer was born into a family of 12 children in the tiny mountain community of Pittman Center, Tennessee.

Though she went on to become one of the world's most successful and admired entertainers, Parton never forgot her roots, opening a theme park, Dollywood, in her home state in the 1980s and donating millions of dollars over the years to support her fellow Tennesseans.
When she turned 80 in January, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee declared her birthday, Jan. 19, as Dolly Parton Day in the state, calling her "Tennessee's favorite daughter."

Following her death on Tuesday, tributes to the star popped up across Tennessee, from her home in Brentwood to her star on the Music City Walk of Fame in Nashville to her hometown and the Grand Ole Opry, where Parton first found fame more than 50 years ago.

Parton left her small mountain hometown immediately after high school for Nashville, where she set out to become a superstar, as she told ABC News' Barbara Walters in a 1977 interview, early in her career.
She spent the rest of her life based in the Nashville area, leaving a lasting impact, according to the city's mayor, Freddie O'Connell.

"While Nashville wasn't her original home, she helped change it forever with an incredible, unprecedented thing: filling a little library in every childcare center in the city with books from her Imagination Library," O'Connell said in a statement Tuesday. "She's given Nashville -- and the world -- story and song and done so in a way that she remained universally beloved in challenging times."

Parton's Imagination Library initiative began in her home county of Sevier County, Tennessee, inspired by her father Robert Lee Parton, who could not read or write. The program, which provides free books each month to children from birth to age 5, regardless of their family's income, eventually expanded across the U.S. and internationally.
Parton was also known to give back to her home state when natural disasters struck.
When devastating wildfires swept through East Tennessee in 2016, Parton established the My People Fund, which provided $1,000 per month for six months to families who lost their homes.
Years later, in 2024, she announced she was donating $1 million of her own money to relief efforts in Tennessee following Hurricane Helene, with another $1 million donated by her businesses.

In 2020, Parton donated $1 million to Tennessee's Vanderbilt University Medical Center to support COVID-19 research. Two years later, she donated another $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center to support pediatric infectious disease research.

Fittingly, Parton's last public in-person appearance before her death was in Tennessee. She made a surprise appearance in June at the grand opening of a gas station and restaurant called Dolly's Tennessean Travel Stop in Cornersville, a town around 60 miles outside of Nashville.

title: Country music legend Dolly Parton dies at 80 after 'brief battle with cancer'
summary: The singer, songwriter and philanthropist enjoyed a more than six-decade career.
story: Dolly Parton, the beloved country music superstar known as much for her philanthropy and theme park business as she was for her chart-topping hit songs, has died at 80.

Parton's death on Tuesday was announced by her publicist, who said the singer "died peacefully" in Nashville. No cause of death was initially provided, but a later statement provided by her publicist said Parton died at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones after "bravely facing a brief battle with cancer."
A small private service will be held for immediate family, the publicist said.

"As many of you know, I have been dealing with some health challenges, and my doctors tell me that I must have a few procedures," Parton wrote on Instagram in September 2025, though she never specified the nature of her health issues. Nearly six months later, at the seasonal opening of her Dollywood theme park, she said that she was still dealing with "a few little health issues" from which she was taking time to recover.

Parton also shared that she was still navigating her grief over the March 2025 death of her husband of nearly 60 years, Carl Dean, saying that she had been taking time since to rebuild herself "spiritually, emotionally and physically."

Just 10 days before her passing, Parton canceled a scheduled appearance to celebrate the opening of a new attraction at her Dollywood theme park in Tennessee, saying her doctor had told her not to travel due to health issues.
"Now I’ve told you before, all my fans, that I have had a few little health issues. And sometimes I get a little dizzy, and I get dehydrated," Parton said in a video message played at the park.

"Dolly also opened doors for generations of singers, songwriters, musicians and dreamers from every walk of life and across every continent," her nephew, Bryan Seaver, shared in a video statement he said Parton asked him to prepare. "By her example, we believed that anything was possible. She never saw a door she couldn't open, and the doors she opened made and changed history."

"Dolly was a farmer, just like her daddy. He farmed the soil; she farmed songs and happiness," Seaver said, adding that Parton told him that "she wants to rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because after a life of wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest."
"May god bless Dolly Parton and may god bless you all. She will always love you," the video concluded.

President Donald Trump called Parton "one of the greatest Country singers, and far beyond, EVER" in a social media post reacting to her passing. "There has never been anyone like her, and never will. In her honor, I am lowering the American flag throughout the United States for a one week period beginning tonight at 6:00PM."

In a music career that began when she was still a child, born into poverty in the tiny mountain community of Pittman Center, Tennessee, Parton went on to become one of the world's most successful and admired entertainers, regarded as a country music living legend. Her trademark style – big blonde hair, flamboyant clothes and makeup – was cultivated early in her career, while she was still in her teens.

"I take my negatives and try to make them into positives, and I always feel better being more flamboyant," Parton wrote in her 2023 book "Behind the Seams: My Life in Rhinestones." "Maybe I looked cheap, but I knew I wasn’t cheap."

Parton's style helped her get noticed but her musical gifts made her unforgettable. She wrote and recorded many of country and pop's most enduring songs, including the hits "Jolene," "Coat of Many Colors" – added to the Library of Congress National Recording Registry in 2011 – "Here You Come Again," "Love Is Like a Butterfly," "9 to 5" and more.

Parton's biggest hit, however, was inarguably "I Will Always Love You," which topped the charts three times, most notably when Whitney Houston's 1992 cover became a global smash. Houston's performance remains the best-selling song by a solo female artist of all time.
Dolly Parton's life in pictures

In 2014, the Record Industry Association of America recognized Parton for sales of over 100 million units worldwide, including 19 RIAA-certified gold, platinum and multi-platinum albums out of the more than 100 studio, live and compilation albums she released during her six-decade-plus recording career.

Parton was also an actress, making her big-screen debut in the 1980 hit comedy "9 to 5," opposite Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin, and wrote and performed the film's chart-topping, Grammy-winning theme song. Not including cameos as herself, she appeared in some nine films in all, among them the enduring 1989 comedy-drama "Steel Magnolias."

A savvy businesswoman, Forbes magazine in June 2025 estimated Parton's net financial worth at $450 million, placing her No. 78 on their list of America's wealthiest self-made women. In addition to her extensive publishing catalog – Parton was careful to retain ownership of the songs she wrote, the recordings of which number over 1,000 – the bulk of her wealth came from her Dollywood theme park and other entertainment and hospitality holdings under her Dollywood Company.

Dolly Parton was also generous with her money. Through her nonprofit Dollywood Foundation, "Saint Dolly," as her fans dubbed her, supported education by providing scholarships and financial assistance to people in need. Her Imagination Library, begun in 1995, has provided nearly 308 million books for free to children in the U.S., the U.K., Ireland, Canada and Australia, according to its official website.

When wildfires in 2016 ravaged the Great Smoky Mountains in Eastern Tennessee, where she grew up, Parton created a fund that gave $1,000 a month for six months to some 900 families affected by the fires to help them get back on their feet, and also organized a telethon to raise money for the fires' victims. Four years later, Parton donated $1 million to Tennessee's Vanderbilt University Medical Center to help fund the search for a COVID-19 vaccine, and later urged Americans to get vaccinated against the virus in a video that showed her receiving the shot as she sang her hit "Jolene," with the refrain updated to "vaccine."

Parton was one of only 17 people to be inducted into both the Country Music Hall of Fame and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, a rarified list that also includes fellow greats Elvis Presley, Johnny Cash, Willie Nelson and Ray Charles; with Brenda Lee, Parton was one of only two female artists so honored. She was one of fewer still artists inducted into the Country, Rock and Roll and Songwriters Halls of Fame.

In 2004, the Library of Congress honored Parton with its Living Legend Award in recognition to her contributions to American culture. The following year, she received the National Medal of Arts, the U.S. government's highest honor for an artist, as well as the Kennedy Center Honors in 2006. In 2025, she was presented with the Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences in recognition of her philanthropic and humanitarian endeavors.

Parton received a Lifetime Achievement Grammy in 2011, in addition to her 10 Grammy wins out of more than 50 nominations. Additionally, her songs "Jolene" and "I Will Always Love You" were inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame. In 2024, Billboard magazine placed Parton in the No. 1 spot on their list of the "100 Greatest Country Artists of All Time."

Born in January 1946, the fourth of 12 children born to Avie Lee Owens Parton and Robert Lee Parton, a sharecropper, Dolly Parton attributed her musical talents to her mother's influence and her business acumen to her father who, despite being illiterate, Parton often said had the best business sense of anyone she'd ever known.

Her early life and hardscrabble but loving upbringing inspired her songwriting throughout her career, but Parton's early hits particularly reflected those years, including 1972's "My Tennessee Mountain Home" and "Coat of Many Colors," released the year before. The latter song, written when she was 23 and which tells the true story of her mother sewing Parton a winter coat made of scraps of cloth out of necessity, became one of her most endearing and enduring hits. It was added to the Library of Congress National Recording Registry in 2011 and is considered one of her signature compositions.

By age 10, Parton was already a local star, performing on radio stations in Knoxville, Tenn. She made her debut at the storied Grand Ole Opry just three years later, introduced by Johnny Cash, and moved to Nashville when she was 18, the day after she graduated from high school. She found initial success as a songwriter, landing a publishing deal and penning hits for country stars of the day including Kitty Wells and Skeeter Davis. Her first album release – 1967's "Hello, I'm Dolly" – featured two country top-40 hits, including her first charting single, the tongue-in-cheek "Dumb Blonde."

The success of "Hello, I'm Dolly" was boosted by her joining the cast of TV's "The Porter Wagoner Show" just two weeks before the album's release. Parton, then 21, and Wagoner, 20 years her senior, remained TV co-stars and recording partners for the next seven years. They released 12 duet albums, all but two of which were country top-10 hits and four of which were Grammy nominated, and scored 12 top-10 singles, including the 1974 No. 1 hit "Please Don't Stop Loving Me."

Wagoner's mentorship was instrumental in getting Parton signed to country giant label RCA. She released 13 solo albums during their partnership, including her 1967 debut disc, all to increasing chart success. Her first solo country No. 1 single came with the Grammy-nominated title track from 1971's "Joshua," which was followed up that same year with the top-five hit "Coat of Many Colors," from the album of the same name.

But Parton's star skyrocketed with the release of 1974's "Jolene." The album was a top-10 country smash, while the Grammy-nominated title track – inspired, Parton often recounted, by witnessing a red-headed bank teller flirting with her husband – topped the country singles chart and went on to be RIAA-certified triple-platinum for sales of more than three million units. In the decades since, "Jolene" has been recorded by dozens of artists in multiple genres, including a top-10 2024 cover by R&B superstar Beyoncé, and is broadly considered one of the greatest country songs ever written.

The album "Jolene" also included the first recording of "I Will Always Love You." Written as a loving farewell to Wagoner after telling him she was ending their partnership in favor of her solo career, Parton recorded the song several times, twice topping the country singles chart with it. But it was Whitney Houston's 1992 recording for the soundtrack to the hit film drama "The Bodyguard" that enjoyed the greatest commercial success. A worldwide smash, it notched a then-record 14 weeks atop the Billboard Hot 100 singles chart and earned Houston two Grammy Awards.

"I Will Always Love You" also spotlighted Parton's business savvy. Elvis Presley was set to record the song after its initial release but Parton nixed the deal at the last minute after being informed by Presley's manager, Tom Parker, that she would have to sign over 50% of the publishing rights to Elvis.

"I was so disappointed because I was going to have to tell my friends Elvis didn't record it," Parton later recalled of her decision. "But I just knew that was not right. … I couldn't give somebody half of a song that had already been number one."

Nearly 20 years later, that decision paid off. It's estimated that Houston's recording of "I Will Always Love You" earned Parton over $10 million in royalties, with a further $10 million pocketed from other recordings of the song, including her own.
"That's fine – you can give her the credit," Parton joked when addressing how the song ultimately came to be so closely identified with Houston. "I just want the cash!"

Parton's popularity soared from the mid-1970s onward, with her music and bubbly, over-the-top glam personality propelling her into mainstream appeal. She continued to write and record hit albums and songs – nearly 50 career solo albums in genres including pop, bluegrass and even rock, earning her first Grammy win with the 1979 No. 1 single "Here You Come Again" and an additional nine Grammys either solo or in collaboration with other artists, including 1987's Grammy-winning "Trio" collaboration with Emmylou Harris and Linda Ronstadt. Her biggest commercial music success came in the 1970s and 80s, with standout singles also including the chart-topping Kenny Rogers duet "Islands in the Stream."

Parton also enjoyed success in film, beginning with the 1980 workplace comedy smash "9 to 5," opposite Jane Fonda, Lily Tomlin and Dabney Coleman, playing one of three women who turn the tables on their overbearing boss. The film was the most commercially successful in which she appeared, grossing over $103 million globally. It also spawned the Oscar-nominated, platinum-selling song "9 to 5," which became one of Parton's biggest-ever hits, topping numerous charts and winning two Grammys.

Not including cameos as herself, Parton appeared in eight films in all, the most notable of which after "9 to 5" was the 1989 comedy-drama "Steel Magnolias," in which she was part of an all-star cast that included Julia Roberts, Sally Field, Shirley MacLaine, Olympia Dukakis and Daryl Hannah.

As Parton built her music and entertainment brand, she was simultaneously building a business empire separate from her publishing and performing. In 1986, she purchased a co-ownership in a small theme park in Pigeon Forge, Tenn., a short drive from her Pittman Center birthplace. The theme park's name was changed to Dollywood, while Parton created The Dollywood Company to oversee the park and subsequent ventures, which ultimately included additional parks, restaurants and other attractions in Tennessee, Missouri, Florida and South Carolina.

Parton was married but once, to Carl Dean, whom she met the day after she moved to Nashville at age 18. She described that meeting while speaking with "Good Morning America" co-anchor Robin Roberts in 2019.

"There was a laundromat down from my little apartment where I was gonna be staying. So, the very day I go down to the laundromat, this good-looking man just drives by and he says something like, 'Well, you're gonna get sunburned out here.' And I said something stupid like, 'Well, what's it to you?' We start talking and, two years later, we married and we're still married, and that was that."

Though Dean shunned the spotlight, electing to keep working at his asphalt-contracting business until his retirement, Parton said he was unfailingly supportive of her and her career throughout their nearly 60 years together. When he died March 3, 2025, at the age of 82, Parton's announcement was brief but heartfelt: "Carl and I spent many wonderful years together. Words can't do justice to the love we shared for over 60 years. Thank you for your prayers and sympathy."
A small, private service for Parton will be held for immediate family, according to her death announcement, with a request to make donations to Parton's Imagination Library in lieu of flowers.
Parton and Dean had no children together. She was godmother to singer Miley Cyrus.

title: Dolly Parton talks career, fame and more in her own words
summary: The country music legend's death at age 80 was announced on Aug. 25.
story: Country music legend Dolly Parton spent more than six decades in the public eye before her death at age 80 following a "brief battle" with cancer.
Parton's death, announced Tuesday by her family and publicist, put a spotlight on her long career, which included 50 albums, 11 Grammys, three Emmys and two Oscar nominations.
The "Jolene" singer propelled herself from a poverty-stricken childhood in Tennessee to being one of the world's most successful entertainers.
Along the way, Parton became just as well known for her quick one-liners and the wise life lessons she often shared in interviews.
Take a look back at Parton reflecting on her life, career and legacy in her own words in interviews over the years.
On how she wanted to be remembered
"I think probably what I'd like people to say 100 years from now is, 'Boy, she looks great for her age,'" Parton told ABC News' Barbara Walters in a 1982 interview.
Decades later, in a 2023 interview with ABC News' Linsey Davis, Walters said she wanted to be "remembered well," noting that she did all she could to give back to the world.
"I just want to see how much I can do in a lifetime," she said. "And I've been blessed, and I've been lucky, and I don't take any of that for granted, but I just wanted to be remembered well."
On finding inspiration in cemeteries
In a 1984 interview, Parton said she often found peace and quiet -- and inspiration -- in cemeteries.

"I like to go sit under trees and things. I walk around and I read the stories and I get a lot of ideas of lives," she said. "I imagine lives for all the people, you know, behind the stones there, and where they died and how they lived and if somebody was a little kid. And I get a lot of ideas."
She continued, "It's just a peaceful, beautiful place to go ... I don't hang out there at night."
On her dreams of stardom
In a 1977 interview with Walters, Parton predicted the versatile entertainer she would go onto become, saying she dreamt of becoming a "superstar."

"I would like to be a superstar. I guess all people dream of that. So in order to be a superstar you can't be just a superstar in one area. That means to you have to appeal to a majority of people, and that's what I'm trying to do."
On her marriage to Carl Dean
Parton told Walters in a 1982 interview that her nearly 60-year marriage to Carl Dean, who died in 2025, gave her a "very special kind of sacred freedom."

"It's somebody to plan with, somebody to grow old with, somebody to have fun with. We have a lot in common. We're good friends," Parton said of Dean, who largely stayed out of the spotlight of his wife's career.

"I just know there's not another person in this world that could give me all those things that I've grown up with, that I've been with so many years," she said. "There may be some people that might turn my head a time or two, and have, but that don't mean that they could take Carl's place."
On the 'excitement' of touring
Early in her career, in a 1977 interview, Parton told Walters that she loved being on the road and would get "restless" if she was home for more than two weeks at a time.

"It's excitement to me," she said. "I guess being brought up in the mountains, where you have little time to do anything but work, and things are so quiet and things are so calm that you grow restless if you have restless blood, and you grow more restless as the years go on, and you want to get out. And when you do, you enjoy it."
She continued, "I love to go home, but if I'm home more than two weeks straight, I get restless and bored, and I want to get back on the bus and I want to go."
On never giving up her dream to open Dollywood
Parton opened Dollywood, a theme park in her home state of Tennessee, in 1986, fulfilling a dream she said she accomplished against the odds.

"My lawyers, and my accountants and a lot of people that I was working with at the time said I was making a big mistake," Parton told ABC News' Robin Roberts in 2019. "But I just knew it was right and…I got rid of all those people, started over with new people that did believe in my dreams."
"Dolly Parton: An American Original - A Special Edition of 20/20" airs Tuesday, Aug. 25, at 10 p.m. ET on ABC and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

title: Taylor Swift, Beyonce and other celebrities react to death of Dolly Parton
summary: Celebrities and politicians are offering their condolences following the death of country music superstar Dolly Parton.
story: "So glad she's with her Carl Dean," Kacey Musgraves wrote on social media.
Celebrities and politicians are offering their condolences following the death of country music superstar Dolly Parton, who died Tuesday at the age of 80.
President Donald Trump wrote on social media that he would be lowering the American flag for one week in honor of Parton, calling her death "a true loss for millions of people."
"There has never been anyone like her, and never will," Trump wrote.
"Dolly Parton: An American Original - A Special Edition of 20/20" airs Tuesday, Aug. 25, at 10 p.m. ET on ABC and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

"A world without Dolly doesn’t feel possible, real, or right. But because of the eternally generous way she spent her time on this earth and the countless lives she changed for the better, her legacy will be an everlasting one," Taylor Swift said in a lengthy statement.

"She was truly the gift that kept on giving. Dolly gave us someone to look up to while encouraging us to be who we are as individuals," the statement continued. "Somehow she was able to give us her lessons about the world gently and honestly, simultaneously, and oftentimes hilariously. She managed to give the world the ultimate mystery and fantasy in some corners of her life, but to give full transparency in the ways that counted. Somehow she was true grace and true grit, all in one dazzling person. She possessed the softest heart when it came to the struggles of others, and a backbone of steel to defend her own self worth as an artist."

Swift said she was grateful for Parton's music and philanthropy and saluted the music legend "For the tightropes she walked so that young girls like me could grow up dreaming of joining the circus too."
Beyoncé honored the "Queen of Country" in a heartfelt message shared on her official website.

"You were the barometer. The North Star. Bold and brilliant. Talented and tenacious. You taught so many lessons on how to be uniquely oneself," Beyoncé wrote. "I am grateful for your art, your heart, your generosity, your humor, your entrepreneurship. I'm honored that I had the privilege to work with you."
"You are truly one of one. Rest peacefully," she added.
Sabrina Carpenter, who collaborated with Parton on a version of "Please Please Please" from Carpenter's "Short n' Sweet" deluxe album, remembered Parton as "an angel walking the earth."

"I will cherish our laughter and conversations and i will keep your wisdom, your playful outlook on life, and perfect sense of humor in my pocket for the rainy days," Carpenter wrote on Instagram. "there will never be another you and how lucky are we all to have experienced your singular magic as well as your once in a lifetime voice, songs, and heart."
"your light will be something the world will search forever to find again 🦋🦋🦋 i will always love you," she added.
Jane Fonda, Parton's friend and co-star in the 1980 hit comedy "9 to 5," wrote on Instagram, "I am devastated."

"Dolly will always be with us because she was so present, so powerful, so generous and playful that she is woven into all our lives and hearts forever," Fonda wrote. "We have our memories of her, her songs, Dollywood, '9to5,' the millions of books she got into the hands of children, all the iconic images that bring her to us. And they are all blessings. Let's be grateful for all that she has left us to ease our sadness now."
"... To her gay and trans fans, I want you to know that she loved you," Fonda added. " ... And you know she doesn't want y'all to mourn now. Dress up and celebrate her spirit."
Lily Tomlin, Parton's longtime friend and her other "9 to 5" co-star, wrote on Instagram, "No words ... 💔."
The movie was Parton's big-screen debut, and she wrote and performed the film's chart-topping, Grammy-winning theme song.

Tomlin said at the 16th Annual Governors Awards in 2025 that the song "9 to 5" was "so much bigger than any singular theme song on a movie soundtrack," saying it "became an anthem for our culture of the time."

She added at the time that Parton's "humanitarian achievements are as staggering as her formidable singing career" and called her "one of the few people who remains in this world that everyone loves and respects."
Country singer Kacey Musgraves wrote on social media on Tuesday, "This really really hurts."
"The world feels a lot less sparkly all of a sudden," Musgraves said, adding, "So glad she's with her Carl Dean."
Dean, who was Parton's husband of nearly 60 years, died last year at the age of 82.

Parton's fellow country singer and actress Reba McEntire wrote on Instagram, "Dolly, thank you for all the wonderful things you did for us here on earth. Your love, your music and you gave so much with your huge huge heart."

"There will never ever be another you. We will remember and cherish every memory and every note you ever played and sang," she continued. "... I'll never forget the first time I met you and I'll never forget our last conversation. I hold it with love in my heart."
Former President Barack Obama reflected on Parton's life and wide-ranging impact in a statement on X.

"It's hard to imagine many people having a bigger impact than Dolly Parton," Obama wrote. "Born in a one-room cabin, she earned 11 Grammys and an Emmy, built a business empire, helped millions of kids learn to read, and — as if that wasn't enough — helped accelerate the research that led to the Moderna COVID vaccine. What a life."
"Michelle and I are thinking of Dolly's family and her many, many fans," he added.
Former President George W. Bush also remembered Parton as both an entertainer and philanthropist.

"Laura and I, along with thousands of her fans, mourn the passing of Dolly Parton. We loved her music and her style. She was a great entertainer and even greater person," Bush said in a statement shared by the George W. Bush Presidential Center on X.
"We respected her work to promote literacy, advance health, and strengthen communities. Dolly was a talented and hardworking American who will be missed," he added.
Former President Bill Clinton described Parton as "a great songwriter and performer who told the stories of everyday Americans with honesty, humility, and heart."

"She rose high from her East Tennessee roots and never forgot where she came from. And she always believed in giving back, especially in her efforts to promote literacy," he wrote in a statement. "Hillary and I were big fans and first saw her in 1974, and will always be grateful for the music and the memories. Our thoughts and prayers are with her family, her legion of fans, and everyone who loved her."

Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton added, "Dolly Parton did all the good she could, for all the people she could, for as long as ever she could. From her legendary songwriting to the Imagination Library -- which sent 1 million books a month to children across the country -- she was the best of America. Dolly, we'll miss your great heart."
The Jacksons called Parton a "true trailblazer" in a statement on Instagram.

"Through her extraordinary talent, kindness and generosity, she opened doors and inspired generations around the world. We share this special memory from 1977, when we had the honor of meeting Dolly in England on the same day we also met Queen Elizabeth II," the Jacksons wrote alongside a carousel of images. "Thank you, Dolly, for the music, the joy and the light you shared with us all."
"Our prayers are with Dolly's family, friends and everyone whose life she touched. ... Your beautiful spirit and remarkable legacy will live on forever," the Jacksons said.
Comedian and actress Carol Burnett took to social media to reflect on one of her "favorite memories," taping the "Dolly & Carol in Nashville" special in Parton's home state of Tennessee.
"We shot the week of Thanksgiving and Dolly made individual turkey dinners for every one of us, that she cooked herself," Burnett said.
"That's who she was," she said, adding, "I'm so sad right now."
Former Vice President Kamala Harris called Parton a "true American icon" in a statement Tuesday.

"Her career accolades included 11 Grammy awards, an Emmy, an honorary Oscar, and -- my favorite -- more than 300 million books sent to millions of children around the world through her Imagination Library," Harris wrote. "All at once she was kind, modest, and funny. With her music, her philanthropy, and her style, Dolly was one of one."
"Doug and I send our prayers to her family, friends, and all those who have been touched by her magic," she said. "We will always love you, Dolly."
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said Parton was "one of a kind, who loved people, her work, her family, and her Lord."
"Tennessee has forever been changed -- enhanced -- by her, and will never be quite the same without Dolly," the governor said on social media.

Reese Witherspoon wrote on social media, "When I was playing June Carter Cash in 'Walk the Line,' [Parton] took me to dinner and told me stories of how June Carter charmed everyone in country music. Dolly gave me the courage to put my whole spirit into that performance and made me see how lucky I was to be a storyteller."
Witherspoon said throughout her career, Parton sent her "notes of encouragement and support, telling me to be the light in people's lives and listen to my angels."
"Dolly, I miss you already. Your talent, your wisdom and your beautiful spirit lit up our lives," the actress said.
Khloe Kardashian, a Parton superfan, wrote in an Instagram story post, "Some people are so extraordinary, their existence feels almost impossible. Dolly was one of those people."

"A once-in-a-lifetime soul. A woman whose light, heart, talent and humanity changed this world forever," Kardashian wrote. "To have admired her was a gift. To have met her, spent time in her presence, and somehow been lucky enough that Dolly Parton knew my name... I will never have words big enough for what that means to me."
"What an astronomical human being. What a legacy. What a loss," she added. "There will never be another Dolly."
Singer Kelly Clarkson also honored the legendary singer, writing on social media that Parton "had a way of making everyone feel special, and seen, and welcomed, and as if you were old friends."

"I will miss her heart and her voice as I am sure millions will," Clarkson said. "What an incredible gift and talent she was and still is with an amazing catalogue of art she has left behind for all of us."
Jack White of The White Stripes, who covered Parton's hit song "Jolene" in 2000, posted a photo of Parton on Instagram with the caption, "Instant Sainthood."
Actress and singer Kristin Chenoweth wrote on Instagram that she was "heartbroken," calling Parton her "ultimate inspiration."

"I met Dolly on several occasions and she always made me feel like one of her own. She even agreed to sing with me on one of my records," Chenoweth said. "... The world has lost one of the best but I know we will never forget her because she is impossible to forget. I love you Dolly and I will ALWAYS love you."

The Muppets also honored the iconic performer, saying in a statement on Facebook, "There will never be another quite like Dolly Parton. She was the ultimate singer, songwriter, actress, performer, and philanthropist. She filled the world with light and we are so grateful for every second we got to spend with her onstage and off."

Actress Octavia Spencer called Parton "a gift to the world," writing on social media, [Y]our voice, your philanthropic heart, and warmth made us ... feel seen and that the world was a pretty decent place."

Actor Colman Domingo wrote on social media, "Dolly taught us that you can be anything and do anything and to do it with kindness. What a light. We are all grateful that we lived in a time of Dolly Parton. We will always love her."

title: Dolly Parton gave millions to help others: Here's where her money went
summary: The country music icon supported childhood literacy, medical research and more.
story: Dolly Parton, the country music legend who died Tuesday at age 80, leaves behind a legacy that extends far beyond her music.
Throughout her life, Parton gave back through philanthropic efforts that supported childhood literacy, medical research and people in need, particularly in her home state of Tennessee.
Parton's death was announced by her publicist. No cause of death was provided.
One of Parton's philanthropic efforts was Dolly Parton's Imagination Library, the book-gifting program she started in 1995.
Parton launched the program in her home county of Sevier County, Tennessee, inspired by her father, who could not read or write.
The program, which provides free books each month to children from birth to age 5, regardless of their family's income, eventually expanded across the U.S. and internationally.
"If you can read, you can self-educate yourself, and you're just lost if you can't," Parton told "Good Morning America" in 2021.
"I just think it's important for children to learn to read in the early years, to learn to love books and all that," she said at the time.
Following Parton's death, the Library of Congress remembered her in a post on X as a "music legend and titan of children's literacy."

The Library of Congress noted that Parton's Imagination Library received multiple Library Literacy Awards and that in 2018, Parton visited the library to donate the program's 100 millionth book to its collection and host a story time.
Parton's philanthropic efforts were also remembered by current and former world leaders.

President Donald Trump said he directed American flags to be lowered for the next week, writing in a social media post in part: "This is a true loss for millions of people. There has never been anyone like her, and never will."

Former President Bill Clinton remembered Parton in a social media post Tuesday, writing, in part: "She rose high from her East Tennessee roots and never forgot where she came from. And she always believed in giving back, especially in her efforts to promote literacy."
Parton's philanthropy also extended to medical research.
In 2020, Parton donated $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center to support research into COVID-19.

The donation created the Dolly Parton COVID-19 Research Fund and helped support early research connected to Moderna's COVID-19 vaccine. Vanderbilt later confirmed that Parton's money funded what a researcher described as "critical" early stages of the vaccine research.
Two years later, Parton donated another $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center to support pediatric infectious disease research.
The donation supported research into infectious diseases, antibiotic resistance, and the diagnosis and treatment of infections in children with cancer.

"I love children," Parton said in a statement announcing the donation. "No child should ever have to suffer, and I'm willing to do my part to try and keep as many of them as I can as healthy and safe as possible."
Parton also stepped in to help communities affected by natural disasters.
After devastating wildfires swept through East Tennessee in 2016, Parton established the My People Fund, which provided $1,000 per month for six months to families who lost their homes.

Years later, Parton again gave back following Hurricane Helene. In 2024, she announced she was donating $1 million of her own money to relief efforts, with another $1 million donated by her businesses.
Her decades of charitable work earned Parton the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy in 2022.
For Parton, giving back was closely tied to where she came from and the people she hoped to help.
"I'm just so proud to have been a part of anything that's good and that's making life a little better for people," she told "GMA" in 2021.

title: A look back at Dolly Parton's legendary career
summary: Dolly Parton's career spanned music, movies, entertainment, business ventures and more
story: As the world mourns Dolly Parton, the legendary country music megastar whose stardom transcended genre and industry, fans and followers are taking a look back at her unparalleled career.

Parton, whose death at 80 was announced on Tuesday by her publicist, leaves behind a career that spans music, books, movies, television, amusement parks, business ventures, and more, all of which serve to further memorialize the iconic singer and songwriter.
Read on for everything to know about Parton's unforgettable career.
The 'Queen of Country'
Parton's success in the music world is implicitly tied to Music City -- Nashville, Tennessee -- where Parton moved in her early adult years to pursue her dream of country music stardom.
After moving to Nashville, Parton notched her very first Top 40 hit with her song "Dumb Blonde" in 1967, according to the Country Music Hall of Fame.
Parton's success would not be short-lived: Her star continued to rise after she earned a spot as a singer on "The Porter Wagoner Show," a music variety show, also in 1967.

The 1970s and the decade that followed would see Parton solidify her musical career into the stuff of legends. Parton's fame soared to meteoric heights with the release of hit singles including "Jolene," "Love Is Like a Butterfly," and "I Will Always Love You," as well as popular albums like 1971's "Coat of Many Colors," 1973's "My Tennessee Mountain Home."
In 1980, she released the album "9 to 5 and Odd Jobs." The album included the title track "9 to 5," which served as the theme song for the film of the same that debuted that same year.

More recently, Parton released an album of rock 'n' roll songs and covers, simply titled "Rockstar." The album featured collaborations with names such as Ann Wilson, Rob Halford, Nikki Sixx, John 5, Paul McCartney, Ringo Starr, Linda Perry, Pink, Brandi Carlile, Chris Stapleton, Miley Cyrus and more.
Parton is the recipient of 10 Grammy Awards out of 55 total nominations, according to the Recording Academy website.

In 2014, the Record Industry Association of America recognized Parton for sales of over 100 million units worldwide, including 19 RIAA-certified gold, platinum and multi-platinum albums out of the more than 100 studio, live and compilation albums she released during her six-decade-plus recording career.
Parton on TV, movies and stage
Parton's career is notable for more than just her music.

She jumpstarted her TV and film career with her singing role on "The Porter Wagoner Show" and saw continued success with the 1980 film "9 to 5," in which she starred alongside Jane Fonda, Lily Tomlin, Dabney Coleman, Elizabeth Wilson and Sterling Hayden.

Further big screen success followed, with Parton's starring role in 1982's "The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas." The film, based on the 1978 stage musical of the same name, also starred Burt Reynolds, Jim Nabors, Charles Durning and Dom DeLuise.

In 1984, Parton starred in "Rhinestone" alongside Sylvester Stallone, and in 1989, she snagged a leading role in the film "Steel Magnolias" alongside co-stars Sally Field, Shirley MacLaine, Daryl Hannah, Olympia Dukakis and Julia Roberts.
Parton made additional TV appearances later in her career, with spots on "Designing Women," "Hannah Montana," "Reba," and more recently, "Grace & Frankie."
She has also appeared in a wide variety of television specials and television films throughout her career.

In June 2024, Parton announced plans for an autobiographical stage musical based on her life. "Dolly: A True Original Musical," with music and lyrics by Parton and a book by Parton and Maria S. Schlatter, is set to open at the St. James Theatre in New York City on Tuesday, Jan. 19, 2027 -- what would have been Parton's 81st birthday.
Dolly Parton, businesswoman
Parton's career interests did not end with the world of entertainment.

In June 2025, Forbes estimated Parton's net financial worth at $450 million, placing her at No. 78 on its list of America's wealthiest self-made women. Patron notably retained ownership of the songs she wrote, recordings of which number over 1,000.
However, much of Parton's wealth came from her theme park, Dollywood, located in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, which she bought an interest in back in 1986, adding her name to the park itself.

The park, which first opened under different ownership in 1961, "remains rooted in the authenticity and warmth Dolly Parton envisioned when she partnered with the Herschend family in 1986," the Pigeon Forge chamber of commerce wrote in an article on its website last year.

Following her death on Tuesday, the Dollywood team shared a statement on the park's website, writing, "Dolly's heartfelt wish was that Dollywood always remain a place of joy, hope and togetherness -- a space where families and friends could honor her memory, not with silence, but with laughter, music and shared dreams."

"Dolly's enduring legacy extends beyond her music and generosity to her remarkable work ethic -- an inspiration to people everywhere," the statement read in part, noting that the park would remain open on Wednesday, "as Dolly wanted."

Parton also authored several books in her lifetime, including memoirs, a number of children's books, and even a cookbook, "Good Lookin' Cookin," which she wrote with her sister Rachel Parton George. She also authored a novel, "Run, Rose, Run," with James Patterson in 2022.
One of Parton's final business ventures was a gas station and restaurant, Dolly's Tennessean Travel Stop, located off exit 22 on I-65 in Cornersville, Tennessee.

"I'm sure some of you are wondering why I wanted a truck stop. Well, I couldn't leave it to beavers," Parton said in remarks at a grand opening ceremony for the travel stop, referencing the popular gas station chain Buc-ee's, whose mascot is a beaver named Buc-ee.
Parton's philanthropic ventures
Parton prided herself on her philanthropic endeavors throughout her life.

In 1995, she launched the nonprofit Dolly Parton's Imagination Library, which gifts books to children from birth until age 5. The organization, which has since gone global, has gifted more than 304 million books since its inception, according to the its website.

In 2020, Parton donated $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center to support research into COVID-19. Vanderbilt later called the donation "critical" to the early stages of its COVID-19 vaccine research.
Parton donated another $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center in June 2022 to support pediatric infectious disease research.

Vanderbilt University Medical Center president and CEO Jeff Balser, M.D, Ph.D., the dean of the Vanderbilt University School of Medicine, said in a statement at the time that Parton's donations over the years had saved "countless lives."
Parton also left her mark in the aftermath of natural disasters across the country, donating wherever she could to help communities get back on their feet.

"These are special people here -- they're my people," she said in October 2024, after donating $1 million to help Hurricane Helene flood victims in Tennessee. "...I can't stand to see anyone hurting, so I wanted to do what I could to help after these terrible floods."
She added at the time, "I hope we can all be a little bit of light in the world for our friends, our neighbors, even strangers during this dark time they are experiencing."
