title: SEEING DOUBLE: Second Dan Sullivan advances, setting up bizarre Alaska Senate ballot
summary: Dan Sullivan Jr. advances to Alaska's general election, complicating the race for Sen. Dan Sullivan as ranked-choice voting amplifies name confusion.
story: Florida Young Republicans Chair Brandon Ludwig joins 'Fox & Friends First' to analyze far-left campaigns pushing to abolish ICE. Democratic socialist candidates challenge established Democrats as the Florida primary elections take center stage. Meanwhile, Alaska's primary features incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan facing a challenger with the exact same name.

Dan J. Sullivan Jr., a Senate candidate in Alaska who has made headlines for sharing a name with incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, R-Alaska, has officially advanced to the general election, The Associated Press announced on Wednesday.
He joins Sen. Sullivan and former Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska, as the third of the final four candidates.
Alaska has yet to announce the fourth.

Sullivan Jr.’s advance, which seemed likely after the polls closed last Tuesday, complicates the picture for Republicans as they work against the clock to explain why two candidates have the same name — as well as which one to vote for. Unlike the primary, the general election picture is further clouded by ranked-choice voting (RCV), which raises more questions about how voters will react to the name overlap.
MORNING GLORY: ALASKA’S 'REAL' SENATOR DAN SULLIVAN STOOD UP OVER CHALLENGER
Dan J. Sullivan, who has filed to run for U.S. Senate in Alaska, poses for a photo in Petersburg, Alaska, on June 26, 2026. (Katie Holmlund/Associated Press)

Under this system, voters rank their preferred candidates. If their top choice is eliminated, their support passes on to their next-ranked option. While supporters of the process argue it expands voters' power and greatly increases the influence of candidates that may not otherwise be a top choice, critics — like Sen. Sullivan — believe it also introduces confusion.

"Like many others who did not support ranked choice voting in 2020, I still believe that this new election system has created unnecessary confusion among voters," Sullivan told local Alaskan media in 2024.
Fears of that confusion were amplified by the emergence of the second Sullivan.

Sullivan Jr., a logger, appeared among the 16 candidates on the ballot as an independent in last week's primary, snapping up 2.5% of the vote. Sullivan Jr.’s campaign announcement did not list a party affiliation. His website does not state his position on any political issues.
Instead, it leaned into the name overlap. "Dan Sullivan challenges Dan Sullivan for U.S. Senate Seat, urges Alaskans to defeat incumbent, elect a Sullivan who stands up for Alaska," it read.
ALASKA REPUBLICANS SCRAMBLE TO EDUCATE VOTERS ON SUSPECTED DEM PLANT AS 'BALLOT FATIGUE' THREATENS RACE
US Senator Dan Sullivan (R-AK) goes to vote on the Laken Riley Act at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on January 9, 2025. (ALLISON ROBBERT/AFP via Getty Images)

According to his biography, Sullivan Jr. spent his early career working blue-collar jobs like logging, construction, bartending and forestry but decided to enter his bid for Senate after growing frustrated with government mismanagement.

A Fox News Digital review of the campaign earlier this year uncovered that Amber Lee, a progressive consultant, had helped author some of Sullivan Jr.’s campaign materials. Lee previously supported Peltola, the former congresswoman.

The campaign has drawn criticism from Republicans who believe it’s an effort to put two "Dan Sullivans" on the ballot in November and, through ranked choice voting, intentionally draw away votes from the senator.
Alaska state Sen. James Kaufman, a Republican, said he personally remains worried about conflation between the two.
He believes there are still some voters in Alaska, especially Republicans, who refuse to use the RCV system, citing disagreements with its implementation.
"Some people have a pretty strong traditionalist perspective: one person, one man, one vote," Kaufman said.
JUDGE RULES REPUBLICAN WITH SAME NAME AS SEN DAN SULLIVAN CAN STAY ON ALASKA PRIMARY BALLOT
Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican from Alaska, stands in the Senate Subway of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on June 17, 2026. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg)

"And so, the ballot fatigue where people just don’t rank because maybe they disagree with it; there’s a pretty strong segment of the population here that just patently disagrees with the ranked-choice voting system we ended up with. And they don’t necessarily believe in utilizing it."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Having cleared the primary, Sen. Sullivan, Sullivan Jr. and Peltola will face off in the general election on Nov. 3.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Tap-to-pay charity scam can cost you thousands
summary: A tap-to-pay charity scam is turning small $15 or $20 donations into charges of nearly $5,000, with victims losing thousands before they notice.
story: ScamSkeptic founder Matt Sanner discusses the growing urgency of protecting vulnerable seniors from AI-powered scams. He shares tips for recognizing high-pressure phone tactics and helping parents avoid fraud on ‘America’s Newsroom.’

Tap to pay has become one of my favorite modern conveniences. I use it all the time. In fact, I rarely need to pull out a physical wallet anymore because contactless payments are accepted in so many places.
There's a security advantage, too. Mobile wallets can use tokenization or virtual card numbers, so your actual card number does not need to pass directly to a merchant during a transaction.

That makes what's happening with a tap-to-pay charity scam especially frustrating. Criminals are taking a technology designed to make paying easier and using a moment of distraction to turn a small donation into a potentially massive charge.

You may think you're giving $5 or $20 to a good cause. Then you check your account and discover hundreds or even thousands of dollars are gone. Here's how the scam works and what you can do to protect your money.
APPLE PAY TEXT SCAM THREATENS $8,250 LOSS IN 35 MINUTES
Scammers are using tap-to-pay charity requests to trick people into authorizing charges far larger than the donations they intended to make. (ZeynepKaya/Getty Images)

How the tap-to-pay charity scam works

The setup can feel completely ordinary. You're leaving a store, walking through a busy shopping area or heading through a public event. Someone approaches you and claims to be raising money for a youth group, school fundraiser or another cause. They ask for a small donation. Maybe you agree to $5. Maybe you offer $20. Then they tell you they can accept tap to pay. That's when you need to pay very close attention.

One version of the scam involves the solicitor entering a much larger amount into a smartphone or payment reader before you tap your phone or card. You think you're approving $20. The payment screen may actually say $2,000. If you tap without carefully checking that amount, you could authorize the larger transaction. Brentwood police warned in January 2026 about a version involving people approaching shoppers outside stores for small donations. Police said victims could be charged significantly more than expected after using tap to pay, Square or Cash App.

The numbers can get ugly fast. The Washington state attorney general issued a warning after receiving reports involving solicitors near the Seattle waterfront. In one case, a person agreed to donate $15 and later discovered a $4,800 charge. Another person agreed to give $20 and later found a charge of nearly $5,000. Those examples show why you should never treat the final tap as a formality.

There's another risk worth keeping in mind. If someone claims the transaction failed and asks to take your phone to help, end the transaction. A scammer does not need to take your phone for the inflated-payment scheme to work. However, handing over an unlocked phone creates a much bigger security problem. Depending on your settings, that person may be able to reach email, messages, payment apps or financial information. I would never hand an unlocked phone to a stranger during any financial transaction.
Why tap-to-pay security may not stop this scam

Tap to pay itself remains a secure way to make legitimate purchases. The weakness here involves what you approve. If a scammer puts $2,000 on the payment screen and you authenticate that transaction, the payment system sees an approved purchase.

The criminal is counting on you to skip one very important step: reading the amount before tapping. We use contactless payments so frequently that the gesture can become automatic. Pull out the phone. Authenticate. Tap. Walk away. That routine gives a scammer an opening.
CyberGuy has previously covered how quickly mobile payment scams can turn into serious financial losses through services such as Venmo, Zelle and Cash App.
How to protect yourself from a tap-to-pay charity scam
You do not need to stop using tap-to-pay. I certainly don't plan to. Instead, change how you handle unexpected payment requests.

Never give a stranger your unlocked phone to complete or troubleshoot a payment. If something supposedly went wrong with a transaction, cancel it and move on. When your financial information is involved, you should stay in control of your device from beginning to end.

This may be the single most important habit. Stop for a second and look at the amount displayed on the merchant's phone or payment terminal. Do this before your phone or card goes anywhere near the reader. If you agreed to donate $10, make sure the screen says $10. The FTC also recommends reviewing your financial statements after making donations to confirm you were charged only the amount you intended.
NEW BANK SCAM LAWS COULD STOP SUSPICIOUS PAYMENTS
Tap-to-pay technology remains secure, but scammers can exploit distracted donors who approve a transaction without checking the amount first. (iStock)

A legitimate cause will still exist five minutes from now. If someone tells you that you need to donate immediately, I would walk away. Scammers often rely on pressure because they do not want you thinking too carefully about the request. The FTC specifically advises people against letting fundraisers rush them into making a donation.

Ask for the organization's name, then look it up independently. Do not rely on a website, QR code or social media account the solicitor hands you. Search for the charity yourself and check whether it is registered. Look for independent reviews and see how the organization says donations should be made. The FTC recommends researching unfamiliar charities before sending money.

If the cause sounds worthwhile, you can still donate. Go directly to the organization's official website after you have verified it. That gives you time to confirm who will receive your money without someone standing over you waiting for a tap.

I'm a big fan of account alerts because they can tell you the moment something happens with your money. Turn on notifications for card purchases and withdrawals. Also, consider alerts for transfers or other significant account activity. If you intended to donate $20 and immediately get an alert showing $2,000, you can contact your financial institution right away.

Check the security settings inside apps such as Venmo, Cash App, PayPal and your bank's mobile app. Enable Face ID, fingerprint authentication or a separate PIN when the app offers those protections. That creates another barrier if someone ever gets access to your unlocked phone.
What to do if you already fell for the scam
If you spot an inflated charge or realize you approved far more than you intended, move quickly. The sooner you respond, the sooner your bank can tell you what options are available.

Call the bank or card issuer connected to the transaction. Explain exactly what happened. Tell them how much you agreed to pay and how much was actually charged. Ask whether the transaction can be stopped, disputed or reversed. If your banking app allows it, consider locking the affected card while you investigate. Brentwood police specifically advise suspected victims of this scam to contact their bank or card issuer immediately.

Take screenshots of the transaction and save any payment confirmations. Write down where the encounter happened and approximately what time it occurred. Also record the merchant name shown with the charge. Those details can help your bank or law enforcement investigate.

If the scammer ever handled your unlocked phone, review the financial apps installed on it. Look for unfamiliar transfers or purchases. Then check whether anyone changed your email address, phone number or other account information. Continue watching those accounts over the following days because suspicious activity may appear later.

If a stranger had access to your unlocked device, change passwords for sensitive accounts that may have been exposed. I would start with your primary email account because criminals can use email to reset passwords elsewhere. Then secure banking and payment accounts. Use a password manager to create and store strong, unique passwords for each account, and turn on multifactor authentication wherever it is available.
HOW FLORIDA RETIREE LOST $200K IN FAKE PAYPAL REFUND SCAM
A tap-to-pay donation scam can turn a $10 or $20 gift into a charge worth thousands if you fail to check the amount before tapping. (Clara Margais/picture alliance via Getty Images)

Make sure your phone requires Face ID, fingerprint authentication or a strong passcode. Also protect sensitive apps when your device offers that option. The goal is to keep someone from turning a few seconds with your unlocked phone into access to your financial life.

Antivirus software will not reverse an inflated tap-to-pay transaction. However, it becomes much more relevant if the scammer convinced you to click a link, visit a website or download something. Strong antivirus protection can help detect malicious software and warn you about dangerous links used in follow-up scams. I recommend running trusted security protection across your devices and keeping it updated. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Fraudsters often come back for a second attempt. If they learn your name, phone number or other personal details, they can combine that information with data already available online to make the next scam more convincing. Data brokers and people-search sites can expose personal information about you. You can remove much of this information yourself. However, the process can take time and information may reappear. A data removal service can automate many of those removal requests and continue checking for your information. It cannot erase information a criminal already obtained. Still, reducing your online footprint gives scammers less material to work with. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

If someone gained access to sensitive information on your phone, you may want an additional set of eyes watching for signs of fraud. Identity theft protection services can monitor for suspicious activity and alert you when certain personal information appears in places it should not. Some services also provide recovery assistance if your identity gets misused. That can be especially useful if you believe the incident exposed more than a payment card. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

A fraudulent tap-to-pay charge by itself does not automatically mean someone can open credit in your name. However, the situation changes if a scammer also obtained sensitive personal information that could be used for identity theft. In that case, consider placing a credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze can make it harder for a criminal to open a new credit account in your name.

If you lost money, report what happened. Contact local law enforcement when appropriate, especially if the amount is significant or the same solicitors appear to be targeting other people. You can also report fraud to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If the person claimed to represent a charity, consider contacting your state attorney general or charity regulator as well.
The safest way to donate with your phone
I still like mobile wallets and I still plan to use tap to pay. The technology gives us convenience along with useful payment protections.
What changes for me is how I handle a stranger asking for a quick donation. I want to know exactly who is getting my money before I approve anything.

If I decide the cause deserves support, I can look up the organization later and donate directly through its verified website. That approach removes the pressure and gives me time to make sure my money reaches the people I intended to help.
Kurt's key takeaways

Tap to pay remains one of my favorite ways to check out. I like the speed and I like the added security mobile wallets can provide. Still, technology cannot protect you from every number you personally approve. That's what makes this scam effective. Most of us have become so comfortable tapping that we barely think about the final transaction screen. I want that habit to change. Before you tap, look at the amount. If a stranger is asking for a donation, give yourself time to verify the organization first. And if anyone asks to take your unlocked phone during the process, my answer would be an immediate no. Your generosity should reach the cause you chose, rather than a scammer counting on a few distracted seconds.
Would you still tap your phone to donate to someone who approached you in public after seeing how easily a small gift can become a four-figure charge? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Hurricane Katrina taught me how to prepare for any storm
summary: Kurt Knutsson shares seven emergency preparedness lessons from surviving Hurricane Katrina inside a New Orleans hotel as conditions turned desperate.
story: Twenty-one years after Hurricane Katrina, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares his experience surviving the storm.

Aug. 29 marks 21 years since Hurricane Katrina struck the Gulf Coast in 2005. I had gone to New Orleans expecting a fun weekend with my parents. Instead, I ended up trapped inside a hotel during one of the most devastating hurricanes in U.S. history.

At the time, I had no idea the experience would change the way I prepare for emergencies for the rest of my life. Katrina remains the costliest hurricane in U.S. history and one of the deadliest hurricanes in U.S. history.

For me, though, the story began before the flooding. As Katrina grew stronger in the Gulf, I realized we needed to get out of New Orleans. I got my parents onto what I remember as the last flight out. My dad even offered me his ticket because I still had no way out. I told him to get on the plane. Then I headed to a rental car company. That plan fell apart fast.

There were about a hundred people there trying to do exactly what I was trying to do. So I eventually returned to the Ritz-Carlton in New Orleans after being told it was extremely well-prepared for a hurricane. I was told it had upgraded windows, generator power and plenty of food. I should not have gone back.
NORTH CAROLINA MOUNTAIN COMMUNITY BRACES FOR HURRICANE SEASON TWO YEARS AFTER HELENE'S BRUTAL IMPACT
Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson reports from Louisiana in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina, where flooding, power failures and widespread damage left the city in crisis. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Want to hear what it was really like? Listen to The CyberGuy Report podcast at Cyberguy.com/ as I revisit Hurricane Katrina with Carlos Amezcua, who was anchoring at KTLA in Los Angeles while I was trapped in New Orleans.

No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.

When the hotel's hurricane plan began to unravel

The hotel looked prepared on paper. It had upgraded windows, a generator and food supplies meant to keep people sheltered through the storm. Then the situation changed fast. As Hurricane Katrina approached, hotel employees were allowed to bring their families inside so they could stay together while staff continued working. That decision brought hundreds more people into the property than the original emergency plan had anticipated. Suddenly, the food, beds and other supplies had to stretch much further. Then the flooding came.

Water surrounded the hotel and made leaving impossible. Food was rationed. At one point, the hotel was so desperate to keep refrigeration running that staff asked guests with diesel vehicles in the elevated garage if they could siphon fuel for the generator. Outside, I heard gunfire and watched looting unfold on Canal Street. Hotel officials repeatedly warned us not to leave because the streets were unsafe. Communication was breaking down too. Cell service was unreliable, and text messages could take hours to reach the other end. Somehow, I managed to MacGyver the hotel's phone system enough to get a dial tone and report back to KTLA in Los Angeles, where I was working at the time.

What kept running through my mind was this: If conditions were becoming this desperate inside one of New Orleans' luxury hotels, what were families trapped in their homes going through? That question became personal as I got to know Jesse and Emma Ruiz, a couple from the Los Angeles area who had saved for an anniversary trip to New Orleans. Their celebration had suddenly turned into a disaster. I became close to them while we were trapped and even tried to make sure they knew where I had stashed some food and water. Years later, seeing them safe again brought all of those emotions right back.
Hurricane Katrina taught me to control the information I could

One of my biggest lessons from Katrina had nothing to do with buying expensive survival equipment. It was about information. Rumors spread constantly. People were scared, and nobody seemed to know what would happen next. As a journalist, I kept trying to verify what I was hearing. I described the situation on the podcast as "information chaos."
That mindset helped me focus. Instead of getting overwhelmed by everything happening around me, I tried to figure out what I could confirm and what problem needed solving next.

I also formed an alliance with Richard Rhodes, a man from Washington who became what I later called my survival partner. We started thinking ahead together about what we would need and how we might get ourselves out. At one point, Richard and I decided we would pack what we could and try to walk out along the levee system toward Baton Rouge. We headed down the hotel stairwell, but a security guard told us we were not going anywhere. I kept going until I could see floodwater around the second-floor level. There was simply no way out on foot.

Then I ran into an information problem I never expected. A helicopter might be able to get me out, but the pilot needed my exact latitude and longitude. I did not know it. Without electricity and the smartphone tools we take for granted today, it took nearly two days to determine my GPS coordinates. Once the helicopter crew had those coordinates, the pilot finally knew exactly where to find us. As I said on the podcast, "Now I don't go anywhere without knowing how to get my GPS coordinates." Today, your smartphone makes that much easier.
Hurricane Katrina changed what I keep ready

Katrina also changed the physical gear I keep nearby. You do not have to turn your garage into an emergency warehouse. Instead, I focus on equipment that helps me communicate, see what is happening and keep essential devices working.

During Katrina, I found an uninterruptible power supply that normally backed up a computer in the hotel. We used it to charge phones when regular power was unavailable. That experience made backup power a permanent part of my emergency planning. I also learned something much simpler. A zip-top plastic bag can become one of the most useful things you own when water is getting everywhere.
ARMY BLACK HAWKS AIRLIFT 200-PLUS STRANDED CAMPERS AS MISSOURI FLOODS TRIGGER MORE 350 RESCUES
Hurricane Katrina left New Orleans flooded and communications crippled, forcing Kurt Knutsson to rethink how he prepares for disasters. (U.S. National Archives / Michael B. Watkins, U.S. Navy)
7 storm season tips I learned the hard way
You cannot control what a major storm does. However, you can make it easier to communicate and function when normal services disappear.

Do not wait until you need rescuing to figure out where to find your latitude and longitude. Open Google Maps and zoom in on the location you want to save. Then press and hold an unlabeled spot to drop a pin. Google says this will display the location's coordinates on both Android and iPhone. Take a screenshot or save the coordinates somewhere easy to access.

I would do this for your home and any other place where you expect to ride out a major storm. You can also save the coordinates in a note along with your address and other emergency information. If familiar landmarks disappear or rescuers cannot easily identify where you are, those coordinates can give them your exact location. As I said during the podcast, "Timing with information is everything."

This is one feature I desperately wish I had during Katrina. Apple's Emergency SOS via satellite is available on iPhone 14 and later models. It can help you text emergency services when you are somewhere without cellular or Wi-Fi coverage. However, do not assume you will instinctively know what to do in an emergency. Apple provides a demo so you can practice ahead of time.
On a current iPhone, you can:
Open SettingsTap Emergency SOSScroll to the Emergency SOS via satellite sectionTap the option to try the demoFollow the onscreen instructions
Open Settings
Tap Emergency SOS
Scroll to the Emergency SOS via satellite section
Tap the option to try the demo
Follow the onscreen instructions

You can also open the Control Center, tap the Cellular control, tap Satellite and choose Try Demo. Most importantly, Apple says you need to be outside with a clear view of the sky and horizon. Dense foliage, tall structures and some terrain can interfere with the connection. During a real emergency, Apple says you should first try calling your local emergency number. If the call cannot connect and you are off the grid, your iPhone can offer the satellite option. For more details, see my guide to getting your phone ready for an emergency.

Some newer Samsung Galaxy phones can also connect to emergency services by satellite when cellular and Wi-Fi service are unavailable. However, unlike Apple's system, availability depends on your Galaxy model and wireless carrier. Samsung says satellite communication is expanding across supported Galaxy phones in the U.S. through carriers including Verizon and T-Mobile. On a supported Samsung Galaxy phone with Verizon, you can practice using Satellite SOS before you need it. Verizon specifically provides a Satellite SOS demo for compatible Android phones.
On a supported Galaxy phone, check:
Open SettingsTap Safety and emergencyTap Satellite SOSSelect the option to try the demoFollow the onscreen instructions
Open Settings
Tap Safety and emergency
Tap Satellite SOS
Select the option to try the demo
Follow the onscreen instructions

During a real emergency, first try calling 911. If you have no cellular or Wi-Fi connection and your phone and carrier support Satellite SOS, your Galaxy can prompt you to connect by satellite. You will need to be outside with a clear view of the sky and follow the onscreen directions to establish the connection. Verizon says Google Messages must be the default messaging app for its Satellite SOS service.

One caveat: If you do not see Satellite SOS under Settings > Safety and emergency, that does not necessarily mean your Galaxy is out of date. Your particular model or carrier may use a different satellite service or may not support the feature.
FATAL AIR AMBULANCE CRASH EXPOSES GROWING GPS DANGER FACING US FLIGHTS
Backup power, GPS coordinates, drinking water and satellite communication are among the tools Kurt Knutsson now keeps ready for severe weather. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Your smartphone is an incredible emergency tool. Still, I would not make it your only source of warnings. NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts official National Weather Service warnings, watches, forecasts and other hazard information 24 hours a day. When shopping for a weather radio, look for one with Specific Area Message Encoding, known as SAME.

SAME-capable receivers can be programmed for specific geographic areas. Some can also activate from a silent mode when an alert for that area is transmitted. That is the type of feature I want available when the power goes out in the middle of the night. You can find more options in my storm survival essentials guide at CyberGuy.com.

Charge your phone and portable batteries before severe weather reaches you. Ready.gov recommends planning for batteries and alternative power sources during outages, including portable chargers or power banks.

I also keep spare charging cables available. That became a habit after Katrina because sometimes you may find a source of electricity but not have the cable you need. A larger portable power station may also be useful depending on your equipment and household needs.

This is where the humble zip-top bag earns a permanent place in my emergency kit. I keep small electronics and other essentials protected from water whenever severe weather is approaching. During the podcast, I pulled out one of these bags because the idea is so simple. "A Ziploc bag is your best friend in any weather."

I also keep a serious flashlight nearby. A lantern-style light can be useful during an outage, while a whistle can give you another way to signal for help. The important part is knowing exactly where those items are before the lights disappear.

Water can become a problem surprisingly fast after a disaster. Ready.gov recommends storing one gallon of water per person per day for several days for drinking and sanitation. If you have pets or service animals, include their needs in your emergency planning as well. Personally, I try to keep about a week's worth of water available when possible. That is the approach I described on the podcast.

One thing Katrina taught me is that trouble may begin when you are nowhere near your emergency supplies. That is why I duplicate some of my basics. I keep emergency gear at home and useful supplies in the car. Ready.gov also recommends keeping an emergency supply kit in your vehicle.

I also keep some emergency cash available. During Katrina, Richard had the foresight to get cash before access to normal payment systems became a problem. Ready.gov recommends including cash in an emergency kit because ATMs and credit card systems may not work during a prolonged outage.

For me, the idea is flexibility. If I have to leave quickly, I do not want every flashlight, charging cable and useful piece of emergency gear sitting inside the house. You can also read my guide to getting survival-ready in any storm at CyberGuy.com for more ways to prepare before severe weather arrives.
Staying calm became part of my emergency plan too

Carlos reminded me during the podcast that I somehow seemed calm while all of this was unfolding. I did not feel calm. There was fear. There was uncertainty. At times, I genuinely did not know how I was going to get out. However, focusing on the next solvable problem helped. Eventually, we arranged for a helicopter to land on the hotel roof. Looking back, I remember exactly how desperate I felt. "I was willing to grab the skid of the helicopter in any way I could just to get out."

Then the helicopter lifted off. For a few seconds, I felt enormous relief. That feeling disappeared when I looked down. Across the flooded area, I could see people stranded on rooftops. They were waving whatever they could find, desperately trying to signal for help. That image has stayed with me ever since.
Kurt's key takeaways

Hurricane Katrina taught me that preparedness is really about giving yourself options. You cannot know exactly what a major emergency will take away. That is why I want more than one way to receive information. I want backup power available. I also want the information rescuers could need saved before I am under pressure. Most of these preparations are remarkably simple. Know how to find your coordinates. Practice the emergency features already built into your phone. Keep the equipment you rely on charged and accessible. Then think about what happens when your original plan stops working. That may be the biggest lesson Katrina taught me. A hotel that appeared prepared became overwhelmed. Cell service became unreliable. Roads became useless as an escape route. Eventually, getting out required a helicopter landing on a rooftop. I could never have planned that exact sequence. What I could do, and what I do now, is give myself more ways to solve the next problem. You can hear the full story, including Carlos Amezcua's memories of watching everything unfold from the KTLA anchor desk in Los Angeles, on The CyberGuy Report podcast at CyberGuy.com. The conversation brought back moments I had not thought about in years.
If a storm knocked out your power and cell service tonight, how long could you actually manage with what you have on hand right now? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Google Docs password leak reveals a costly security mistake
summary: A contractor stored credentials in a Google Doc set to "Anyone with the link," and Google Search autocomplete eventually surfaced the password string.
story: Google General Counsel Halimah Delaine Prado joins 'Fox & Friends' to detail how Google is fighting AI-powered phishing scams.

Passwords have a way of ending up in places they were never meant to live. Sometimes convenience wins in the moment, and security becomes tomorrow's problem. One company learned that lesson after a contractor stored credentials in a Google Doc so they could access them from different devices.

Then something happened that should make anyone who uses Google Docs take a closer look at their sharing settings. A developer searching the company's domain on Google saw one of its staging hostnames appear in autocomplete alongside what looked like a credential string. The company investigated and found a Google Docs URL that anyone with the link could access.

That's a rough way to discover that a password has traveled much farther than you intended. Here's how the exposure happened, what Google says about Docs privacy and the simple steps you can take to keep your own passwords and shared files safer.

WORLD PASSWORD DAY: CHECK IF YOUR PASSWORDS ARE SAFE
A computer screen displaying text related to a Google Docs password leak security incident. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How company credentials ended up in a Google Doc

The story was reported by The Register and comes from Siim Kostabi, co-founder of Pageloot, a company that provides QR codes for businesses. Kostabi said his company brought in an outside contractor to help with back-end API integrations. The contractor had credentials for the company's staging environment, which is essentially a test version of its system.

The contractor wanted easy access to those credentials from multiple devices. So they put the information into a Google Doc and set the document so anyone with the link could view it. Later, a Pageloot developer was working on an unrelated problem and typed the company's domain into Google Search. Autocomplete surfaced one of the staging hostnames followed by what appeared to be a credential string.

The team checked and found the accessible Google Docs URL. The Register reported that Google Search had indexed the document and offered information from it as a search suggestion. Pageloot quickly cut off the contractor's access and rotated the exposed credentials. The company also adopted a rule against storing passwords in Google Docs, Slack or Notion and other collaboration tools.
Google explains how Docs privacy settings work

Before you start worrying that every Google Doc you have ever created could suddenly appear in a search, there is an important piece of context. Google told CyberGuy that Google Docs are restricted by default. The person who creates the document controls how it gets shared.

Google's current Drive guidance says Restricted means only people with access can open a file. If you select Anyone with the link, anyone who gets that link can use the file without signing in to a Google Account. Google separately lists a Public setting, when available, that allows anyone to find the file through Google Search.

Google also told CyberGuy that a link to a publicly shared Doc may be indexed if someone posts that link somewhere public where a search engine crawler can find it. The Register says the Pageloot document eventually surfaced through Google Search autocomplete. However, the report does not explain how Google first discovered the Docs URL. For the rest of us, the useful lesson is simple: pay attention to the sharing setting before putting anything sensitive in a cloud document.
A former employee caused another access problem
Kostabi also described a separate incident involving one of Pageloot's customers. The midsize retailer discovered that its QR codes had started sending shoppers to a competitor's website.

According to Kostabi, the company investigated and found that a former employee's credentials had never been revoked. He said the former employee used that lingering access to redirect the retailer's URLs. That mistake carries a very familiar lesson.

When someone no longer needs access to an account or shared file, their access should go away too. That applies at work, but it can also apply at home. Maybe you once shared a financial document with an accountant. Perhaps an old household file still includes someone who no longer needs it. Shared access can be easy to forget because the file quietly remains in Google Drive.
WHAT YOUR INTERNET PROVIDER, WEBSITES AND ADVERTISERS SEE
A company discovered staging credentials stored in a Google Doc had surfaced through Google Search autocomplete after the file was shared too broadly. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why this Google Docs password leak should get your attention

You do not have to run a business to learn something from this story. Plenty of people use Google Docs and Drive to keep household information, travel plans or tax documents and other details they want available across devices.

The danger comes when sensitive information lands in a file with broader access than you realize. A Google Doc can feel private because you remember sending the link to only one person. What really counts is who currently has permission to open it and what the General access setting says. That makes this a good time to check the files you would least want a stranger opening.
Tips to keep passwords and Google Docs safer
A few small changes can reduce the chance that an old shared file or exposed password turns into a much bigger security problem.

If you have passwords sitting in a Google Doc right now, move them to a reputable password manager. Password managers are designed to securely store logins and make them available across your devices. They can also help you create unique passwords instead of reusing the same one. Check out the best expert-reviewed password managers of 2026 at Cyberguy.com for options and what to look for. After moving a password, delete it from the document. If other people may have had access to the file, change that password too.
Start with documents containing financial information or account details.
On a computer:

Open Google Drive.Find the file you want to check.Click Share.Look at the people listed under access.Remove anyone who no longer needs the file.Check General access.Select Restricted if you want access limited to people you specifically approve.
Open Google Drive.
Find the file you want to check.
Click Share.
Look at the people listed under access.
Remove anyone who no longer needs the file.
Check General access.
Select Restricted if you want access limited to people you specifically approve.
Google says switching General access to Restricted means only people with access can open the file.
On iPhone, iPad or Android:
Open the Google Drive app.Open or select the file.Tap Manage access.Under General access, tap Change.Select Restricted.
Open the Google Drive app.
Open or select the file.
Tap Manage access.
Under General access, tap Change.
Select Restricted.

This setting can be handy when you need to share something quickly. However, anyone who gets the link can access the file without signing in to a Google Account. That link can also get forwarded or copied somewhere you never expected. For sensitive documents, share the file directly with specific people instead.

Open the sharing settings on important files and scan the list of people who can still get in. If someone no longer needs access, remove them. This is especially worth doing after you finish working with a contractor or service provider. At home, the same idea applies when you have shared a document temporarily and the reason for sharing it has passed.

Changing a Google Doc from broad access to Restricted helps close the door, but it cannot undo exposure that may have already happened. If a password was sitting in a document other people could access, change it. Then check the account's recent login or security activity for anything you do not recognize.

Two-factor authentication adds another step when someone tries to sign in to your account. That can help protect you if a password gets stolen. CyberGuy's guide to multifactor authentication apps can help you strengthen accounts that support this added protection.

Strong antivirus software adds another layer of protection on your computer and phone. It cannot fix a Google Doc with the wrong sharing setting. However, it can help detect malicious downloads, phishing attempts and other threats that may follow if criminals get hold of your login information. Keep your security software updated and make sure real-time protection stays turned on. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Identity theft protection makes the most sense when an exposed document contained more than a password. For example, you may want extra monitoring if someone gained access to your Social Security number, financial account information or other highly sensitive personal data. Identity theft protection services can watch for signs that your information is being misused. Some also alert you to suspicious activity tied to your identity. If the exposure involved only one account password, changing that password and securing the account may be enough. The level of protection you need depends on what information was actually exposed. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

You probably have old Google Drive files you have not opened in months or even years. Spend a few minutes checking the sharing settings on documents containing sensitive information. You may find an old permission you completely forgot about. For more ways to lock down cloud files, see our guide on protecting sensitive documents and controlling file access.
What Google says about private Docs and Gemini

Google also addressed a separate privacy question with CyberGuy. The company told us that it does not use private Workspace content, including Drive and Docs, to train its foundational AI models such as Gemini. Google's published Workspace guidance likewise says Workspace data isn’t used to train or improve the underlying generative AI models that power Gemini, Search and other systems outside Workspace without permission. That issue is separate from what happened in the Pageloot story. This case centered on how the document was shared and how credentials were handled.
FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK
Google Docs are Restricted by default, but changing sharing permissions can expose sensitive information to anyone who gets the link. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Kurt's key takeaways

What gets me about this story is how ordinary the original decision probably felt. Someone needed a password on more than one device and chose an easy place to put it. That shortcut eventually left company credentials where Google Search autocomplete could surface them. The second incident carries another lesson I think all of us can use. Access should have an expiration date. When somebody no longer needs to open one of your files or accounts, remove them. I would also take five minutes today and look at the Google Docs you care about most. Check the people who can open them and look at the General access setting. You may find nothing wrong. Great. But if you uncover an old shared link or a person who should no longer have access, you will be glad you looked before somebody else did.
When was the last time you checked who can still open the Google Docs and Drive files you've shared over the years? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: AI may answer some New Orleans 911 calls
summary: New Orleans 911 uses Carbyne AI to triage repeat auto crash calls, but strict limits keep human call-takers in control of all other emergencies.
story: Fox News host Emily Compagno discusses New Orleans' deployment of AI to answer 911 calls on 'Outnumbered.'

Calling 911 is one of those moments when you expect a human voice on the other end. In New Orleans, though, an artificial intelligence system may answer in a limited situation involving certain calls about already reported auto crashes.

The Orleans Parish Communication District handles 911 emergency communications in Orleans Parish. OPCD says the AI helps manage repeat crash reports while keeping human call-takers available for other emergencies.
Hearing an automated voice after dialing 911 could make anyone pause. So, here is what the system actually does, when it steps in and where humans remain in control.

No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.
Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.
SMART STREET SENSORS COULD BE WATCHING YOUR CITY NEXT
New Orleans uses artificial intelligence to help handle certain repeat 911 calls about auto crashes already reported to emergency dispatchers. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How New Orleans 911 AI works

OPCD began working with emergency communications company Carbyne on AI-assisted call triage before launching the system in 2023. Carbyne calls the technology AI-V Emergency Call Triage. The company designed it to help emergency communication centers deal with sudden floods of calls about the same event.

A car crash can create that problem quickly. OPCD says one accident can generate numerous calls from nearby drivers. During busy periods, those repeat reports can pile up while call-takers handle other emergencies. The AI gives OPCD another way to manage some of those repeat calls.

The system checks whether an incoming call comes from within 200 meters, or about 650 feet, of a crash that 911 already knows about. It can step in only when every human call-taker is occupied. OPCD says it has not deployed the system this way for any other category of 911 call.
What happens when the AI answers

The conversation starts simply. OPCD says the AI identifies the call as New Orleans 911. It then asks whether you are calling about an accident at a specific location. Your response determines what happens next.

Answer anything other than yes, and the system returns your call to the 911 queue for a human call-taker. OPCD says this safeguard works regardless of the language you use. Confirm that you are calling about the known crash, and the AI tells you that 911 already knows about it.

Someone involved in the accident or a caller with more information can stay on the line for a human. Otherwise, the system tells the caller that they may hang up. OPCD says the AI itself cannot end the call. The caller decides when to hang up.
What the AI cannot do

The limits of the system become especially important when you are talking about 911. OPCD says the AI cannot dispatch emergency responders. It also cannot determine how urgently a call should be handled.
Its role focuses on identifying this specific type of repeat crash call and determining whether the caller needs to remain in the human queue.

OPCD also says the technology isn’t a large language model like ChatGPT. The system performs a much narrower task within the emergency communications network. Comparing it directly with a general-purpose AI chatbot can therefore create the wrong impression of what it actually does.
What happens when the system does not understand you?
This was one of my first questions about the technology. OPCD says the system sends a call back to the queue or a human operator when it cannot understand the caller.

It also defaults to a human when a call falls outside the limited crash scenario it was designed to handle. The system supports multiple languages. OPCD also trained it using local 911 recordings to better understand New Orleans accents and local street names. That local training can help in a city where a street name could challenge an unfamiliar voice system.
AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU
Visual representation of artificial intelligence systems or technology interface related to emergency services dispatch. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What happens if you hang up while waiting?
There is another safeguard worth knowing about. OPCD says the AI system keeps the 911 center's normal callback procedures in place.

Once your call enters the queue for a human, hanging up does not erase it. The call center can contact you after staff work through the queue. Still, OPCD advises callers to stay on the line whenever possible. A call waiting in the queue will eventually reach a call-taker.
Calls still get recorded
An AI interaction does not disappear from the system. OPCD says it logs these calls with the normal metadata and audio recording. Those records remain available when investigators need them.

The agency also says calls handled through the system do not get uploaded to an outside large language model. That addresses an obvious privacy question whenever AI becomes part of an emergency communications system.
Has the New Orleans 911 AI made mistakes?

OPCD says it tested the technology for several months before putting it into live use. The agency says its team reviewed 100% of the calls handled by the system during its first three months. During that review period, OPCD says it found no false positives or false negatives.

In practical terms, the system handled the calls OPCD expected it to handle without taking over calls outside its intended use. That result is encouraging, although it covers a defined review period rather than every call handled since the system launched. OPCD says its compliance team continues to audit the technology closely.
Has the system helped?

Carbyne has published performance figures from its work with OPCD. Because Carbyne provides the technology, these numbers are vendor-reported rather than findings from an independent study. In a Carbyne case study, the company says its AI-V Emergency Call Triage system triaged more than 3,500 events during a 90-day period.

Carbyne reports that redundant calls among those triaged calls dropped by more than 30%. The company also says distressed callers got their calls answered up to 40 seconds faster on average. Those numbers suggest the approach has potential. Still, I would like to see OPCD continue releasing its own performance data over time.
Is AI replacing New Orleans 911 call-takers?

OPCD says no. The agency has struggled to fill all of its available call-taker positions. Staffing shortages also remain a broader problem across the 911 industry. OPCD says it views AI as a tool to support its human call-takers rather than replace them.

For New Orleans, the goal is to reduce repeat crash reports during call surges so human call-takers can reach other people waiting for help. The agency says it has not expanded AI triage to other categories of 911 calls.
Could New Orleans expand its 911 AI later?
OPCD is studying what else the technology might eventually do. However, those experiments are taking place in a testing environment rather than on the live 911 system.

The agency says it has explored whether AI could help with other types of call clusters. It has not put those uses into operation. OPCD also says it will not expand the AI triage tool to additional 911 categories unless the agency can ensure the technology works properly. For now, its live use remains focused on the specific auto-crash scenario.
What this means to you

New Orleans may be the test case here, but this story reaches far beyond one city. AI is starting to move into public services that people rely on during emergencies. That means your community could eventually face the same questions. When should AI step in? What should it be allowed to handle? How quickly can you reach a human when something goes wrong?

For now, New Orleans keeps the system on a very short leash. It handles only certain repeat calls about known crashes, and human call-takers remain available for anything outside that narrow use. The bigger question is what happens next.

As more emergency centers look for ways to handle staffing shortages and call surges, AI could become part of the conversation where you live. If that happens, you should know exactly what the system can do, what it cannot do and how easily you can reach a person. That is what I would be watching most closely.
LAGUARDIA AIRPORT AI HOLOGRAM ANSWERS TRAVELER QUESTIONS
An AI system can answer some New Orleans 911 calls when human call-takers are busy, but its role is limited to repeat reports of known crashes. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Kurt's key takeaways

Hearing AI on a 911 call would make a lot of people uneasy. I understand why. In an emergency, you want help fast and a clear way to reach a person. New Orleans has given its AI a narrow job. It can help filter repeat reports of an accident that 911 already knows about while human call-takers are busy. I can see the benefit. One crash may generate many calls while someone elsewhere needs help with a completely different emergency. Still, 911 deserves an extremely high standard. OPCD says its early audit found no false positives or negatives, and the agency continues to monitor the system. I want that scrutiny to continue. Any move beyond this limited use should come with clear safeguards and solid performance data.

Would you feel comfortable hearing an AI system after dialing 911 when it could help human call-takers reach other emergencies faster, or would you always want a person to answer first? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Card skimming scam is stealing food benefits nationwide
summary: A single card skimmer can generate $1 million in stolen funds, and Secret Service video shows criminals installing them in under two seconds.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

You swipe your card at the checkout, grab your receipt and walk away. Nothing looks unusual. However, a device sitting right on top of that payment terminal may have copied your card information and PIN.

U.S. Secret Service agents recently swept hundreds of retailers across Los Angeles looking for skimmers. What they found shows how sophisticated these devices have become and how difficult they can be to spot.

This card skimming scam is especially serious for people who rely on Electronic Benefit Transfer, or EBT, cards. Many of those cards still depend on magnetic-stripe technology that criminals know how to exploit.
INSIDE NYC'S 'PERFECT SCAM': LUXURY CARS, DUSTY SHELVES AND THE EBT SECRET BEHIND THE COUNTER
U.S. Secret Service agents found sophisticated skimmers on payment terminals during a Los Angeles sweep targeting suspected fraud. (U.S. Secret Service)

Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.

Secret Service finds skimmers hiding in plain sight

One of the most unsettling parts of the investigation is how quickly criminals can install a skimmer. Surveillance video from the investigation captured a suspect placing one over a payment terminal in less than two seconds. From there, the fake reader sits directly over the real terminal. When someone swipes a card, the device can capture account information and the PIN used during the transaction.

We have previously shown you how skimmers and shimmers can steal your payment information. What stands out now is how convincing these newer devices can look. During the Secret Service sweep, agents found a skimmer that blended closely into the legitimate payment terminal. It even had what appeared to be a security hologram.

Agents had to pry the device off. Inside, they found miniature electronics and a wireless transmitter. That transmitter can send stolen information to a criminal nearby. The person who installed the skimmer may not have to return and remove it to collect the data.
A single skimmer could lead to huge losses
The numbers behind this crime are staggering. The Secret Service says a single skimmer can generate as much as $1 million in stolen funds.
Across the country, 32 active federal investigations span 15 states. Meanwhile, the Secret Service estimates that skimming costs consumers and financial institutions more than $1 billion each year.

The agency has also stepped up its nationwide enforcement efforts. During 2025 operations, law enforcement removed more than 400 illegal skimming devices. The Secret Service says skimming activity has increasingly targeted EBT cards.

A recent Los Angeles sweep shows how widespread the problem has become. Law enforcement visited 328 businesses and inspected 1,749 payment devices. Agents seized 16 skimmers. The Secret Service estimated those removals prevented about $16.6 million in potential fraud losses.
Why criminals are targeting EBT cards

This is where things take a troubling turn. The Secret Service says criminals intentionally target locations with heavy EBT use. That includes stores where people use government benefits to buy groceries.

Many credit and debit cards now offer chips or contactless payment. However, many EBT transactions still require a magnetic-stripe swipe. That gives criminals an opening. A skimmer can capture the information stored on the magnetic stripe. Criminals can then copy that information onto another magnetic-stripe card. If they also capture the victim's PIN, they can use the cloned card to steal benefits.

For people who rely on those benefits, the impact can be immediate. Victims may discover their accounts have been drained when they try to buy groceries or pay for everyday necessities. Recovering stolen benefits can also take time, leaving families without money they were counting on.
VENEZUELAN NATIONALS CHARGED IN $529K ATM JACKPOTTING SCHEME AT I-95 REST STOPS, FEDS SAY
Tiny electronics hidden inside a skimmer can capture card data and help criminals steal information without altering the real terminal. (U.S. Secret Service)
Why EBT card security is changing

Federal officials know the magnetic stripe is a weak point. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food and Nutrition Service says EBT fraud involving skimming is rising. The agency is working with states on modernizing SNAP EBT systems, including introducing chip cards.

Chip technology makes card information harder to copy than data stored on a magnetic stripe. Still, that transition takes time. Until more EBT systems support newer payment technology, millions of people may continue using cards that require a swipe. That leaves benefit recipients with fewer ways to avoid the very payment method criminals are targeting.
Organized crime groups are behind some skimming operations

The Secret Service says organized criminal groups are involved in some of these skimming schemes. Investigators have linked some operations to groups that travel into the United States and move between locations installing devices.

The agency has been conducting skimming operations across the country throughout 2026. Recent sweeps have focused on payment terminals at stores and ATMs where skimming activity is suspected. That kind of coordinated activity can make the devices harder to track and allow criminals to target multiple locations in a short period of time.
How to protect yourself from card skimmers
You may never spot a well-made skimmer by sight alone. Still, you can lower your risk and catch suspicious activity faster.

If a payment terminal supports contactless payments, use them. The Secret Service recommends tap-to-pay when possible. You can also use a digital wallet on your phone if the retailer supports it. For more ways to protect your cards in stores and online, see our guide on how to protect your credit and bank cards from getting hacked.

Take a few seconds before inserting or swiping your card. Look for a reader that appears loose or crooked. Also watch for damage, unusual gaps or parts that do not seem to line up correctly. The Secret Service recommends avoiding a reader if something looks altered or damaged.
IDENTITY THEFT RARELY ANNOUNCES ITSELF: 6 SIGNS YOU MISSED
Card skimmers can steal payment information and PINs in seconds, putting EBT users and other consumers at risk of fraud. (U.S. Secret Service)

Some overlay skimmers sit directly on top of the legitimate card reader. Before swiping, gently check whether anything feels loose or moves unexpectedly. Do not try to rip apart a terminal. If something seems suspicious, stop using it and notify the store.

A skimmer may capture card information while another device records your PIN. Use your hand to shield the keypad whenever you enter a PIN. That simple habit can make captured card information less useful to a criminal.

Enable alerts through your bank or card issuer so you know when your card gets used. Pay attention to small charges too. If you see something you do not recognize, contact your financial institution using the number on your card or its official app. If money has already disappeared from an account, follow our steps on what to do if your bank account is hacked.

EBT users should review their account history for transactions they do not recognize. The Food and Nutrition Service recommends checking EBT accounts regularly. It also advises changing your PIN at least once a month, particularly before your benefits are issued. If you spot an unauthorized transaction, change your PIN immediately and contact your state EBT agency.

Government agencies should not need your PIN to verify your eligibility. Do not provide your EBT card number or PIN in response to an unexpected text, phone call or email. Federal officials warn that criminals use several methods to steal benefit information, so protecting the PIN remains important even when no physical skimmer is involved.
What to do if you think a skimmer stole your card information
Act quickly once you notice suspicious transactions.

Contact the bank or organization that issued the card.Ask them to block the compromised card and review unauthorized transactions.If an EBT card is involved, contact the agency that manages benefits in your state.Change the card's PIN immediately.Also write down where you last used the card. That information may help investigators or the retailer locate a compromised terminal.Do not assume one unauthorized charge will be the end of it. Criminals who successfully copy card information may try using it again.
Contact the bank or organization that issued the card.
Ask them to block the compromised card and review unauthorized transactions.
If an EBT card is involved, contact the agency that manages benefits in your state.
Change the card's PIN immediately.
Also write down where you last used the card. That information may help investigators or the retailer locate a compromised terminal.
Do not assume one unauthorized charge will be the end of it. Criminals who successfully copy card information may try using it again.
Kurt's key takeaways

What bothers me most about this scam is that criminals are going after people who may have the fewest options to protect themselves. If I can tap my credit card or pay with my phone, I can avoid swiping altogether. Many EBT users cannot make that same choice because their cards still rely on older magnetic-stripe technology. That needs to change. These skimmers have become convincing enough to fool almost anyone, and some can transmit stolen information without the criminal ever coming back for the device. You can check the reader and keep an eye on your account, but there is only so much you can do when the payment system itself leaves you exposed. Moving benefit cards to more secure technology should be a priority, especially when families are depending on that money for food.
