The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: US military plane lands in Moscow, with Kremlin claiming it has no information: report
summary: A video has emerged showing a U.S. military C-17A Globemaster III aircraft approaching for a landing at Moscow, Russia's Vnukovo airport on Wednesday.
story: A video captured a U.S. military C-17A Globemaster III aircraft coming in for a landing on Wednesday, Aug. 25, 2026, at Moscow's Vnukovo airport. (Credit: Reuters)
Video captured a U.S. military transport plane coming in for a landing Tuesday at Moscow's Vnukovo airport, in a flight that the Kremlin reportedly claimed it had no information about.

Data from the website Flightradar24 showed that the Boeing C-17A Globemaster III left Joint Base Andrews in Maryland early Sunday afternoon on a flight to Riga, Latvia. The aircraft then traveled from Riga to Moscow, Russia on Tuesday morning.

The last time a U.S.-registered jet made a direct flight to Russia from Europe was in January when special envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, visited Moscow for a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin about the war in Ukraine, according to Reuters.

A Department of War spokesperson told Fox News Digital on Tuesday, "We have nothing to provide on this subject." Fox News Digital also has reached out to the White House and the U.S. Embassy in Moscow for comment.
PUTIN 'PANICKED' AS DEFIANT UKRAINE MARKS INDEPENDENCE DAY UNDER RUSSIAN BOMBARDMENT
A U.S. military transport plane approaches Moscow, Russia, on Wednesday, Aug. 25, 2026, in this screen grab taken from a social media video. (Reuters)
The Kremlin said it had no information about the latest flight, Reuters reported.

Yury Ushakov, an aide to Putin, said following January’s meeting with Witkoff and Kushner that "our counterparts arrived from Davos after taking part in a series of events together with President Donald Trump, including those concerning the Ukraine settlement."
MARINE VETERAN ROBERT GILMAN RETURNS TO US SOIL AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION FULFILLS REQUEST: 'NO AMERICAN LEFT BEHIND'

Russia’s President Vladimir Putin meets with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner and Federal Acquisition Service Commissioner Josh Gruenbaum at the Kremlin in Moscow on Jan. 22, 2026. (Alexander Kazakov/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

"They offered what can be called their first-hand accounts of these events and shared their impressions, as well as their latest thoughts and assessments regarding the meeting between the President of the United States and [Ukraine President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy in Davos" during the World Economic Forum, he added.
A Boeing C-17 Globemaster III plane is seen departing Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport. (Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Overall, I can say that the focus of the meeting between the President of Russia and US representatives was to obtain information resulting from the contacts the United States had with the Ukrainians and Europeans in order to define further steps between our two countries," Ushakov also said.
Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Denmark's left-wing PM warns: 'Big enemy has started to grow from within' as Europe faces migrant reckoning
summary: Mette Frederiksen's stance on Denmark immigration and border control puts her at odds with Spain's PM, as she names failed integration and Islamist extremism as key threats.
story: Fox News host Mark Levin issues a warning about leftist immigration ideology in wake of a recent wave of illegal immigration into Spain on 'Life, Liberty & Levin.'

Denmark's left-wing prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, has sent shock waves throughout the European left after recent comments about the Scandinavian nation's — and the continent's — failure to deal with radical Islam among migrant communities.

Her comments come after the mass migration chaos in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, when Frederiksen criticized the actions of Spain's leftist leader, Pedro Sánchez, during a special session on Ceuta in the Danish Parliament.

Responding to a question from a far-left legislator on Denmark’s apparent lack of "solidarity" with Spain against "anti-democratic forces" pressuring Europe, Frederiksen said, "If we talk about undemocratic forces, then Russia is our biggest enemy. The problem is that a big enemy has started to grow from within, and it is foreigners who have come to Europe," according to an English translation.
MIGRANT CRISIS PUSHES ITALY TO RESTORE BORDER CHECKS WITH SPAIN, TESTING EUROPE'S OPEN-BORDER SYSTEM
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen addressing the Danish Parliament. (Mads Claus Rasmussen/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP via Getty Images)

While not singling out Denmark's integrated immigrant population, she continued, "It is Hamas supporters. It is people who commit terror against European societies. It is people who do not recognize our fundamental European values. It is people who sympathize with some of the darkest forces in this world. So, Europe is threatened. The problem is that we are threatened both from outside and now from within, but it is not because of a disagreement between the Danish and Spanish governments, but because of people with an Islamic background who do not want the open, free European society, unfortunately."

Sweden-based foreign policy expert and author Daniel Schatz told Fox News Digital, "What is striking is not that a conservative politician is talking about illegal immigration, failed integration and Islamist extremism, it is that one of Europe’s leading center-left prime ministers is saying it in such blunt terms. That tells you how far the European immigration debate has shifted."
PORTUGAL ENACTS 'BURQA LAW' LARGELY PROHIBITING FACE COVERINGS IN PUBLIC

Frederiksen came to power in Denmark’s 2019 elections on what Reuters called a "platform of radical reforms to reach climate targets, lowering the pension age for manual workers - and stricter migration policies." Denmark already had some of the strongest asylum laws in Europe before 2019, including a 2018 law targeting "parallel societies." That law allowed the government to "demolish or sell off social housing areas where more than half of residents are from a ‘non-Western’ background," if certain criteria were met, and refugees in those areas are not eligible for family reunion.

In 2021, Frederiksen introduced a new deportation law allowing for refugees to be returned to their country of origin, if Denmark deemed it safe, even if Denmark had no diplomatic relations with that country, and even as the European Commission deemed Danish legislation on transferring asylum seekers to third countries while their claims were processed "incompatible with EU law."
Escorted by the Spanish army, migrants who crossed into Spain return to Morocco from the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. (AP Photo/Antonio Sempere)

Since June, Frederiksen has been a leading voice in opposition to the immigration policies of Spain’s Pedro Sánchez, telling Parliament, "It is no secret that I and the Spanish Prime Minister deeply disagree on immigration policy… I and we will not accept that Danish society has to pay the price for decisions in Spain that we fundamentally disagree with."

On Aug. 1, Frederiksen joined conservative Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and 20 other EU government leaders in a letter saying the EU "cannot allow mass crossings, the instrumentalization of migration or other hybrid threats to create the perception that illegal entry into the European Union is possible."

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and the Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Denmark Mette Frederiksen addressed the media during a joint press conference after a meeting at Palazzo Chigi. (Stefano Costantino/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
ITALY-SPAIN BORDER FEUD EXPOSES EUROPE’S DEEPENING IMMIGRATION DIVIDE

The two, currently the only female heads of government in the EU, followed that letter with an Aug. 10 joint statement saying they "are both proud of Europe’s Christian cultural heritage and we want to protect it. We expect that those who arrive in our countries and choose to make Europe their home respect our values and do not try to impose ways of life that we do not share. We believe that this is the right path to protect Europe and our common values. And we believe that millions of Europeans share this conviction."
File photo showing men praying at a Mosque in Denmark. (Davut Colak/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images)

Emma Schubart of the Henry Jackson Society told Fox News Digital, "Frederiksen is right to name the ‘enemy within’. Europe has spent years pretending that uncontrolled migration and failed integration come without consequences. They do not… Parallel societies have taken root, Islamist extremism has been allowed to fester and support for groups such as Hamas is no longer confined to the margins. Denmark understands the cost."

Daniel Schatz said Frederiksen "is essentially arguing that Europe faces threats from two directions: Russia from outside and anti-democratic extremism from within. For a center-left European leader, that is remarkably strong language." He noted Frederiksen’s "political formula has been straightforward: protect Denmark’s generous system of public benefits and social services, control the border and deny the populist right a monopoly on immigration. For an American audience, that is probably the most important thing to understand about the Danish model."
A police vehicle is seen near the Israeli embassy in Copenhagen, as police investigate two explosions near the site, on Wednesday, Oct. 2, 2024. (Emil Helms/Ritzau Scanpix via AP, File)

Frederiksen’s position is important, he said, because she did not move politically "because Danish voters suddenly became concerned about immigration. She moved because she realized years ago that many of them already were." He added, "The important distinction is that this is not an argument that immigrants are inherently criminal. It is an argument that a democratic society must be willing to confront failed integration when it occurs."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Schubart added, "Other leaders now need to show the same courage, secure their borders, deport those with no right to remain and make clear that integration into our laws and values is not optional."
Reuters contributed to this report.

Tyler Speicher is an American journalist living in Slovenia after spending 25 years covering stories ranging from the Little League World Series to hurricanes, 9/11 and its aftermath for New York City news outlets, including 20 years on the Fox News Channel assignment desk.

title: Could Iran’s regime collapse? Experts assess Bessent’s bid to sever financial lifelines
summary: Scott Bessent's "Economic D-Day" against Iran sent the rial to an all-time low as experts debate whether maximum pressure can trigger regime change.
story: Former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo analyzes Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent launching 'Operation Economic Outcast' against Iran. Pompeo discusses the powerful impact of sanctions and argues that the era of funneling money to Iran is over. The economic offensive aims to achieve complete global isolation by holding Iran's partners accountable under strict U.S. sanctions.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s Monday announcement that America will impose the economic equivalent of the military campaign that defeated Nazi Germany on the Islamic Republic of Iran could set off a series of events leading to the dissolution of the nearly 47-year-old dictatorship in Tehran, according to Iran experts.

Bessent’s declaration of economic warfare follows President Donald Trump’s commitment last week to launch an "economic D-Day" against the Tehran regime. The comprehensive U.S. economic pressure point campaign targeting Iran’s already troubled economy could have dramatic effects on the restive population in the country of over 90 million people.

"In the Second World War, D-Day marked the historic beginning of a campaign with our allies to target and drive the enemy from its positions, including those in third countries. Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe," said Bessent. He added, "Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone. Iran's fanatics devote themselves to death to America and seek nuclear weapons to do just that. They have murdered and maimed more of our citizens and service members than any other terrorist regime on Earth."
TRUMP THREATENS 'UNPRECEDENTED' ECONOMIC CONSEQUENCES FOR ANY NATION AIDING IRAN
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent speaks at a news conference, Monday, Aug. 24, 2026, at the Treasury Department in Washington. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)
Just hours before Bessent spoke, Iran’s currency, the rial, plunged to an all-time low. The rial fell to 2.02 million to the U.S. dollar. Iranians are struggling to afford basic goods.

Jonathan Harounoff, an Iran expert and British author of Persian heritage, told Fox News Digital that "Ultimately, this pressure campaign will likely continue to cripple the regime and set the stage for perhaps yet another domestic uprising. The precise timing of such a revolt is impossible to predict."

Harounoff, who has written extensively on upheavals in Iran against the clerical leadership, added, "What isn't impossible to predict is that the regime is governing brutishly over a repressed population that has endured sustained economic and social immiseration. It's only a matter of time before more protests break out, and the real question is whether international organizations like the U.N. and Western governments will choose to stand by — or tangibly support the Iranian people and actively sever any cooperation they maintain with the regime."
LEAKED IRAN REPORT FINDS RECORD PUBLIC ANGER AS REGIME FOCUSES ON HOLDING POWER
Iranians gather while blocking a street during a protest in Kermanshah, Iran on Jan. 8, 2026. (Kamran/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)

He warned that, "Too often, outsiders speak of regime change as if it were a passive exercise. Certainly, only the people of Iran can bring about organic, homegrown, transformational change — and they have 47 years of turmoil and repression driving them toward it. But there are real ways to support the Iranian people (Starlink, supporting think tanks and foundations, raising awareness of the plight of Iranians, etc.) and help them achieve what has, until now, been a quixotic dream."

Jason Brodsky, policy director at United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), told Fox News Digital, "The question is often asked: what makes this iteration of the maximum pressure campaign different from all other iterations? The answer is this iteration is taking place against a backdrop where there is a synchronization of economic and military pressure against the Iranian regime — a combination which has never been deployed by a U.S. administration until now. The U.S. naval blockade currently in place against Tehran is unprecedented. The Iranian regime's industrial base — for example, steel plants — has also been damaged following kinetic strikes. The Iranian regime’s military capacity has likewise been degraded."
IRAN ACCELERATES EXECUTION CAMPAIGN AGAINST ANTI-REGIME ACTIVISTS AMID INTERNET CENSORSHIP
Buses that were burned during Iran's protests, in Tehran, Iran, Jan. 21, 2026. (Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via Reuters)

He noted, "So Operation Economic Outcast is being launched at a time of true weakness in terms of its national power. The regime's risk tolerance may be increasing, but so is its desperation. The drivers pushing the Iranian people into the streets to protest have only gotten worse since January — with political, economic and social forces all deteriorating. The regime is seeking to use the tussle over the Strait of Hormuz as a distraction from all of this."

Alireza Nader, an independent Iran expert, however, expressed skepticism that the tightening of the economic screws could provoke a mass revolt. "I don’t think starving the civilian population in Iran will lead to an American victory. The regime has demonstrated an extreme brutality toward the population, having massacred thousands of unarmed protestors this past January. And Iranians are less likely to rise up when the promised help to them from Trump and Netanyahu never materialized."
Nader said, "The Woman, Life, Freedom movement against the regime prior to the war had the best chance of overthrowing the regime. This war has disrupted the Iranian people’s struggle for freedom."
Iranians block a street while gathering during a protest in Tehran, Iran, on Jan. 9. (MAHSA / Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)

Beni Sabti, an Iran expert at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) in Israel, told Fox News Digital that "there are some protests inside Iran for pensioners and those who did not get their salaries."

He said the January protests began with "economic problems." President Trump has said that the Iranian regime murdered 52,000 Iranian demonstrators during the Jan. 8 and 9 mass protests against the regime.

Sabti, who was born in Tehran and has deep sourcing in Iran, said Trump’s economic offensive campaign against Iran could "bring out the people again." He said there were some "rumors" that lower-rank army soldiers did not receive their salaries.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The U.S. Treasury Secretary Bessent seized on the point that the regime will have payroll problems today. He said, "To the ordinary soldiers supporting this regime, as more and more of your paychecks stop or are supposedly just delayed, ask whether your commanders are leading your country to triumph or to ruin, and recall that the Berlin Wall fell when ordinary soldiers decided not to shoot at their own people."
Benjamin Weinthal reports on Israel, Iran, Syria, Turkey and Europe. You can follow Benjamin on Twitter @BenWeinthal, and email him at benjamin.weinthal@fox.com

title: Syria off US terror blacklist after nearly 50 years as Trump admin clears investment hurdle
summary: The United States formally removed Syria from its state sponsors of terrorism list after Marco Rubio authorized the rescission and delisted HTS.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The United States on Monday formally removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, a move Secretary of State Marco Rubio said eliminates the final major barriers to investment and economic recovery in the country.
Rubio said in a statement that he had authorized the formal rescission after a mandatory 45-day congressional notification period ended.
President Donald Trump had initiated the countdown in July after confirming to Congress that Syria’s government had ceased supporting acts of international terrorism.
"I have also delisted Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham’s (HTS) designation as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist (SDGT)," Rubio said Monday.
FORMER ASSAD-ERA PRISON CHIEF CONVICTED OF TORTURE IN US FEDERAL COURT, MARKING A HISTORIC FIRST

Syria’s president secured a major diplomatic boost as the U.S. removed the country from its terrorism blacklist, clearing key barriers to investment. (BING GUAN/POOL/AFP via Getty Images; Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The actions, he said, represent "another historic step by President Trump to give the Syrian people a path to prosperity."
Rubio said Washington had taken unprecedented steps over the past year to provide sanctions relief to the Syrian people.

He pointed to Trump’s June 2025 executive order, "Providing for the Revocation of Syria Sanctions," which accelerated sanctions relief by terminating the Syria Sanctions Program and the national emergency with respect to Syria while directing reviews of other Syria-related sanctions and terrorist designations.

"These actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism," Rubio said of the Syrian government.

Al-Sharaa ousted President Bashar al-Assad in December 2024 in an offensive led by HTS rebels. Syria had been on the State Sponsors of Terrorism list since 1979, with the designation in force throughout al-Assad’s rule.
BRIEF ALCOHOL BAN IN DAMASCUS SPARKS CONCERNS ABOUT PRESIDENT AL-SHARAA'S VISION FOR SYRIA

Secretary of State Marco Rubio shakes hands with then Syrian interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa at the Lotte New York Palace Hotel, on the sidelines of the 80th United Nations General Assembly at the United Nations headquarters, Monday, Sept. 22, 2025. (Bing Guan/Pool Photo via AP)

"In the past year, the Government of Syria has taken significant steps to counterterrorism, to include formally joining the Global Coalition to Defeat ISIS in November and conducting operations to disrupt the terror networks of ISIS, al-Qa’ida, Hizballah, and Iran-aligned groups," Rubio said.

He added that rescinding Syria’s designation as a state sponsor of terrorism and HTS’ designation as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist "eliminates the final major barriers for private-sector investment in Syria and promotes Syria’s economic recovery and reintegration into the global economy."
EVANGELICAL LEADER SAYS US MUST PROTECT SYRIAN CHRISTIANS FROM ATTACKS BY JIHADI TERRORISTS

Syrians gather in Umayyad Square, waving the Syrian revolution flags as they continue their celebrations after the overthrow of the 61-year Baathist regime and the end of the Assad family era in Damascus, Syria on Dec. 27, 2024. (Emin Sansar/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani told Reuters on Aug. 22 that lifting the designation would help restore Syria’s links to the global financial system and encourage investment following nearly 14 years of war.
"There is no longer any obstacle to investment, doing business and rebuilding economic life in Syria," he said.

"Today’s action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also said in a statement, adding that it is "in line with President Trump’s promise to deliver sanctions relief to Syria."

The governor of the Central Bank of Syria said Monday that lifting Syria’s designation as a state sponsor of terrorism is a "historic step that returns it to its natural place within the global economic system."
On Monday, Trump also posted a photo on Truth Social of al-Sharaa and al-Shibani holding his signed June 2025 executive order directing sanctions relief for Syria.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
Cuba, Iran and North Korea remain the three countries designated by Washington as state sponsors of terrorism.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Putin ‘panicked’ as defiant Ukraine marks Independence Day under Russian bombardment
summary: Ukraine celebrated 35 years of independence amid fresh Russian attacks as an expert said Kyiv’s deep strikes and battlefield pressure have left Putin rattled.
story: Ukraine's Independence Day faced heightened security risks as former Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Carrie Filipetti, now executive director of the Vandenberg Coalition, says Vladimir Putin is "panicked."

Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day on Monday under the shadow of continued Russian attacks, with one regional security expert arguing that Russian President Vladimir Putin is "panicked" as Ukrainian forces strike deeper inside Russia.

The anniversary, commemorating Ukraine's Aug. 24, 1991, declaration of independence from the Soviet Union, came amid intensified Russian strikes on civilian infrastructure and heightened security concerns after Ukraine's Security Service warned of possible terrorist attacks ahead of the holiday.

European leaders joined Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv for Independence Day events in a show of support as the war grinds on. Zelenskyy declared that Ukraine wants peace but is not prepared to surrender to Moscow's demands.
A Russian drone strike Friday on a packed shopping center in Kryvyi Rih, Zelenskyy’s hometown, killed at least 16 people and injured 130, according to The Associated Press.
'PURE HELL' IN MOSCOW AS UKRAINIAN DRONES STRIKE MAJOR REFINERY SUPPLYING CAPITAL'S FUEL MARKET

FILE - Russian President Vladimir Putin chairs a meeting aboard the missile cruiser Varyag in Russia's far eastern Sakhalin region on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. Putin previously said Russia is not waging a sabotage campaign against Europe. (Reuters)
Putin has warned that Ukrainian strikes on Russian economic targets open a "Pandora’s box," while Kyiv maintains deep strikes are vital to disrupting Moscow’s logistics.
Ukraine has targeted Russian economic infrastructure, including warehouses belonging to online retailers Wildberries and Ozon.

"The war with Russia has seen a lot of advances for the Ukrainians over this year," former Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Carrie Filipetti, now executive director of the Vandenberg Coalition, told Fox News Digital.
"They've recently been able to actually penetrate much deeper into Russian territory, including close to Moscow and St. Petersburg."

"Their success on the military front has now resulted in the Russians getting panicked and starting to attack more inside Ukraine and what they're really trying to do is weaken their will and capabilities," Filipetti said, adding that Putin "gets very anxious when he's put in a corner."

"What we're seeing is these sorts of gasps at trying to retain some kind of control," Filipetti added. "This is why he recently targeted a shopping mall inside Ukrainian territory. He is not focused on targeting military assets. He is really focused on trying to defeat the will of Ukrainians by attacking them."
RUSSIA UNLEASHES NEARLY 600 MISSILES AND DRONES ON KYIV IN DEADLIEST STRIKE SINCE MAY
The anniversary came amid intensified Russian strikes. (REUTERS /Gleb Garanich)
Filipetti warned the targeting of civilian areas created heightened security risks as Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day, more than four years into Russia's full-scale invasion.

Several European leaders traveled to Kyiv for Ukraine’s Independence Day events, including European Council President António Costa and leaders from Finland, Lithuania, Norway, Denmark, Estonia and Latvia.
Filipetti said the high-level participation underscored continued international support for Ukraine.
TRUMP'S TURKEY ARMS SALE PROPOSAL SPARKS CONGRESSIONAL QUESTIONS BEFORE NATO SUMMIT

Ukrainian authorities urged citizens to stay vigilant on public transport and guard against potential sabotage or sharing media that could reveal military positions, as well as possible attacks, Ukrainian News reported. (HENRY NICHOLLS / Pool via REUTERS)

"Independence Day is a really important moment for the allies of the Ukrainians to really show that we are not losing steam, that we continue to support their operations, to continue to support their sovereignty," Filipetti said. "But anytime there's massive public gatherings, particularly to demonstrate patriotism and support for the Ukrainian state, it increases the security risk."

Ukrainian authorities urged citizens to stay vigilant on public transport and guard against potential sabotage or sharing media that could reveal military positions, as well as possible attacks, Ukrainian News reported.
"They should be particularly mindful about sharing any videos or photographs that could betray the locations of some of their frontline soldiers," Filipetti warned.
DRONE OFFENSIVE HITS RUSSIAN OIL TANKERS AND REFINERIES AT 'INDUSTRIAL SCALE' AS MOSCOW BANS DIESEL EXPORTS

Russian glide bombs strike food processing plant in Zaporizhzhia Rescuers work at the site of a reported strike on a food processing plant in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on July 8, 2026.  (Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Monday's holiday came after a lethal exchange of drone and missile strikes. Ukrainian officials reported at least seven deaths from Russian attacks, while a Ukrainian drone strike in Russia's Krasnodar region killed three, according to Russian officials, The Associated Press reported.

"The Russians really want to bleed the Ukrainians of people, equipment, and will before the Russians are bled of those same three things," Filipetti said. "And what we've seen over the course of this year is almost no territorial gains on behalf of the Russians."
They are losing more soldiers each month than they can recruit, forcing them to rely on North Korean, Cuban and other foreign fighters to fill the gap, Filipetti added.
ZELENSKYY SAYS PUTIN 'LOST THE INITIATIVE' AS UKRAINE'S TECH INDUSTRY RESHAPES THE WAR

President Vladimir Putin prioritizes Russia's nuclear triad strengthening as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warns the Russian leader has launched "World War III." (Genya SAVILOV / AFP via Getty ImagesContributor / Getty Images)
"Remember, Putin thought that this was going to be a special military operation that was going to last a matter of weeks," Filipetti said.
Ultimately, she emphasized that Ukraine's resolve delivers a firm deterrent beyond Moscow.

"It sends a message to the Russians that any invasion of sovereign territory, like their invasion of Ukraine, is going to create more consequences for them," Filipetti said. "We are not losing steam, and we continue to support their operations, to continue to support their sovereignty."
Filipetti said it also sends an important message to other American adversaries like China.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"These adversaries of the United States really learned from how the United States handles conflicts in other theaters. It's really important that our adversaries of China, Russia, Iran, and others understand that if they invade another country unilaterally, there are going to be consequences, not rewards."

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Iran tried to assassinate one of Netanyahu's sons, prime minister says
summary: Benjamin Netanyahu claims Iran tried to murder one of his sons, urging enhanced protection for prime ministerial candidates during the election campaign.
story: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warns Iran of a forceful response to any future attacks, emphasizing Israel's right to self-defense after recent clashes. The segment explores the volatile Middle East situation, including Iran's use of Hezbollah and the US administration's role in fostering regional alliances. Internal protests against the Iranian government are also discussed.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused Iran of attempting to assassinate one of his sons on Monday.
Netanyahu made the accusation during an interview with Israel's Channel 14, saying he has asked Israeli law enforcement to boost protection measures for any prime ministerial candidate.
"This is an unbelievable case. Iran targeted one of my sons. Iran tried to murder him, tried to murder one of my sons," Netanyahu told the station, as reported by the Jerusalem Post.

title: Massive garbage heap collapses onto homes, killing at least 30 as rescuers search for survivors
summary: A mountain of garbage collapsed after heavy rain at a major landfill site in Conakry, Guinea, burying nearby homes and launching a search for survivors.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
At least 30 people were killed in a massive landslide in Guinea on Sunday when a mountainous open-air landfill collapsed and buried nearby shacks, trapping numerous victims beneath a mass of garbage.
The incident happened at Dar Es Salam, the largest waste dump in the West African country's capital, Conakry, according to a report from The Associated Press (AP).
Guinea News reported that the weight of the waste caused a three-story building beneath it to cave in.
Authorities said heavy rainfall also washed over the refuse overnight, creating hazardous conditions at the landfill, according to the AP.
EARTHQUAKE SHAKES PERU'S ANDES REGION, KILLING AT LEAST 5, DISPLACING HUNDREDS
Residents and rescuers use an excavator to search for victims after a landslide struck the Dar Es Salam dumpsite in Conakry, Guinea, on Aug. 23, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
Six people were seriously injured and several homes were destroyed in the incident, according to reports. Officials launched a search-and-rescue operation to find any survivors.

The AP reported that the landfill was originally scheduled to close Sunday after officials warned of hazardous conditions, citing Lt. Col. Baldé Mamadou Bailo, the sanitation officer for the military engineering battalion.
The decision followed reports of a similar incident at the landfill in recent years, raising concerns about its safety.
Thirty people were killed and six others seriously injured after a landslide struck the Dar Es Salam dumpsite in Conakry, Guinea, on Aug. 23, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
As a precautionary measure, residents who lived near the site had also been given eviction notices and were forced to vacate the area, the AP said.
However, many people remained nearby at the time of the disaster, according to reports.

"We will ensure that the remaining families are relocated elsewhere," Dienabou Touré, the minister of territorial administration and decentralization, said at the scene, according to the AP.
Reuters reported that the landfill suffered a similar incident in 2017, when torrential rains caused a mudslide that killed at least eight people.

title: Mexican governor facing US drug charges seeks leave just one day after returning to office
summary: Embattled Sinaloa Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya's abrupt reversal follows pointed remarks from Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum about putting nation above personal interest.
story: Mexican Senator Lilly Tellez discusses the indictment of a Sinaloa governor and nine officials for alleged fentanyl trafficking. She blasts President Claudia Sheinbaum's refusal to extradite, asserting Mexico operates as a 'narco-state.' Tellez warns of deep corruption and the dire implications for bilateral relations and border security.

Embattled Sinaloa, Mexico, Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya abruptly requested an indefinite leave of absence Saturday, just one day after returning to office following a three-month absence triggered by U.S. drug trafficking charges against him.
Rocha, 77, shared a letter on social media asking for "temporary leave of an indefinite nature, for more than 30 days" from his position as governor.
The letter, dated Aug. 22 and stamped received by the Sinaloa State Congress that day, does not say when Rocha plans to return or why he is stepping away again.
MEXICAN SENATOR ACCUSES SHEINBAUM OF SHIELDING 'NARCO-POLITICIANS' AFTER US CARTEL INDICTMENT

Sinaloa Gov. Ruben Rocha Moya speaks as he leaves the inauguration ceremony of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum in Mexico City, Mexico, on Oct. 1, 2024. (Jose Luis Torales/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
The request came just a day after Rocha announced his return and said it was his "duty to fulfill the mandate" of voters who elected him to serve through Oct. 31, 2027.
"Today, I return to the exercise of my responsibility as Governor of Sinaloa with a clear conscience and head held high, with the strength of truth on our side," Rocha wrote Friday on X.
Rocha said he spent 112 days away from office while making himself available to Mexican authorities investigating what he called "false accusations" by the U.S. government.
He said he personally appeared before Mexico’s Attorney General’s Office and answered investigators’ questions.

Rocha insisted the investigation had produced no evidence that he committed a crime and accused political opponents in Mexico and abroad of trying to damage both the country’s sovereignty and the left-wing movement he represents.
MEXICAN PRESIDENT IN THE DARK ABOUT DRUG OPERATION AFTER WHICH US, MEXICAN OFFICIALS WERE KILLED
"I am unrelated to and innocent of the fabrications woven against me," Rocha wrote.
Rocha’s return Friday did not get a warm reception from Mexico’s ruling Morena party or the government of President Claudia Sheinbaum.

Morena said it had no advance knowledge of Rocha’s decision and distanced itself from the move, according to Reuters. Mexico’s Interior Ministry said returning to office was Rocha’s decision alone and noted that the attorney general’s investigation remained open.
5 MEXICAN CARTEL BOSSES CHARGED IN WEAPONS, DRUG TRAFFICKING, TIMESHARE FRAUD SCHEMES, DOJ SAYS
Sheinbaum also posted a pointed message on X.
"No personal interest can ever stand above the interests of the people and the Nation," she wrote.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum responded to Rocha's return to office on Saturday. (Daniel Cardenas/Getty Images)
"Mexico deserves public servants who understand that positions are temporary, but responsibility to the Nation is eternal," Sheinbaum added.

U.S. prosecutors charged Rocha and nine other current and former officials in April with drug trafficking and related weapons offenses. The current and former high-ranking government and law enforcement officials are alleged to have partnered with the Sinaloa cartel to distribute massive quantities of narcotics to the United States.
U.S. prosecutors charged Rocha and nine other current and former officials in April with drug trafficking and related weapons offenses linked to the Sinaloa cartel. (Solidago/Getty Images)
Rocha is the first sitting Mexican governor to face charges from the U.S., according to Reuters.

title: Hormuz crisis hides a deeper oil threat that could outlast the war
summary: Art Berman warns that 8 million barrels shut in near the Strait of Hormuz may never fully recover, even after a ceasefire reopens the waterway.
story: Art Berman says millions of barrels of production remain shut in and warns some wells could take months to restart — while others may never fully recover.

As global attention remains fixed on tankers moving through the Strait of Hormuz, a petroleum geologist is warning that the more consequential energy story may be unfolding thousands of feet underground — and could continue long after any political agreement ends the fighting.

Art Berman, a petroleum geologist and energy consultant with more than four decades of industry experience, told Fox News Digital that millions of barrels of Persian Gulf oil production remain shut in and warned that restoring those wells is far more complicated than simply reopening the strategic waterway.
"This is potentially a kind of a world-changing event, even if we resolve the political issues," Berman said.

"The bigger story and the more important one long term is that 8 million barrels of Persian Gulf production is currently shut in and world production is down about 10 million barrels a day," Berman explained.

In an aerial view, Marathon Petroleum Corp's Los Angeles Refinery, one of the largest oil refineries in North America, operates as gas prices rocket upward due to worldwide oil supply disruptions caused by the U.S. and Israeli attack on Iran, on March 10, 2026 in Carson, California. (David McNew/Getty Images)

"We can move tankers around and we can obsess about, you know, are there 4 million barrels getting through or are there 6 million or 9 million or whatever the right number is," he added. "But eventually, those tankers have to be filled with oil."

A White House official, speaking on background, pointed to the sharp decline in oil prices following the signing of the MOU and said the Strait of Hormuz is open, with the U.S. naval blockade in full effect.

Berman's estimate of Gulf shut-ins is broadly consistent with the latest assessment from the International Energy Agency. The IEA said in its Aug. 12, 2026, Oil Market Report, "Gulf oil production rose by a further 2.5 mb/d in July to 23.9 mb/d, still 8.3 mb/d below pre-war levels."
Global oil supply remained 6.3 million bpd below year-earlier levels, according to the agency.
The U.S. Energy Information Administration offers a somewhat different estimate.

EIA assessed production shut-ins at an average 5.5 million bpd in July, while warning that continuing constraints on Hormuz transit had forced the agency to increase its forecast for shut-in production in August. EIA expects production and trade patterns to generally return to pre-conflict conditions in early 2027, but says some Gulf producers may not regain their previous output during its forecast period.
Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, on Aug. 3, 2026. (Reuters)

The distinction is important because much of the public discussion has centered on what the industry calls the midstream problem — whether tankers can safely transport oil through Hormuz — while Berman argues that the upstream problem of producing the oil itself could prove more enduring.
"The very last thing in the world I ever want to do is to shut in a well," Berman told Fox News Digital.

Restarting a well requires restoring communication between equipment at the surface and reservoirs thousands of feet underground, he explained, and extended shutdowns can create complications inside the reservoir and well.
"This is not like turning on a switch for a light bulb," Berman said. "It's a complicated, high-risk, relatively long-term process, and we don't know the outcome."

Berman estimated that roughly 80% of affected wells could return close to their previous production levels, although he said that could take weeks or months. He said many of the remainder could require additional engineering work and some could ultimately produce at lower rates.
"Some of that production will never come back," he predicted.
Other energy analysts agree that restarting Gulf production presents substantial technical challenges. But Wood Mackenzie is more optimistic than Berman about the ultimate recovery.

Its analysis projects that fields affected by the Hormuz closure could return to approximately 70% of their previous production within three months and 90% within six months, assuming a controlled restart. The final roughly 1 million bpd could take considerably longer.
Oil tankers and cargo ships line up in the Strait of Hormuz as seen from Khor Fakkan, United Arab Emirates, Wednesday, March 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Altaf Qadri)
Berman also warned against assuming that a ceasefire or political agreement would immediately restore pre-war energy flows.

Shipowners, insurers and crews would first have to become confident that tankers could safely navigate the waterway, while other logistical and security issues could continue even after governments reached an agreement.
"A simple political agreement doesn't mean the problem's over," Berman said.
Berman's argument goes considerably further than predicting a slow oil-market recovery.
He contends that the Persian Gulf conflict represents a fundamental shock to the global energy and economic system — one whose consequences will persist even after the immediate crisis ends.

Asked about his comparison with the COVID-19 pandemic, Berman told Fox News Digital that the scale of oil production affected by the current crisis makes it comparable to the largest economic disruptions of recent years.
"This is not just a news cycle," Berman said. "This is potentially a kind of a world-changing event, even if we resolve the political issues."
IRAN DEAL CLOCK HITS ZERO AS TRUMP DEMANDS ‘WHITE FLAG’ WITH NEW PRESSURE CAMPAIGN LOOMING
The ConocoPhillips Oil Refinery is seen in Wilmington, California on April 11, 2026. (Etienne Laurent / AFP via Getty Images)
The United States is the world's largest oil producer, but Berman argues that does not isolate American consumers from the disruption.
"The oil market and the refined products market is global," he told Fox News Digital.

Berman noted that U.S. refineries require different grades of crude to produce the country's mix of gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other petroleum products, meaning domestic production alone cannot eliminate America's exposure to international markets.
"The problem for the U.S. isn't that we don't have enough oil, we almost do," Berman said. "It's that the oil we have isn't the right kind" for everything American refineries produce.

EIA reported July 15 that Hormuz disruptions had already pushed international buyers toward alternative sources of petroleum products, contributing to higher U.S. refinery margins, production and exports.

Whether that recovery proceeds as EIA expects or encounters the technical obstacles Berman warns about could determine how long the economic consequences of the conflict linger after the shooting stops.
For Berman, the question is no longer simply when tankers return to Hormuz. It is whether the global energy system that emerges afterward will ever operate quite the way it did before.

The White House pushed back on concerns that the disruption represents a lasting threat to U.S. energy security, pointing to record American production and blaming Iran for instability in the critical shipping corridor.

"Thanks to President Trump, the United States is now the world’s number-one producer and exporter of oil and gas. Record oil and gas production strengthens our energy independence and national security," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital.

"The Iranian regime’s terrorist actions in the Strait of Hormuz have proven that our allies need to invest in reliable, affordable, and secure energy sources and advance new partnerships with the United States that enhance the world’s energy security," Rogers added.
Children swim as ships are seen anchored in the Strait of Hormuz on August 10, 2026 off the coast of Bandar Abbas, Iran. ( )
Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House, U.S. Energy Information Administration and Defense Intelligence Agency for comment.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Woman in her 30s who pretended to be a child and lived with family found guilty of fraud

story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
A woman in Brazil was found guilty this week of living with a foster family for more than a year while pretending to be a child, officials said.

Amanda Maria Souza de Oliveira, who is in reality 37 years old, was convicted of fraud and false identity on Thursday, according to a translated release from the Court of Justice of Santa Catarina in Brazil.
Oliveira, who the family took in as their daughter for 14 months until her scheme was uncovered, claimed she had fled abuse.
FEDS BUST ONE OF LARGEST ALLEGED MARRIAGE FRAUD SCHEMES IN US HISTORY INVOLVING 1,000-PLUS CHINESE SHAM UNIONS
Amanda Maria Souza de Oliveira was convicted of fraud and false identity in Brazil. (Campo Grande Civil Police)

COLLEGE FOOTBALL NATIONAL CHAMPION WHO WORE WIGS IN FRAUD SCHEME PLEADS GUILTY TO CHARGES
She was sentenced to one year, six months and 10 days in prison, along with four months and 18 days of detention.
One of her lawyers, Lúcio Sousa, said that Oliveira’s scheme was how she "survived."
Amanda Maria Souza de Oliveira was sentenced by a court in Brazil to one year, six months and 10 days in prison, along with four months and 18 days of detention for fraud and false identity. (iStock)
"She admits that she invented an identity," Sousa said before the verdict, according to the Post. "It was the way she found to survive. But she has been a vulnerable person for more than 20 years.

"She has lived on the streets, and there has been no allegation that she obtained any financial advantage, or committed robbery or theft, which, in theory, means the elements of fraud have not been established."
Oliveira said she never meant to hurt anyone.

Amanda Maria Souza de Oliveira is photographed in jail after she was convicted of fraud and false identity by pretending to be a child while living with a foster family in Brazil. (Campo Grande Civil Police)
She said she wanted to experience the love she never got as a child.

title: Portugal enacts 'burqa law' largely prohibiting face coverings in public
summary: Portuguese President António José Seguro has enacted a measure that bans people from covering up their face while in public places, with some exceptions, AFP reported.
story: Laura Ingraham, Jesse Watters, Sean Hannity and Greg Gutfeld bring Fox News viewers their fresh takes on the top news of the day.

Portuguese President António José Seguro has enacted a measure that largely prohibits individuals from covering up their faces while out in public, a restriction broadly viewed as aimed at Muslim women, according to AFP.

But the report noted various carve-outs to the prohibition, including for health, professional, artistic or weather-linked issues and for when people are at locations of worship, diplomatic missions or aboard planes.

title: A near-total lunar eclipse will be visible across the U.S. Thursday night
summary: Two weeks after a total solar eclipse wowed skywatchers in Europe, a near-total lunar eclipse is in store Thursday for people in North and South America.
story: Two weeks after a total solar eclipse wowed skywatchers in southern Europe, a near-total lunar eclipse is set to put on a show Thursday night for people across North and South America.

Lunar eclipses occur when Earth slips between the sun and the moon and casts a shadow on the lunar surface. During this week’s event, nearly the entire moon — 96.2% at the eclipse’s peak — will be shrouded in Earth’s shadow.
Weather permitting, skywatchers in the continental U.S. will have some of the best views. The eclipse will also be visible elsewhere in North America, South America, parts of Europe and Africa.

During the eclipse, Earth’s shadow will appear reddish orange on the lunar surface because of the way Earth’s atmosphere scatters light from the sun. That’s why a total lunar eclipse is also known as a “blood moon.”

Thursday’s eclipse will begin at 9:23 p.m. ET, when the moon first enters the outer part of Earth’s shadow. The real action gets underway, however, at 10:33 p.m. ET, when Earth’s shadow starts to envelop the lunar surface, appearing to take a “bite” out of the lunar disk.
The eclipse will peak at 12:12 a.m. ET, when more than 96% of the lunar surface will be shrouded. The event will end at 3:01 a.m. ET when the moon exits the outer edge of Earth’s shadow.

Most viewers in North and South America, except those in Alaska and the northernmost reaches of Canada, will have a chance to see every stage of the lunar eclipse. For those in Europe and Africa, however, the eclipse will begin early Friday, and the moon will set as the event is progressing.
Unlike solar eclipses, lunar eclipses can be viewed safely with the naked eye, and skywatchers can use binoculars and telescopes to catch more dramatic views.

The lunar eclipse follows a total solar eclipse — when the sun, the moon and Earth align, with the moon passing in front of the sun and blocking its light — that darkened skies in Spain, a small part of Portugal, Greenland, Iceland and northern Russia.

Solar and lunar eclipses usually come in pairs because of the fortuitous way the moon, Earth and sun interact. The three celestial bodies happen to align from our perspective on Earth because the sun is 400 times farther from Earth than the moon, while also being 400 times bigger. That makes them appear the same size in the sky.
Solar eclipses occur during the new moon phase. Typically around two weeks later, when the moon is on the other side of Earth from the sun, lunar eclipses occur during the full moon phase.

The next solar eclipse, on Feb. 6, will be visible in parts of South America and Africa. The next lunar eclipse will occur overnight from Feb. 20 to 21. It should be visible in North and South America, Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia and Antarctica, according to NASA.

title: Panda Express’ CEOs are on a ‘mission’ to help workers achieve the dream of home ownership
summary: Panda Express founders Andrew and Peggy Cherng want to be known for helping their workers build careers and eventually buy their own homes.
story: Panda Express is famous for its orange chicken. But the founders of the iconic fast-casual Asian chain also want to be known for something else: helping their workers realize the American dream.

“I always believe that when you do well, you know, personally, then you can go out and take care of other people,” said Andrew Cherng, who is co-founder, co-chair and co-CEO of Panda Express along with his wife, Peggy Cherng.
“You want people to do well,” he said. “And you want to treat them well.”

Cherng measures progress in part by how many of his managers make $100,000 or more annually. He also tracks whether those managers can afford to buy homes, and he considers that a barometer of his own success.
Yet over the past decade, that American dream of homeownership has slipped out of reach for millions of middle-class families.
With low housing stock across the country, mortgage rates hovering at 6.8% and home prices in some cities at record levels, there is little relief in sight.

Immigrant families are also less likely to own their homes than families headed by native-born U.S. residents, according to census data. Experts point to several factors that are likely to contribute to the disparity, including limited employment and income prospects, language barriers and inconsistent access to banks and financing.
Peggy Cherng said the couple recognize elements of their own journeys in those of their employees. “Most of our associates are first-generation immigrants,” she said.
Andrew was born in China and immigrated to the U.S. in 1966 after having grown up in Taiwan and Japan. Peggy was born in Myanmar and raised in Hong Kong.

The couple met at the University of Missouri and opened their first Panda Express in 1983 in Glendale, California. At the time, they envisioned it as a casual offshoot of Panda Inn, the full-service Chinese restaurant Andrew opened with his father in the early 1970s.
That immigrant experience remains central to how the couple run the business today, particularly a focus on investing in their employees, whom they consider their extended family.

Today, Panda Express is America’s largest Asian restaurant chain, with more than 2,500 locations across 49 states and restaurants in 12 countries. The privately held company employs around 55,000 people and generates around $7 billion in annual sales, according to data compiled by market research firm Technomic.
For Andrew, the foundation of that success is built from the ground up — starting with his employees.
“How do we help these people to have a better life? That’s our mission,” he said in an interview at the company’s headquarters outside Los Angeles, part of NBC News’ “Business in America” initiative.

Peggy said, “Our mission, our calling, is how we are able to help more associates realize their American dream, establish their business, their career, but most importantly, mark that accomplishment by owning a home.”
And despite the long list of obstacles to first-time homeownership, Andrew wants to help his Panda Express employees focus on what is possible rather than what stands in their way.
“We actually help everybody to think about owning a home very quickly,” he said.
Many of the managers he hires initially seem to view the position as just another job, he said, not a potential career path.
Managers “have to do a lot of things,” he said. “We teach them [those skills], but to have a good life, you turn that person from being sort of ‘task-based’ to ‘life-based.’”
That transformation, according to Andrew, often instills a deeper sense of purpose in his employees — one that extends to caring for others and their communities.
“We get people to see that quickly and see it clearly,” he said.

title: Secret Service officials placed on leave in inquiry over ‘potential misconduct’
summary: Secret Service communications director Anthony Guglielmi has been placed on leave, two sources familiar with the matter told NBC News on Wednesday.
story: Secret Service communications director Anthony Guglielmi has been placed on leave, two sources familiar with the matter told NBC News on Wednesday.
The news comes as a Secret Service spokesperson revealed that three officials who are not law enforcement personnel were put on leave pending an investigation into potential misconduct.

Gregg Bernstein, a spokesperson for Guglielmi, did not expressly say he was on leave, saying merely that he is a “professional of deep integrity whose decades-long public record advocating for local, state and federal agencies speaks for itself.”
“He holds profound respect for the mission and work of the United States Secret Service and is cooperating fully with everything being asked of him,” Bernstein said in a statement.
CNN first reported the inquiry.

In its statement, the Secret Service did not disclose what prompted the investigation or identify the officials. It said it will continue to “pursue the level of excellence that is worthy” of the organization’s mission.

“The U.S. Secret Service is committed to upholding the highest standards of professionalism and integrity in fulfilling our zero-fail mission of protecting the President and other high-level government officials,” it said.
The spokesperson added, “Our critical work demands that our workforce maintain an unwavering commitment to duty, honesty, and courage in all aspects of their jobs.”

Guglielmi was named communications director in March 2022. He testified before the House Jan. 6 committee later that year, discussing former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson’s testimony to the panel.

title: Gary, Indiana, nears full power restoration more than 2 weeks after violent storms
summary: A powerful derecho struck northern Indiana and other parts of the Midwest on Aug. 11, knocking out power to tens of thousands.
story: More than two weeks after violent storms wiped out power to thousands of customers, the lights and air conditioners were finally back on Wednesday for almost all residents of Gary, Indiana.
As of Wednesday evening, just over 100 utility customers in the city of 69,000 were still experiencing outages, according to the Northern Indiana Public Service Co., known as NIPSCO.

“Storm restoration efforts related to the Aug. 11 storm and subsequent weather events are substantially complete,” the company said in an update on its website Wednesday morning. “While crews continue working through a limited number of individual outage cases, restoration activities have concluded across the broader service territory.”

A derecho — a storm that can produce tornado-strength winds — struck Indiana and other parts of the Midwest with straight-line winds of 70 to 100-plus mph on the morning of Aug. 11, the National Weather Service said.

It tore down power lines and inflicted what NIPSCO called “the worst damage in known company history,” knocking out power to 80% of its customers, around 375,000. Fewer than 150 outages remained Wednesday night in the rest of the company’s service area.

In addition to the derecho, there were also tornadoes, including a 26-mile-long EF2 twister that touched down in Illinois and went into Indiana, according to the National Weather Service. That tornado had an estimated peak wind of 110 mph, and it damaged roofs and uprooted trees, the agency said.
NIPSCO had come under fire for the long delay in restoring power.
In an address Sunday, Gary Mayor Eric Melton said, “The current pace of restoration is unacceptable.”

Some residents of Gary, a Rust Belt city on the shore of Lake Michigan, around 25 miles southeast of Chicago, described people sleeping in their running cars with the air conditioning on to get some relief from the heat.

Calvin Boone, 44, said this week that generators have been stolen in his neighborhood. Joetta Walker, 73, who has asthma, said that with no power, she hadn’t been able to use her nebulizer and had to rely on an inhaler to help her breathe.

Other Gary residents who spoke to NBC News this week said they couldn’t help but wonder whether the reason their city’s power was getting restored last was because it’s a mostly Black city. An executive at NIPSCO’s parent company told The Associated Press that the outages were a result of where the storm hit and had “nothing to do with race or any type of division.”
Add to Google
Add to Google
Gov. Mike Braun, a Republican elected in 2024, criticized the utility company’s response and called for an investigation to be launched.

“NIPSCO is a monopoly utility that Hoosiers pay every month with the expectation that it will use its considerable resources to maintain its system, prepare for severe weather and restore service as quickly as possible when disaster strikes,” Braun said in a news release Monday.
“NIPSCO has failed to keep its end of the bargain,” he said.
Braun said Tuesday that President Donald Trump had approved a request for a major disaster declaration. The declaration allows more aid.
There were seven storm-related deaths in Indiana, according to a count of official reports by NBC News.
One was in Lake County, where Gary is; two were in Delaware County; and one person each died in Jennings, Porter, LaPorte and Henry counties, according to officials and family members.
NIPSCO President and CEO Vince Parisi earlier asked for patience.

“This was the worst damage we have ever seen, and we are grateful for the patience from our customers,” Parisi said in a statement Tuesday. “Thanks to thousands of people working around the clock, restoration is complete, and we’re now focused on supporting the communities still recovering.”

title: A near-total lunar eclipse will be visible across the U.S. Thursday night
summary: Two weeks after a total solar eclipse wowed skywatchers in Europe, a near-total lunar eclipse is in store Thursday for people in North and South America.
story: Two weeks after a total solar eclipse wowed skywatchers in southern Europe, a near-total lunar eclipse is set to put on a show Thursday night for people across North and South America.

Lunar eclipses occur when Earth slips between the sun and the moon and casts a shadow on the lunar surface. During this week’s event, nearly the entire moon — 96.2% at the eclipse’s peak — will be shrouded in Earth’s shadow.
Weather permitting, skywatchers in the continental U.S. will have some of the best views. The eclipse will also be visible elsewhere in North America, South America, parts of Europe and Africa.

During the eclipse, Earth’s shadow will appear reddish orange on the lunar surface because of the way Earth’s atmosphere scatters light from the sun. That’s why a total lunar eclipse is also known as a “blood moon.”

Thursday’s eclipse will begin at 9:23 p.m. ET, when the moon first enters the outer part of Earth’s shadow. The real action gets underway, however, at 10:33 p.m. ET, when Earth’s shadow starts to envelop the lunar surface, appearing to take a “bite” out of the lunar disk.
The eclipse will peak at 12:12 a.m. ET, when more than 96% of the lunar surface will be shrouded. The event will end at 3:01 a.m. ET when the moon exits the outer edge of Earth’s shadow.

Most viewers in North and South America, except those in Alaska and the northernmost reaches of Canada, will have a chance to see every stage of the lunar eclipse. For those in Europe and Africa, however, the eclipse will begin early Friday, and the moon will set as the event is progressing.
Unlike solar eclipses, lunar eclipses can be viewed safely with the naked eye, and skywatchers can use binoculars and telescopes to catch more dramatic views.

The lunar eclipse follows a total solar eclipse — when the sun, the moon and Earth align, with the moon passing in front of the sun and blocking its light — that darkened skies in Spain, a small part of Portugal, Greenland, Iceland and northern Russia.

Solar and lunar eclipses usually come in pairs because of the fortuitous way the moon, Earth and sun interact. The three celestial bodies happen to align from our perspective on Earth because the sun is 400 times farther from Earth than the moon, while also being 400 times bigger. That makes them appear the same size in the sky.
Solar eclipses occur during the new moon phase. Typically around two weeks later, when the moon is on the other side of Earth from the sun, lunar eclipses occur during the full moon phase.

The next solar eclipse, on Feb. 6, will be visible in parts of South America and Africa. The next lunar eclipse will occur overnight from Feb. 20 to 21. It should be visible in North and South America, Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia and Antarctica, according to NASA.

title: PGA Tour CEO blasts ‘concerning’ ad depicting a man shoving a female golfer
summary: Good Good Golf took down the ad, saying it “depicted actions that are not aligned with our values as a brand.” PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp called the brand’s response “disappointing.”
story: Good Good Golf is facing the wrath of the golf industry after it posted a controversial ad that depicted one of its co-founders shoving a female golfer to the ground.

The commercial, which promoted Good Good Golf and Callaway Golf’s Quantum Driver collaboration and has since been taken down, sparked outrage online, with viewers saying it appeared to promote domestic violence and violence against women.
PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp condemned the commercial Tuesday, calling it “concerning” and “clearly not aligned with PGA Tour values.”

The commercial showed golfer Alexis Miestowski trying to grab a driver out of a golf bag, only to be shoved to the ground by Good Good Golf co-founder Garrett Clark. After having pushed her, he stands over her and warns: “Do not touch my new driver.”
Good Good Golf said in a statement Saturday that the ad “ultimately depicted actions that are not aligned with our values as a brand.”
“We have since taken that content down, and sincerely apologize,” it said.
The public, however, wasn’t pacified by the apology. Neither were some sponsors.

An X user responded to Good Good Golf’s statement, “Why would a company take the time to shoot, produce, and then put out a video on all their social channels that isn’t aligned with their values as a brand?”

Good Good Golf started out as a YouTube channel and grew into an independent media and apparel company. The premiere Tuesday night of its Golf Channel reality show, “Big Break X Good Good,” was postponed because one of the sponsors wanted to drop out following the ad fallout.
PGA Tour leadership didn’t buy the apology statement, either.
Rolapp told reporters Tuesday that Good Good Golf’s initial response was “disappointing” and “a bit defensive and late.”
“But I think the responses are getting better. I think we’ve seen some things this morning; we had some conversations with them,” Rolapp continued. “But no, we were disappointed with what we saw.”
He said the PGA Tour will continue to “monitor” and work with Good Good Golf. It comes at a critical time as Good Good Golf is the title sponsor of a new PGA Tour event in Austin, Texas, this fall.

On Wednesday, Clark posted an 8-minute video in which he admitted the ad was “in poor taste.” He said the hate the ad received was “very justified” and appeared to cast blame to the company’s marketing department.

“The way that this ad was received is not how Good Good is, and it’s not what we stand for,” he said. “I do sincerely apologize for playing the role that I did in that ad, and I want you guys to know that I in no way, shape, or form support DV abuse or anything of the sort.”
He said the Good Good marketing team had pitched the ad as a spinoff of this year’s horror film “Obsession” and Clark’s character would be “obsessed” with the driver.
Clark noted Miestowski has received an onslaught of online hate following the ad, which he called “completely unacceptable.”
“If you guys have any hatred or comments that you’re wanting to send our way, put it towards Good Good, put it towards me personally,” he said.

Clark acknowledged the backlash has raised plenty of “very very valid points” and spurred “important conversations,” especially regarding gender in the sport, which has been predominantly male. He stressed Good Good has been dedicated to “including women in all of our content and pushing our women’s side of the game in hopes to grow the game of golf.”

“Hopefully, you guys can forgive Good Good as well as myself for being a part of it. And hopefully we can move on and grow the women’s side of golf because that is one of our huge, huge goals,” he concluded his video.
Callaway Golf CEO Chip Brewer also apologized for the ad Saturday, saying, “While the video was produced by Good Good, it was approved by Callaway prior to voting.”
“That approval should never have happened. Mistakes were made, and we are taking the matter very seriously,” he continued.

Brewer apologized for the video, saying, “To be clear: we are unequivocally against discrimination, domestic violence, or threatening behavior of any kind.” He said the company is also conducting internal and external investigations and has changed its approval processes to ensure “this will never happen again.”
While Good Good Golf and Callaway are mired in the controversy, another brand is turning it into its marketing punch line.
Parsons Xtreme Golf shared an ad Tuesday showing various women golfing, with the caption: “Our drivers play nice with everyone. #SheGolfs.”

title: Military trial date set for alleged mastermind of Sept. 11 attacks
summary: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, who has been held at Guantánamo Bay since 2006, is scheduled to go on trial in June 2028.
story: A military judge ruled Wednesday that the man accused of being the mastermind behind the 9/11 attacks will stand trial starting in June 2028.
Khalid Sheikh Mohammed will be prosecuted alongside others suspected of conspiring in the attacks: Walid bin Attash, Ali Abdul Aziz Ali and Mustafa Ahmed al-Hawsawi.

Mohammed is accused of orchestrating the plot to crash hijacked planes into the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon on Sept. 11, 2001. A fourth plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania during the attacks.
He has been held at the U.S. naval base at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, since 2006.
Air Force Lt. Col. Michael Schrama, a military commissions judge, on Wednesday rejected the January 2027 start date proposed by prosecutors and instead set the trial date for about 18 months later.

The trial date was announced after a split federal appeals court last summer threw out a potential agreement that would have allowed Mohammed to plead guilty in exchange for sparing him the risk of execution.
Mohammed was charged and arraigned in 2008 with war crimes and murder in connection with the nearly 3,000 people who died in the 9/11 attacks.

The road to prosecute Mohammed and other conspirators has dragged on for years, with the Obama-era military commissions system being tested for the first time — at times leading to lengthy challenges to its rules.

Defense lawyers have also argued that the holdup comes from what they say are the government’s efforts to hide details of torture used against detainees at secret CIA prisons before they were transferred to Guantánamo Bay.
Mohammed was captured in Pakistan in 2003 before being transferred to Guantánamo Bay three years later.

A Senate report from 2014 found that the CIA had used what it called “enhanced interrogation techniques” against Mohammed and other conspirators, including waterboarding Mohammed 183 times in what was described as “a series of near-drownings.”

title: Serena and Venus Williams set to play doubles together at U.S. Open
summary: Serena and Venus Williams received a wild card to play doubles together at the U.S. Open next week, the United States Tennis Association announced.
story: Four years after a pseudo-retirement, Serena Williams is back in the U.S. Open for a shot at redemption. And this time, she’s teaming up with her older sister, Venus.
The Williams sisters got a wild card Wednesday and will play doubles together next week, the U.S. Tennis Association announced.
It will be the 10th time the pair have played alongside each other in the U.S. Open, a doubles event they have won twice, in 1999 and 2009. The duo have captured 14 major titles together.

Serena Williams, 44, teamed up with 23-year-old phenom Carlos Alcaraz in a dramatic mixed doubles run Tuesday. Both returning from injury, Williams and Alcaraz — who boasts seven Grand Slam singles titles — wowed fans with dazzling rallies and impassioned play in an opening-round win before they were knocked out in the quarterfinals by Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli.
After the loss, Williams told NBC News she was just happy to be back on the court.

“It felt great,” she said. “I haven’t played a ton of tennis, but it still felt good to kind of get back out there and just kind of feel your groove. I honestly never, ever thought I would be back here playing tennis. So it’s kind of surreal.”

Williams is widely considered the greatest women’s tennis player of all time. She has 39 Grand Slam titles (23 singles, 14 women’s doubles and two mixed doubles) and spent 319 weeks ranked No. 1 in the world. Along with Steffi Graf, she is one of only two women to win all four Grand Slam singles titles and an Olympic singles gold medal.
Though she never officially retired, she said she was “evolving away from tennis” in 2022.
Alcaraz, the world No. 3 player, called it a “privilege” to play alongside Williams this week at the U.S. Open.
“I felt the pressure,” he said. “It’s kind of as if I was playing the final of the Grand Slam. I just loved it, and I enjoyed every single second.”
Alcaraz is coming off a four-month layoff following a right wrist injury he sustained at the Barcelona Open in April.

Williams, meanwhile, returned to competitive tennis in June after a four-year break, only to injure her right knee during her first-round singles match at Wimbledon. Given the time away from the game and additional recovery, she said, her relationship with the game has evolved.

“My relationship with tennis is like a love-hate thing,” she told NBC News. “I love it, and then I hate to lose. ... But it’s definitely more fun now. I just try my best not to put as much pressure on myself.”
The first round of the women’s doubles tournament begins Sept. 3.

What is the best way to clean a dishwasher?

The best way to deep clean a dishwasher involves hand washing the different components of the machine, including the racks, filter and spray arms. I spoke with Ryan Knoll, the owner of cleaning company TidyCasa, for the best step-by-step way to clean a dishwasher. Here’s what he recommends:

Remove the racks, spray arms and filter from the dishwasher. Use mild dish soap, a scrub brush and warm, soapy water to scrub them. If needed, use a toothbrush to scrub parts of the filter. Rinse the racks, spray arms and filter with water and set those aside.

Wipe away any debris from the bottom of the dishwasher. With mild dish soap and a scrub brush, scrub the interior of the dishwasher with warm soapy water. Add the racks, spray arms and filter back into the dishwasher.

Fill a dishwasher-safe measuring cup with one cup of distilled white vinegar and place it on the top rack of the dishwasher, making sure it’s sitting upright. Close the dishwasher and run it on the hottest cycle. Remove the vinegar after the cycle is complete and then run the dishwasher again.

As an alternative to step three, use a dishwasher cleaner. Follow the instructions on the label. If you use the Finish Dishwasher Deep Cleaner or Glisten Dishwasher Cleaner, remove the top of the container, place the bottle upside down on the bottom rack or wherever it says in the directions and run the dishwasher on the hot water cycle. If you’re using a dishwasher cleaning tablet, then simply place it in the compartment before running the appliance.

If it’s a stainless steel dishwasher, use a stainless steel cleaning spray and microfiber cloth or stainless steel cleaning wipe to clean the outside of the dishwasher door. Otherwise, use mild dish soap and a damp microfiber cloth to wipe the outside. Wipe away the residue with a dry microfiber cloth.
How we picked the best products for cleaning a dishwasher

Your dishwasher may appear clean on the outside, but many of its parts — such as the filter and spray arms — collect debris and minerals over time. Our experts recommend keeping the following tips in mind when looking for products to clean a dishwasher:

Find specialized detergent: Dulude recommends against filling the detergent compartment of the dishwasher with regular liquid dish soap in general because it produces too much foam and suds. Instead use dishwasher detergents and/or tablets from brands like Finish, Affresh, Cascade and Glisten. These cleaners get rid of soap scum, food debris and limescale (residual minerals leftover from hard water), all of which are common causes of a smelly dishwasher. In fact, hard water residue buildup can decrease water pressure and affect the function of appliances, according to the United States Geological Survey. Go with acidic cleaning agents: You should also use acidic ingredients like distilled white vinegar to clean the inside of your dishwasher and its parts. That’s because the acidic nature of vinegar helps to lift and remove the stuck-on debris. Look for abrasive cleaning products: Abrasive ingredients and products, such as baking soda or a scrubbing brush, are ideal for cleaning parts of your dishwasher because they lift grime.
