How to keep a dishwasher clean

Once your dishwasher is clean, it’s important to maintain that cleanliness. Incorporating the simple steps below into your kitchen routine can help you stretch out the time between cleanings, which also saves you money on cleaners or ingredients in the long run.

Pre-rinse dishes: Even though some brands may say that rinsing dishes before putting them in the dishwasher isn’t necessary to get them clean, it’s still a good idea to rinse them to prevent small particles of food from getting stuck in the filter. This also helps prevent rotting food smells from forming in your appliance.Unload dishes immediately: You should remove the dishes from the machine as soon as the cycle finishes. That’s because, even though the dishes are technically clean, they can develop water stains. Using a rinse aid can also prevent this. Use a rinse aid: Speaking of rinse aids, picks like Finish Jet-Dry Rinse Aid, help your dishes dry faster, which ultimately prevents  them from developing hard water stains.

title: Gary, Indiana, nears full power restoration more than 2 weeks after violent storms
summary: A powerful derecho struck northern Indiana and other parts of the Midwest on Aug. 11, knocking out power to tens of thousands.
story: More than two weeks after violent storms wiped out power to thousands of customers, the lights and air conditioners were finally back on Wednesday for almost all residents of Gary, Indiana.
As of Wednesday evening, just over 100 utility customers in the city of 69,000 were still experiencing outages, according to the Northern Indiana Public Service Co., known as NIPSCO.

“Storm restoration efforts related to the Aug. 11 storm and subsequent weather events are substantially complete,” the company said in an update on its website Wednesday morning. “While crews continue working through a limited number of individual outage cases, restoration activities have concluded across the broader service territory.”

A derecho — a storm that can produce tornado-strength winds — struck Indiana and other parts of the Midwest with straight-line winds of 70 to 100-plus mph on the morning of Aug. 11, the National Weather Service said.

It tore down power lines and inflicted what NIPSCO called “the worst damage in known company history,” knocking out power to 80% of its customers, around 375,000. Fewer than 150 outages remained Wednesday night in the rest of the company’s service area.

In addition to the derecho, there were also tornadoes, including a 26-mile-long EF2 twister that touched down in Illinois and went into Indiana, according to the National Weather Service. That tornado had an estimated peak wind of 110 mph, and it damaged roofs and uprooted trees, the agency said.
NIPSCO had come under fire for the long delay in restoring power.
In an address Sunday, Gary Mayor Eric Melton said, “The current pace of restoration is unacceptable.”

Some residents of Gary, a Rust Belt city on the shore of Lake Michigan, around 25 miles southeast of Chicago, described people sleeping in their running cars with the air conditioning on to get some relief from the heat.

Calvin Boone, 44, said this week that generators have been stolen in his neighborhood. Joetta Walker, 73, who has asthma, said that with no power, she hadn’t been able to use her nebulizer and had to rely on an inhaler to help her breathe.

Other Gary residents who spoke to NBC News this week said they couldn’t help but wonder whether the reason their city’s power was getting restored last was because it’s a mostly Black city. An executive at NIPSCO’s parent company told The Associated Press that the outages were a result of where the storm hit and had “nothing to do with race or any type of division.”
Add to Google
Add to Google
Gov. Mike Braun, a Republican elected in 2024, criticized the utility company’s response and called for an investigation to be launched.

“NIPSCO is a monopoly utility that Hoosiers pay every month with the expectation that it will use its considerable resources to maintain its system, prepare for severe weather and restore service as quickly as possible when disaster strikes,” Braun said in a news release Monday.
“NIPSCO has failed to keep its end of the bargain,” he said.
Braun said Tuesday that President Donald Trump had approved a request for a major disaster declaration. The declaration allows more aid.
There were seven storm-related deaths in Indiana, according to a count of official reports by NBC News.
One was in Lake County, where Gary is; two were in Delaware County; and one person each died in Jennings, Porter, LaPorte and Henry counties, according to officials and family members.
NIPSCO President and CEO Vince Parisi earlier asked for patience.

“This was the worst damage we have ever seen, and we are grateful for the patience from our customers,” Parisi said in a statement Tuesday. “Thanks to thousands of people working around the clock, restoration is complete, and we’re now focused on supporting the communities still recovering.”

title: ‘Monster isn’t enough’: Family mourns 8 killed, including 4 kids, in Montana shooting
summary: A man killed eight relatives, including his sister and four children, at a family dinner in Montana weeks after his parents asked him to move out, authorities said Wednesday.
story: A man killed eight relatives, including his sister and four children, at a family dinner in Montana weeks after his parents asked him to move out, authorities said Wednesday.
The attack unfolded early Sunday evening on White Star Circle just outside Billings at a home owned by victims Dana Smith, 73, and Barbara Smith, 72, officials said.
The homeowners were killed along with Megan Ireland-Ghekiere, 39, and her four children, Owen Ireland, 13; Chloe Ireland, 7; Landon Ghekiere, 15; and Charlotte Ghekiere, 12, authorities said.
Evelyn Smith, 92 — whom interim Yellowstone County Sheriff Kent O’Donnell called the “family matriarch” — did not live at the home but was there Sunday for dinner. She was killed.
O’Donnell identified the shooter as Alan Michael Smith, 44, saying he carried out a “very complex” attack. He was found dead as authorities sought the killer.
Smith is the brother of victim Megan Ireland-Ghekiere and thus an uncle to all four of the younger victims, Billings police said.
Dana and Barbara Smith were the killer’s parents and Evelyn Smith was his grandmother, according to police.
Smith had once lived in that house and had been asked to move out weeks earlier, Brad Ireland — Megan Ireland-Ghekiere’s ex-husband — told The Associated Press.
O’Donnell confirmed that Alan Smith had once lived at the house but wasn’t residing there when the violence occurred Sunday.
“This is an ongoing criminal investigation with eight victims, making this very complex,” O’Donnell said.

The killings wiped out members from four generations, said Jennifer Mercer, a neighbor and family friend who set up an online fundraiser to help cover funeral costs and other expenses and was authorized to release the details.

Smith arrived at the home at about 5:49 p.m., and 11 minutes later neighbors believed they heard the sound of fireworks, officials said. That kind of noise, especially in the summer, wouldn’t necessarily alarm anyone, O’Donnell said.
But at 6:02 p.m., dispatchers received a call from a “female” voice inside the house, and Yellowstone County sheriff’s deputies arrived at 6:10 p.m., officials said.
The children were all very close and everyone got along, with their parents remaining amicable even after having divorced, according to Mercer.
“Charlotte was the hero that dialed 911,” Mercer said told NBC News in a statement. “She tried to save her family. She lived by her favorite quote, ‘I love you more.’”
When police officers and deputies arrived, they “confronted the suspect in the front yard, where he retreated into the house,” O’Donnell said.
More “gunshots were heard within the household” before the shooter went to the back of the property, O’Donnell said.
At about 6:13 p.m., a deputy “heard a final shot, which was broken away from the rest of the shots,” according to O’Donnell.
By about 6:22, police officers and sheriff’s deputies “made entrance into the backyard,” found a male victim there with a gunshot wound and began lifesaving measures on him, O’Donnell said.

“At this time, it wasn’t known that he was actually the suspect of all this,” O’Donnell said. “He was just a person down, and law enforcement did what they’re trained to do. They got him out of the hot zone and provided what first aid they could. He was pronounced dead upon arrival at the hospital.”
The blaze continued until about 1 a.m. Monday, Billings Fire Department Chief Matt Hoppel said.
Another complicating factor in the fire was that the house sat outside Billings city limits on county land where fire hydrants were not mandatory.
“They had to haul in truckloads of water, set up a temporary tank and pump out of that tank,” O’Donnell said. “So the fire suppression portion of this was very, very difficult.”
The Smith family moved to Montana from the Seattle area.
When Megan Ghekiere and Ireland divorced six years ago, she moved to Montana with their children, her ex-husband said.
Megan Ghekiere would then meet Adam Ghekiere, who would become her second husband. He was working and not at the Smith home when gunfire erupted.
“We are so grateful for the prayers, the love, the support that we’re getting from the nation,” Ghekiere said.
The blended family appeared to be very close, emotionally and geographically, with Evelyn Smith, Dana’s elderly mother, living in a nearby retirement home, Ireland said.
“They were nice,” neighbor Donna Heisler, 67, told NBC News on Tuesday. “I talked to Barbara, the wife, at a couple of garage sales.”
Heisler said her neighbors appeared to enjoy their privacy.

“They kind of kept to themselves. Really weren’t a very outgoing couple,” Heisler said. “They weren’t the socialites on the block, so you’d see them once in a while, but they weren’t overly outgoing.”
She added: “And coming from a bigger city maybe more the way they preferred to have it.”
Ireland said Alan Smith had moved in with his parents in Montana and stayed with them for years before he was asked to leave a couple of weeks ago.
Ireland called Alan Smith a “hermit” and said, “No one knew what he did in there 24/7.”
Smith’s name was not connected to any criminal records in Montana and Washington.
“We had not been called to this residence before, and we had not had any prior contact with the suspect,” O’Donnell said.
Adam Ghekiere, who works at the airport in Billings, learned of the shootings over dispatch radio, and when he couldn’t reach family on the phone, he raced to the crime scene.
Ghekiere’s children weren’t supposed to be there, he said, because family dinner was usually on Friday.
Ghekiere said police have confirmed to him that Charlotte was the one who dialed 911 from inside the house.
“I keep hearing her — every time I would say, ‘I love you,’ she would say, ‘I love you more,’” Ghekiere told the AP.

title: I Teach a College Class on Dolly Parton. What We Can All Learn From Her
summary: A college professor explains why her class on Dolly Parton has lessons for everyone.
story: “Take It From Me” is a TODAY.com series where experts use their wisdom to explain trends or make recommendations within their fields. In this latest installment, an anthropology professor explains what Dolly Parton has to teach us all.
The news of the Dolly Parton’s passing at the age of 80 led to an outpouring of tributes from peers in the industry and fans.
After hearing the news, anthropology professor Sarah Phillips spent part of the afternoon of “curled in a ball” in her office, “just outright mourning Dolly and all that we’ve lost.”
“It’s been a real roller coaster. Like many people, I think I never really believed she was mortal,” she tells TODAY.com.

For Phillips, Parton’s death felt personal. An associate professor of anthropology at Indiana University Bloomington, Phillips taught a course called “The Anthropology of Dolly Parton” for two years in a row.
“We have graduated around 120 ‘Dolliologists,’” Phillips says.

The course, which is taught every spring semester with the help of four undergraduate teaching assistants and a graduate associate instructor, uses Parton as a lens to study sociocultural anthropology.

Phillips says Parton’s story is one-of-a-kind, in that by following its arc, a person can learn about regional differences in America, class, fame, femininity, workers’ rights, women’s rights, queer culture, education and more.
“I can’t think of anyone else that this approach would work as seamlessly as it does,” Phillips says.

By now, Parton’s rise is the stuff of legend. Born the fourth of 12 siblings in a one-room cabin in Tennessee, Parton exhibited a love of music at an early age. By 13, Johnny Cash had introduced her at the Grand Ole Opry. She moved to Nashville after graduation. Her big break came in 1964, when she was hand-picked by Porter Wagoner to co-star on his syndicated TV show. Her decision to go solo and leave the show inspired the song “I Will Always Love You,” one of her biggest hits.

She was known as much for her song-writing prowess as her distinct appearance, entrepreneurship and philanthropy. She was also a devoted wife, aunt and godmother. Parton was beloved in her home state for many reasons, including investing in the local economy by building Dollywood in Pigeon Forge.
The class uses Parton’s story as a way to talk about, well, America.

“We talk about regional stereotypes. We talk about language and dialect. We talk about the history of different forms of music, especially country music, and how it moved from different parts of Europe through the United States down to the South, and how Dolly and her people were part of that movement.”

At one point in the semester, the class watches “9 to 5,” the 1980 film Parton starred in with Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda and wrote the lead song for, and connects it to the real-life office workers’ movement originating in Boston.
Another class is a lesson on regional stereotypes in the U.S, like how the idea of the hillbilly and redneck are curated and challenged in Parton’s album art and different periods of her career.

She also tries to impart Parton’s message, which she summarizes like this: “If you have a dream and you put in the work, because she sure did work, you can do anything that you want to. Despite the hurdles that are going to be put up in front of you by naysayers, by people who want to see you fail, by people who think they have your best interests at heart but are giving you advice — listen to your heart.”
What also fascinates Phillips is Parton’s undeniably wide appeal, and what caused it.

“She was so genuine beneath the big hair, beneath the rhinestones, the acrylic nails, the over-the-top look that she curated. As she would say, ‘Where it counts, I’m real.’ And she really connected with people on a personal level,” Phillips said. “Dolly Parton often said, ‘When people come to see me, they’re really coming to see themselves,’ and so she knew that people looked to her as a reflection of all that was good in themselves, and she really leaned into that.”
Phillips says the students leave the class inspired by Parton’s story. Many have reached out in the wake of her death, hoping to gather.

“They want to go out and change the world, and they want to do so in a way that is caring and kind and energetic and in line with their moral compass, and they see how Dolly did that, and it really inspires them,” she says.
While not everyone can take “The Anthropology of Dolly,” Phillips provided us with a mini curriculum. She says the course was inspired by the nine-episode podcast “Dolly Parton’s America.”

“Start with ‘Dolly Parton’s America,’ there is a treasure trove. There’s so many wonderful people interviewed in that podcast, so many different perspectives presented,” Phillips says. “Then, go after those authors, see what they’ve written.”
There’s another thing Phillips says we do: “Keep her memory alive.”

“I have no doubt that that’s going to happen, but we also have to think through these questions that you’re asking me,” Phillips explains. “What made her so special? What made her this uniting figure? Something that you know the one person all Americans can agree on, and can we all try to cultivate that just a little bit in ourselves? It would be a much better world if we could.”

title: Tim Curry Honored By ‘Rocky Horror Picture Show’ Co-Stars
summary: Tim Curry’s “The Rocky Horror Picture Show” co-stars are sharing their memories of filming the cult classic with the actor following the news of his death.
story: Tim Curry’s “The Rocky Horror Picture Show” co-stars are sharing their memories of filming the cult classic with the actor following the news of his death.

Curry, who delivered an unforgettable performance of Dr. Frank-N-Furter in the musical, died peacefully at his home in Toluca Lake, Los Angeles, on Aug. 25, his representatives confirmed in a statement to NBC News. His longtime manager and friend Marcia Hurwitz shared the news of his passing, as well. Curry was 80 years old.

The English actor, also known for his roles in “Clue” and the 1990 TV version of “It,” was honored by the many actors he shared the screen with. Members of “The Rocky Horror Picture Show” cast, including Susan Sarandon, posted sweet tributes to Curry.
Read on to see what they said about working with Curry and how they will remember him.
Susan Sarandon
Sarandon, who portrayed Janet Weiss in the 1975 film, uploaded a slideshow of photos of Curry to Instagram. The final picture showed Curry dressed in his Dr. Frank-N-Furter costume.
“What a funny, sexy, original he was. But what I loved about him most was his heart,” Sarandon said about her former co-star.

“Even wheelchair bound he continued to be so sweet and generous with his fans,” she added, referring to the stroke Curry suffered in 2012 that impacted his mobility. “Thank you Tim for meaning so much to so many people. Love you, S.”
Barry Bostwick
Barry Bostwick, who portrayed Janet’s fiancé Brad Majors, referenced lines from “The Rocky Horror Picture Show” in his Facebook tribute.
“The river was deep but you swam it. The road was long but you ran it” Dammit Tim, I love you…” he wrote, a play on lyrics from the song “Dammit Janet.”
Luke Evans

Luke Evans, who took on the role of Dr. Frank-N-Furter for the Broadway production of the musical and earned a nomination at the 79th Tony Awards, shared a letter on Instagram that he wrote to Curry three weeks before his death.

“I want to share it with you, he was a force, a bright fierce flame, an exquisite charm and that rich vocal tone, he was an inspiration to me and so many more people for the roles he played and the effect he had on so many of us. There will only be one Tim Curry. And the rest of us will just have to do our best to emulate some of the magic of that role that I’ve just spent 7 months playing…,” he said before including the message.
In the letter, Evans said although they had never met he felt Curry’s presence since he started working on the production.
“Being compared to you has been one of the greatest compliments I’ve ever received, even though it’s a comparison no one could ever hope to live up to,” he said, in part.
Evans added, “I’ve never tried to recreate what you did. That would be impossible. I simply hoped to honour the extraordinary character you brought to life, while finding my own way through him.”
‘The Rocky Horror Picture Show’
The Instagram account for “The Rocky Horror Picture Show,” which was co-written by fellow cast member Richard O’Brien, described Curry as a “singular talent.”

“A true original. And the man who first brought Dr. Frank-N-Furter to life,” the post said. “When The Rocky Horror Show began in 1973, nobody could have imagined what would follow. But from the moment Tim stepped onto that stage, something extraordinary happened. He didn’t simply play a character. He created an icon.”
The post continued, “Thank you, Tim. For the brilliance. For the courage. For the inspiration. For Frank. And for everything that followed. You were, and always will be, unforgettable.”

title: Dolly Parton Had Many Projects In the Works Before Her Death. Where They Stand
summary: Dolly Parton’s team shares an update on all the projects she was working on and would be releasing.
story: Before her death, Dolly Parton had a slew of projects she was excited about bringing to life and sharing with her millions of fans.
On Aug. 26, a day after the country icon died at the age of 80, her team shared an update on all the plans she had in development.

“Dolly worked up until the day she died. She loved seeing her dreams come to life, and loved knowing her work brought people joy,” her longtime manager Danny Nozell said in a press release. “Ever the planner, Dolly worked with the team that she handpicked, for the past several years to build a project roadmap that will guide us for decades to come.”
Parton died after being diagnosed with cancer, her estate announced Aug. 25 in a statement. She had not publicly disclosed her diagnosis, but had been open about her ongoing health challenges.

While the beloved star’s death came as a shock to many, she prepared for her legacy to live on. Nozell said in his statement that he and Parton’s team will oversee the many projects she had been working on and “ensure the many dreams she had yet to fulfill are brought to life.”
He noted that many projects were in various stages of development, stressing that Parton approved everything that would be shared on her official channels.

“If you see unreleased music, products, books, experiences, and campaigns launched through official Dolly Parton channels, you can have confidence in knowing that she placed her personal stamp on it.”
The “9 to 5” singer’s team also shared a video compilation of Parton hard at work, promoting some upcoming content.

Parton’s team also said that details on additional projects, including an avatar show she previously spoke about, a biopic, docuseries, scripted series, a Billy The Kid animated series and many more “will be revealed soon.”

title: Dolly Parton Had a Well-Documented Love Affair With Food. These Were Her Favorites
summary: Dolly Parton loved to cook and eat foods like chicken and dumplings, funnel cake, fried chicken, potatoes (in any form), milk gravy and more Southern staples.
story: Dolly Parton was a meat-and-potatoes kind of woman.
The iconic singer, songwriter, actor and philanthropist died at the age of 80 on Aug. 25 following a “brief battle with cancer,” her estate announced.
Over her spectacularly rhinestone-speckled life, she appeared on TODAY over 50 times, sometimes with a plate full of muffins or a cake in tow.
After Parton’s nephew Bryan Seaver shared the news of her death in an Instagram video, fans shared their condolences — and many of them made food that reminded them of her.

Parton and the Southern food she grew up on were intrinsically linked, leading to several food partnerships, a line of Lodge cooking pans, and two cookbooks from the “9 to 5” singer, including one with her sister, Rachel Parton George.
In those books and in interviews over the years, the “Jolene” singer shared some of her favorite dishes. Here is a selection of them from over the years — a “Coat of Many Colors,” if you will.
Fried Chicken
Parton told TODAY.com more than once that fried chicken was at the top of her family’s favorite foods list.

“Growing up in the South with my mom being the greatest cook in the world — and my aunts and my grandmas — I just remember things like fried chicken on Sunday was one of the greatest things ever,” she told TODAY.com in January 2022.

Later, in September 2024, she said, “I think there’s something about Sundays and fried chicken — even in the country — that was just a special treat … The preacher in our family happened to be our grandpa, and grandpa loved fried chicken.”
Funnel Cake

Dollywood, Parton’s theme park, offers some irresistible foods. From cinnamon bread at The Grist Mill or pot roast at Aunt Granny’s Restaurant, guests could snack on any of a number of Dolly’s delicacies. In January 2025, Parton revealed which food she always has to have when she sets foot in her eponymous park.

“The funnel cakes we’re famous for, so I never go there … even if I’m in my bus or if I’m in my suite, The Dolly Suite, I say, ‘Run and get me some funnel cakes. I can’t leave here without funnel cakes,’” she said.
Banana Pudding, Coconut Cake and Chocolate Cake
Parton stopped by TODAY in 2022 to chat about her line of cake mixes and frostings with Duncan Hines, and shared her love for another dessert.
“Everybody in the South — but everywhere, really — we love bananas, and we love banana pudding,” she said. “When you have a good banana pudding, it’s great.”
She also expressed her adoration for cake during the segment.

“I always think of Sundays when I think of coconut cake,” she said. “My mom always made either chocolate cake or coconut cake on Sundays, but on Easter, we always had a coconut cake. So we just felt that it was really a nice start for me to do something more Southern, and they’re beautiful.”
Milk Gravy
“Every now and then I’ll make my husband, Carl, an extra special breakfast,” she said on TODAY.com in 2020 while sharing her own recipe.
She added that, when she made Southern staples like sausage patties or flaky biscuits for her husband Carl Dean, who died in 2025, she would make an easy, creamy milk gravy as the “perfect” topping.
Get The Recipe
Taco Bell
Parton told Insider in January and April 2022 that when she wasn’t cooking, she and her husband would sometimes hit up Taco Bell.

“I like soft-shell tacos,” Parton said. “I like the others, but they fall apart so bad, especially if you’re riding around. So I always get a Taco Supreme, with the sour cream and all that, in the soft shell. I love that.”
She also revealed she loved the then-discontinued Mexican Pizza, which may have convinced the chain to resurrect the dish in May 2022.
Potatoes, in Any Form
In 2025, she told TODAY.com that every day, she had “to have something with potatoes.”
“I mean, I’m just one of those people that I have to either have a baked potato, some mashed potatoes, or some french fries, or something to do with potatoes,” Parton told TODAY.com.
Earlier, in 2022, she also said she enjoys the tuberous starch at barbecues, in the form of a mayo-based potato salad, along with a vinegar-based coleslaw.

“When that happened at our church, and that big bowl of potato salad got there, you didn’t have to worry,” she said. “Even it was sunny, it wasn’t gonna last that long! It wasn’t gonna go bad … not if I was around!”
Chicken and Dumplings and Peanut Butter Fudge

Chicken and Dumplings, which appears in her recipe book, “Good Lookin’ Cookin,’” was also a favorite on the movie sets she graced. She would also whip up a sweet treat that co-stars like Lily Tomlin or Jane Fonda may have snacked on while filming “9 to 5”: peanut butter fudge.

“I cook a lot when I’m on my movie sets,” she said in 2022. “So I guess it would be a long list of famous people, because whoever the stars and co-stars are. I have this huge big pot, and I make chicken and dumplings. I’m famous for it, so everybody wants me to make that or a peanut butter fudge that I love and take on set with me. Everybody asks, ‘When are you going to do the dumplings?’ I always announce it a couple of days before so they all look forward to it. So, I’ve had my dumplings eaten by a lot of famous people.”

title: Tim Curry Was the World’s Scariest Clown. It Surprised Him Until the Very End
summary: Tim Curry was terrifying playing the clown Pennywise in “IT,” the 1990 TV-movie adaptation of Stephen King’s book.
story: Coulrophobia is the fear of clowns. There is, however, no known name for the specific condition of coulrophobia, as brought on by Tim Curry.
Curry, of course, may have generated more than a few cases of coulrophobia all by himself, thanks to one of his most memorable parts.
The actor’s manager shared on Aug. 26 that he had died at the age of 80.
In 1990, Curry took on a role that was as frightening as something you would read in a Stephen King book, which is not a coincidence because it came from a Stephen King book.

In “IT,” based on King’s 1986 book of the same name, Curry portrayed Pennywise, the demonic clown terrorizing a group of child outcasts in 1960s Maine, and resurfaces decades later to wreak more havoc.

“IT” was a four-hour movie that aired over two nights. Curry was the linchpin of the film, which also starred John Ritter, Tim Reid, Richard Thomas, Harry Anderson, Annette O’Toole, as well as child stars Jonathan Brandis and Seth Green.
Pennywise is as scary as scary can be, and Curry was often taken aback at the effect the character had long after the movie aired.

“The majority of people who want to talk to me about being Pennywise are either notably odd people, who sort of revel in his evilness, or else they want me to know that I’ve really traumatized them, or made it impossible to sleep, or something of that variety,” he wrote in his 2025 memoir, “Vagabond.”
“I don’t blame them — one of my lines is literally ‘I’m your worst dream come true.’ But I’ve never really known how to respond to that.”
Curry, who already had a following for his work in “The Rocky Horror Picture Show” and “Clue,” seemed to have mixed feelings about “IT,” which was remade for the big screen in 2017.

“I haven’t had much to say about it publicly for many years, which many people misread as my carrying some sort of deep conflict about the role,” he wrote in “Vagabond.” “That’s really not the case, but I didn’t revel in the role, either.”
Imagine, though, if Curry did revel in it. He was mesmerizing in his portrayal of the clown who lured in children with his menacing smile and balloons.

“My job was to give Tim the stage and not get in his way too much,” “IT” director Tommy Lee Wallace told The Hollywood Reporter in 2017. “He was like Robin Williams in the way he brought a spontaneous improvisation to the part.”

This was transcendental stuff. Curry reached a level of terror that the slasher films of the ‘80s aspired to — and he did it in a TV movie that preyed on the visceral over the physical. It would’ve been right at home had people coughed up a few bucks to see it on the big screen.
“Beep beep, Richie.”
“They all float down here.”
“I’m every nightmare you’ve ever had. I’m your worst dream come true. I’m everything you ever were afraid of.”
If you’ve seen the movie, you can see and hear Curry delivering those lines. They still echo more than three decades later.
The Hollywood Reporter applauded the film, calling it “one big kicky ride thanks to the charismatic acting of Curry as savage, sneering malevolence.”

“I don’t like clowns. I never did,” he told The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences earlier this year. “But I liked doing that show a lot because you have immense freedom, really, as a clown.”

Curry was so on point that he recalled scaring Tony Dakota, one of his co-stars, in a scene that takes place early in the movie when Georgie (played by Dakota) chases his toy boat after it goes into the sewer, where Pennywise is holed up.

“He stopped in the middle of the scene and said, ‘Mr. Curry, you’re scaring me.’ I said, ‘Well, ‘I’m supposed to scare you, but I don’t mean to harm you in any way,” he told The Academy, echoing a story he also shared in “Vagabond.”

“IT” earned two Emmy nominations, winning one for outstanding achievement in music composition for a miniseries or a special. It was also nominated for best editing. It’s amazing to think that Curry did not earn a nomination, given the enduring nature of the part.

Interestingly, Curry would earn one Emmy in his career — and it was connected to horror. He garnered a nod in 1994 for outstanding guest actor in a drama series for appearing on the HBO anthology series “Tales from the Crypt.”

Curry called “IT” “very original, very audacious, and yes, legitimately frightening” in “Vagabond.” He would go on to write that fans often ask him to do Pennywise’s voice when he goes to conventions, which he called “a weird phenomenon.” It shows the power of the part and the connection fans still feel to this very day.
“I never would have imagined that out of my whole body of work, that clown would end up being so memorable to audiences,” he wrote.

title: Bob Barker Reflects on 3 Decades of Hosting ‘The Price Is Right’ in 2002 TODAY Interview
summary: On April 1, 2002, Bob Barker stopped by TODAY to look back at his experiences, a mere 30 years into his tenure.
story: Welcome inside the TODAY Vault, where we revisit memories from our show when celebrities and newsmakers started discourse, made us laugh or shaped our culture. This latest installment aired April 1, 2002 and features Bob Barker talking to Al Roker about “The Price is Right” 30 years into his run as host of the beloved game show.
The history of game shows can’t be told without Bob Barker.
Barker, who helped make “The Price is Right” a staple of daytime television during his 35-year run as host, died Aug. 26, 2023, at the age of 99.
He began his stint on the show in 1972 and remained on the job until 2007, a vital part in turning the show into the smash hit it remains to this day with current host Drew Carey.
On April 1, 2002, Barker stopped by TODAY to look back at his experiences, a mere 30 years into his tenure.
“Sometimes it seems much longer,” he said while laughing. “And sometimes it seems like only yesterday that we started.”
Barker also spoke about what had changed over the years, why young people loved the show and how he broke into the business.
How Had ‘The Price is Right’ Changed Since He Began Hosting?
Barker noted that the set remained the same, but the cost of the items on the show had evolved.

“The prices, that’s what has really changed,” he said. “The first car I gave away was $2,465. We had car after car, four digits. Two was the first number. Then 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. Now we’ve had to change our props to accommodate five digits.”
‘The Price is Right’ Appealed to Young People

It’s lore that kids watched the show when they stayed home sick from school. That love didn’t dissipate over time, either, as evidenced by the young people and college students who appear on the show. Barker couldn’t explain why a younger demographic was so drawn to the series, but he was glad it was.
“We’re blessed. It happened. We don’t know how it happened. If we did, we could bottle it and sell it. But it became a cult thing with the college youngsters,” he said.
“And now they come from all over the country — East Coast, Midwest, and, of course, the West Coast — and they give our show great energy. It’s just wonderful,” he added.
How Did Bob Barker Wind Up Hosting Game Shows?

Prior to “The Price is Right,” Barker hosted “Truth or Consequences” for 18 years. He began his career in radio and ultimately made the move to the small screen with encouragement from his wife, Dorothy Jo Gideon.
“I started working at a radio station when I was in college. They didn’t call them game shows. They were audience participation shows,” he said.

“The first audience participation show I did, my wife heard and she said, ‘That’s what you should do.’ She said, ‘You do that better than you’ve ever done anything else.’ Now she didn’t say I was good,” he joked. “She just said I did it better than I’ve ever done anything else. And I set out to do precisely what I’m doing.”

title: Young Dolly Parton Photos: See the ‘Queen of Country’ Through the Years
summary: See pictures of Dolly Parton from the earlier part of her life as a child into adulthood when she posed with some huge stars.
story: The world continues to mourn Dolly Parton’s death of cancer at the age of 80.

Tributes for the icon — who was a TODAY staple and sage speaker — have poured in from across all corners, as the global superstar leaves behind a legacy in which she was known not just for her music and acting, but for her humility and generosity.

Parton was married to Carl Dean for 60 years before his death in 2025. There was another Dolly Parton, though, long before they tied the knot and long before she became a worldwide superstar who wrote over 3,000 songs.

Parton was Dolly Rebecca Parton on Jan. 19, 1946, the fourth of 12 children. She grew up in rural Sevierville, Tennessee and sang on local television and radio while still a child. At 13, Johnny Cash introduced her for her 1959 debut at the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville.

Stardom awaited her. Parton moved to Nashville to pursue a music career after graduating high school in 1964. In 1967, country star and TV personality Porter Wagoner handpicked her to be his new duet partner on “The Porter Wagoner Show.”

That same year, she released her debut solo album, “Hello, I’m Dolly,” which rose to the number 11 spot on the Billboard Top Country Albums chart and announced her arrival as a star for years to come.
Take a look at Parton throughout her younger years below.
Dolly Parton From Her 1st Recording to Co-Starring with Porter Wagoner
Parton’s first single, “Puppy Love,” came out in 1955, when Parton was about 9 years old. When she was 21, Wagoner offered her a life-changing spot on his syndicated show.
Dolly Parton Went Solo in 1974 and Became a Star

Parton became a solo act and rocketed to stardom in the 1970s, propelled, in part, by the success of her songs “Joshua,” “Coat of Many Colors,” “Jolene” and “I Will Always Love You.” Those tracks would remain some of her signature songs throughout her career.
Dolly Parton Hobnobbed With Celebrities for Years

As her star rose, so did her profile. Parton was not known for appearing in the tabloids, but she did cross paths with several stars over the years as she crossed into the mainstream by making the jump into film with ‘9 to 5” in 1980. Even before that, she had emerged as a superstar.

title: Miley Cyrus Honors Late Godmother Dolly Parton After Her Death: ‘I Have an Angel By My Side’
summary: Singer Miley Cyrus shared a heartfelt tribute after the passing of her “fairy godmother,” Dolly Parton.
story: To the world, Dolly Parton was a country music legend. To Miley Cyrus, she was her “fairy godmother.”
Parton’s nephew shared that she died “peacefully” on Aug. 25 at the age of 80. And today on Instagram, Cyrus gave Parton her “flowers.”

“The feeling of losing my Aunt Dolly is beyond what feels right to share. Our most sacred moments were private and they’ll stay there behind the stage, beneath the glamour & between our hearts,” she began.

“What I KNOW is Dolly would want me to feel it, write a song about it, and then continue on and be strong. I have an angel by my side. I always have. One of our last conversations was about music and metamorphosis. 🦋

“I will always love her and want to make her proud. My heart breaks for the world, her family and friends who will miss her deeply. We’re in this loss together and we will see her in all of the most beautiful things. 💖”

Parton had a long-standing friendship with the singer’s parents, Billy Ray Cyrus and Tish Cyrus-Purcell, and she shared the story of becoming a godmother during an interview in 2023 on SiriusXM’s “The Howard Stern Show.”

“We just got to be good friends because he’s a Kentucky boy, I’m from Tennessee,” Parton said at the time. “And he said … ‘We’re having a girl, and you’ve got to be her godmother!’ And I said, ‘Well, I’d be honored.’ So actually, Miley and I took over from there.”
Miley Cyrus and Dolly Parton have a long history of gushing over one another, both personally and professionally.

They collaborated in front of the cameras when Parton guest starred on three episodes of “Hannah Montana” as her character’s fictional on-screen godmother. And together they sang Parton’s 1973 hit “Jolene” with Pentatonix on “The Voice” in 2016.
When Parton was honored by as one of Time’s Most Influential People of 2021, Cyrus wrote a tribute to her.

“There’s a theory that you shouldn’t meet your heroes, but I wish everyone had the chance to meet Dolly Parton, because she’s even better than your sparkliest dreams,” Cyrus wrote. “She may be my fairy godmother, but I think she’s that to everyone else too. I am happy to share her with the world.”
Cyrus shared a message that her godmother sent her a few years later.
“Dolly’s been like a mother to me. Actually, I was just reading this fax that she sent me two Mother’s Days ago,” Cyrus told W Magazine in 2024.
“Dolly wrote to me to say: ‘How much do I love you? As much as my heart can hold and as far as my arms can reach,’” Cyrus recalled. “It gets me choked up. I just love her so much.”
In a Facebook tribute, Billy Ray Cyrus said that he grew up watching Parton on his living room TV, and shared a memory from a meeting with her in 1992.

“I’ll never forget walking into her dressing room to apologize for all the tabloid stories which claimed I was having an affair with her. In true Dolly fashion, she just looked at me, winked and said, ‘Honey, this trash sells records!’” Billy Ray Cyrus wrote.
The singer added that Parton recently sent him a message telling him that she “loved me with her whole heart.”
“I will always love her in the same way ….. with my whole heart … and I always will,” he said.

title: TODAY Anchors Honor Dolly Parton and Her Life Spent Spreading Joy: ‘She Was an Original’
summary: Following the death of beloved country music icon Dolly Parton, the TODAY family took a trip down memory lane to reflect on the many ways she had touched their lives.
story: Following the death of beloved country music icon Dolly Parton, the TODAY family took a trip down memory lane to reflect on the many ways she had touched their lives.
“It goes without saying how much we love Dolly Parton,” Hoda Kotb said on TODAY Aug. 26. “Her music was the soundtrack of so many lives, and that’s just one small part of her incredible legacy.”
Carson Daly highlighted the “rhinestone-studded trail” Parton had blazed for countless entertainers who had followed her, many of whom had shared their personal tributes to Parton.

“It’s crazy, from all walks of life ... all genres of music,” Carson said of the music industry’s admiration for Parton. He recalled how she initially turned down her nomination for the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame because she didn’t feel her music was worthy. Parton later accepted the nomination — and then she proceeded to put out a rock album in 2023.

“I don’t think she cared about any accolades,” Hoda said. “It was as if the accolades didn’t mean much to her because she often said, ‘If I didn’t get paid or if I wasn’t that good, I would still be singing.’”
Kristen Welker also shared about Parton’s legacy, including what her fans meant to her.

“She was just so humble,” Kristen said, reflecting on Parton’s response when asked if she felt bothered when people recognized her. “She said, ‘Are you kidding? That’s why I’m here.’ She loved just being with the people and spreading that love.”
Craig Melvin highlighted Parton’s family background, being one of 12 children, as a possible source of her humility.
Carson then chimed in, further commemorating Parton’s reach.

“Country music was regional, it was walled off of mainstream,” he said. “She comes in and owns her masters, she owns her likeness, she owns her rights. She’s a business savant. ... And by the way, her greatest legacy might be what she’s done for literacy.”

Parton founded the Imagination Library, a book gifting program that grants young children around the country access to free books. Carson continued to list Parton’s contributions to society beyond entertaining, including her donations to fund a COVID vaccine and helping those impacted by natural disasters.
“She didn’t want the accolades,” Carson said. “She wanted to help.”
Later on TODAY, “9 to 5” played on the Plaza, with Craig shouting out Parton as a “national treasure.”
Hoda, who has interviewed Parton many times, reflected on a moment when Parton made an impact on another member of the TODAY family, Megan Stackhouse, who is head of public relations.

“She walked up to Dolly and said, ‘You raised me.’” Hoda remembered. “And Dolly enveloped her, hugged her, and I remember Megan crying. We all got to sit and chat with her, but those are the moments I think stick out the most for me.”

title: What To Know About Dolly Parton’s Relationship With Goddaughter Miley Cyrus
summary: Dolly Parton agreed to be godmother to Miley Cyrus before the “Hannah Montana” star was born. Discover all their is to know about their deep bond.
story: Successful in both music and film, the late Dolly Parton also took on the role of godmother to singer and actor Miley Cyrus.

Parton was “honored” to take on the task when Cyrus’ father, fellow country music star Billy Ray, asked her to ahead of Cyrus’ birth, Parton recalled during a 2023 appearance on “The Howard Stern Show.” “So actually, Miley and I took over from there. We just stayed very, very close through the years.”
The two have collaborated on stage, acted together and revealed details about their shared inner life throughout Cyrus’ upbringing.
Never having had children, Parton said she was able to be “everybody’s mother” in a 1984 interview, a benefit for which Cyrus often expressed gratitude.

“Dolly’s been like a mother to me. Actually, I was just reading this fax that she sent me two Mother’s Days ago,” Cyrus told W Magazine in 2024. “Dolly wrote to me to say: ‘How much do I love you? As much as my heart can hold and as far as my arms can reach,’” Cyrus said. “It gets me choked up. I just love her so much.”
The two musical icons had long shared a loving bond. Ahead, what to know about their relationship.
Parton Has Known Cyrus Since ‘Before She Was Born’
On “The Howard Stern Show,” Parton explained that she became close to Cyrus’ father when he toured with her while promoting his 1992 single, “Achy Breaky Heart.”

“We just got to be good friends because he’s a Kentucky boy, I’m from Tennessee,” Parton said. “And he said … ‘We’re having a girl, and you’ve got to be her godmother!’ And I said, ‘Well, I’d be honored.’”
Parton also described her goddaughter as her “little sweetheart,” adding: “I’ve known her since before she was born, actually.”
Parton Guest-Starred on ‘Hannah Montana’
Parton played Aunt Dolly on three episodes of “Hannah Montana.” She appeared in 2006’s “Good Golly, Miss Dolly,” 2007’s “I Will Always Loathe You,” and 2010’s “Kiss It All Goodbye.”
The country legend said she felt like a “proud mama” as she worked with her young goddaughter on the hit Disney Channel series.
“I was so proud of her. I thought she was sensational,” Parton told Vanity Fair in 2020.

“We just worked so great together. ... And thanks to her, I had a whole new following of people that were turned on to me,” she also said. “These young, little kids that were her fans, and kids that were fans of just the whole show, and the other little artists on the show, but here I am, Miley’s fairy godmother.”
In a 2021 essay for Time magazine, Cyrus reflected on working with Parton on “Hannah Montana.”

“I remember when she came in to do a table read for ‘Hannah Montana’ in all her bedazzled glory. Her smell, the way her nails tapped the table, the sound it made when she flipped the pages of the script — I could see that she fascinated other people too,” Cyrus wrote. “A living fantasy was in front of all of us.”
They Have Collaborated on Music

Cyrus and Parton teamed up to co-host NBC’s “Miley’s New Year’s Eve Party” and ring in 2023. They performed duets of two of their greatest ballads: Cyrus’ ”Wrecking Ball” and Parton’s “I Will Always Love You.”
Parton opened up about the emotional experience of performing with her goddaughter.
“Even when we were rehearsing, Miley was crying,” Parton told Business Insider in 2023.

“The fact that we were singing so well together stirred up our emotions very much,” she added. “Then we went into ‘I Will Always Love You’ and she would just have these tears coming down and it was so emotional.”
Parton and Cyrus also performed a cover of “Wrecking Ball” for Parton’s rock album, “Rockstar,” which came out in November 2023.
This version features a playful change to the lyrics, a nod to Parton’s “I Will Always Love You.”

In the original version of “Wrecking Ball,” Cyrus sings, “I can’t live a lie, running for my life/ I will always want you,” but in the collaboration with Parton, the line is changed to, “I can’t live a lie, running for my life/ I will always love you.”

Cyrus celebrated this collaboration with her godmother in a post on X: “I’ve grown up covering my Aunt Dollys music & it’s an honor to hear her singing one of my songs,” she wrote. “I love you Aunt Dolly! I’m so happy to add another collaboration under our bedazzled (studded leather) belt!”
Parton Is One of Cyrus’ Biggest Cheerleaders
Parton has always jumped at the chance to sing her goddaughter’s praises, both professionally and personally.
The country legend called Cyrus “smart and talented” in an essay she penned when Cyrus was named one of Time magazine’s 100 Most Influential People in 2014.

“She knows what she’s doing. She was very proud of the work she did as Hannah Montana, but people were gonna leave her there forever,” she wrote. “And she was just smotherin’ and chokin’ in it. So she felt she had to do something completely drastic. And she did. She made her point, she made her mark, and more power to her.”
In 2020, Parton spoke to Vanity Fair about Cyrus forging her own path and pointed out their similarities.

“But you know, she’s like me. She’s finding her own space, she’s finding her own things, and she’ll always land on her feet,” Parton said. “I don’t always have to agree with everything she does, but it ain’t my business. That’s her life. I’m just her fairy godmother, and I love her.”
She also praised her goddaughter when Howard Stern asked if Cyrus ever came to her for advice.

“Well, she’s asked me a lot of things. She mostly just runs things by me, and we talk,” she said. “She’s very successful. Miley’s very smart. She’s very intuitive about the business, and I just think Miley’s a spectacular human being and an amazing talent.”
Cyrus Said Parton Is Her ‘Idol’

“Have you ever met anyone who doesn’t love Dolly Parton? I never have,” Cyrus wrote in an essay about Parton when Parton was honored on the Time 100 list in 2021. “Dolly is not only my idol because of her incomparable career — she’s also my role model because of her steadfast morals and values.”
“There’s a theory that you shouldn’t meet your heroes, but I wish everyone had the chance to meet Dolly Parton, because she’s even better than your sparkliest dreams,” Cyrus also wrote.
In her W magazine interview, Cyrus also mentioned thinking about her godmother as she reflected on having children someday.
“I’m 31 now, and I still don’t know if I want kids or not,” she said at the time. “I feel like my fans kind of are my kids in some way. I’ve heard Dolly say that too, because she didn’t have kids.”
Their bond runs deep on stage and off.

“There’s a chemistry, and a realness, and a love, and a connection that her and I have that I really feel,” Cyrus told TODAY ahead of their New Year’s Eve performance in 2022. “You can see our chemistry, and I really don’t think there’s much to write. There’s not much to choreograph. It’s all right there,” she added.
Parton Taught Cyrus to Dream Big
Cyrus credits the 20th anniversary special for “Hannah Montana,” which aired in 2026, to Parton.

Ahead of official announcements for the special, Cyrus teased something was in the works during interviews. Turns out, the special hadn’t yet been greenlit. But Cyrus took a page from Parton’s book and spoke it into existence.

“I learned this terrible habit — but I actually think it was good advice — from Dolly,” Cyrus told Variety. “She told me that if you want something to happen, promote it before it exists. Then no one can say ‘no.’ So I just started promoting a ‘Hannah Montana’ 20th-anniversary special that literally did not exist.”
They Both Worked With Beyoncé on the “Cowboy Carter” Album
When Parton allowed Beyoncé to cover her music on Beyoncé’s first country album, Parton revealed she didn’t imagine Beyoncé would pick “Jolene.”

When E! News asked about the choice, Parton said, “Well, I think it was very bold of her. When they said she was going to do ‘Jolene,’ I expected it to be my regular one, but it wasn’t. But I love what she did to it.”

Parton was happy with the rendition. In fact, Parton praised Beyoncé’s lyric changes, too. In Beyoncé’s version, she warns Jolene to stay away from her man, unlike Parton’s original in which she begs Jolene not to take her man.

Cyrus collaborated with Beyoncé on the same album, lending her voice to the song, “II Most Wanted.” When the album was released, Cyrus sang Beyoncé’s praises. “I’ve loved Beyoncé since long before I had the opportunity to meet & work with her,” Cyrus wrote on Instagram. “My admiration runs so much deeper now that I’ve created along side of her. Thank you Beyoncé. You’re everything & more. Love you.”

She also performed the duet during the Paris leg of Beyoncé’s Cowboy Carter tour. “To have learned from you & loved you my whole life, & then be standing together in matching gold looks is more than I could’ve imagined,” Cyrus wrote on social media.
Cyrus and Parton Are Actually Related

While they already considered each other family, Cyrus and Parton are, in fact, actually related, according to Cosmopolitan. The outlet cited a 2024 Ancestry.com report that states the two stars were seventh cousins.
Parton and Cyrus, the genealogy site found, shared an ancestor who was Parton’s sixth great-grandfather and Cyrus’ seventh great-grandfather.

title: Dolly Parton Once Showed TODAY’s Willie Geist How She Wrote ‘9 to 5’ Using Her Fingernails
summary: During a 2020 interview with Willie Geist, Country legend, Dolly Parton, revealed how she used her acrylic fingernails to help pen her No. 1 hit “9 to 5.”
story: “The Queen of Country” is gone, but Dolly Parton leaves behind a lasting legacy of music, generosity and a catalog of hit songs. Among the most memorable is Parton’s No. 1 hit “9 to 5.”

The 1980 tune was written for the movie by the same name featuring Parton, Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda. The trio starred as Doralee, Violet and Judy, three beleaguered secretaries working for sexist boss Franklin Hart Jr. (Dabney Coleman).
After suffering at the hands of their boss’s relentless demands, they hatch a plan to exact their revenge, and it doesn’t go quite as planned.

While the movie was one of the biggest box-office successes of the year, it was Parton’s song that took home all the awards, earning two Grammys and an Oscar nod, along with spending 26 weeks on the Billboard Hot 100.
Four decades later, it still remains one of the most popular anthems dedicated to the grind of the 9-to-5 worker.
What might be the most interesting fact about the toe-tapper, however, is that it was written, in part, on Parton’s fingernails.
In a 2020 interview with TODAY’s Willie Geist, Parton explained that she penned the hit song while on the set of the movie, but since she didn’t have an instrument, she had to improvise.
“I did it on my fingernails,” Parton tells Willie, scratching her legendary long nails together. “Can you hear that?” she asks, of the rhythmic tapping.

“They sound like a typewriter,” she explained. “I didn’t have my guitar because I didn’t want to get too scattered because we were trying to stay in the mood, and they were doing lights and all that. So, I would just look around and I would get ideas watching whatever was going on on the set.”

As she pondered the song, she says thought about the movie’s storyline; women in the workplace, their race to get out of the house in morning and Parton began tapping out the song’s iconic beat on her nails, washboard style.
“I would just kind of play my little fingers, go back to the hotel at night, write down the words, get my guitar and start singing it,” she recalls. “That’s how it all kind of how that all worked.”
Even though her fingernails were intended as a placeholder for her guitar, the nail-scratching ultimately made it into the final cut of “9 to 5.”

“I played my nails on the real record just for fun because all the girls got a kick out of me singing it to them, running around,” said Parton laughing. “Even Jane (Fonda) and Lily (Tomlin), to this day, every time they see me, they start going (scratching nails together).”
Even so, there’s one caveat, Parton explained. “You’ve got to have acrylic nails though, which I don’t think either of them do, so they don’t play it as good as I do.”

Penning “9 to 5” wasn’t the only time Parton used her fingernails to tap out a tune, either. The Queen of Country memorably performed a nail duet in 1987 with Grammy-winning singer Patti LaBelle on her variety show “Dolly.”

Telling LaBelle that she often tapped out songs on the dashboard of her car when she didn’t have a guitar on hand, Parton invited to singer to join her in singing the classic folk song “Shortnin’ Bread.”
Together, the pair harmonized and scratched their nails in unison. “That’s cute!” said LaBelle of their acrylic collaboration. “We did plan this, but we didn’t know how it was going to sound.”
LaBelle wrapped the brief but iconic moment with a quick nail solo before the pair finished to cheers and applause.

Parton’s “9 to 5” co-stars paid tribute to their long-time friend upon Parton’s passing on Aug. 25 at the age of 80, with Tomlin posting on X, “Friend. Songwriter. The Great Harmonizer of Humanity. Dolly. Dolly. Dolly. Forever Dolly.”

Fonda honored Parton with a long post on Instagram, writing, “More than anyone I have ever known, Dolly will always be with us because she was so present, so powerful, so generous and playful that she is woven into all our lives and hearts forever.”

Fonda summed up her friend’s legacy by saying, “We have our memories of her, her songs, Dollywood, ‘9to5,’ the millions of books she got into the hands of children, all the iconic images that bring her to us. And they are all blessings.”

title: Eminem Shares Letter Dolly Parton Once Wrote Him About Their ‘Unexplained Connection,’ Despite Never Meeting
summary: Among all the tributes to Dolly Parton in the wake of her death, Eminem’s post truly illustrates how she touched people across all walks of life.
story: Among all the tributes to Dolly Parton in the wake of her death, one of them truly illustrates how she touched people across all walks of life.
“Jolene” and “The Real Slim Shady” may have been far apart musically, but even Eminem had a heartfelt remembrance of a time the country icon reached out with some kind words for him.

The legendary rapper, whose real name is Marshall Mathers, shared a thoughtful note on Instagram that Parton sent him following his induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022. It was one of many tributes to Parton following the announcement of her death at 80 on Aug. 25.

“I’m sorry we never got a chance to meet, but getting this note from Dolly really had an impact on me,” he wrote. “She definitely didn’t have to take the time to do it. Even for a kid who mostly listened to rap music, she was an icon. A superstar in every sense. Rest easy Dolly. And thank you for the kind words.”

Parton was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame herself as part of the same class of inductees as Eminem in 2022. Parton sang her iconic hit “Jolene” and Eminem performed a medley of his most memorable songs as part of the induction ceremony.

“Congratulations on your induction to the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame,” she wrote in her note. “Your performance was amazing and everybody said so. Even though I don’t know a lot about rap music, I’ve come to know that you are the very best at it.”

The two performers, who are 27 years apart in age, shared similar hardscrabble upbringings and success as underdogs in the music industry. They are also synonymous with their roots — Parton in Tennessee and Eminem in Detroit.

“Aside from that I hope what I have to say will not seem weird or strange to you but I have always felt some unexplained connection to you like I know you somehow,” Parton wrote in her note. “I had hoped to meet you at the show but you know how nuts those things are, personally I hate ‘em and I missed my chance but maybe someday we’ll meet.
“In the meantime, keep doing what you’re doing because you do it so well and no matter how complex your world may be just know you are very special and touch people in ways you don’t even know.”
Parton signed the letter, “With love & respect.”

In addition to tributes from her peers, Parton also received an outpouring of love from younger artists who respected and collaborated with her over the years. Taylor Swift, Beyoncé, Sabrina Carpenter and goddaughter Miley Cyrus were all artists who had a strong connection to the 80-year-old legend.

title: Taylor Swift Remembers Dolly Parton’s ‘True Grace and True Grit’ in Statement After Her Death
summary: Taylor Swift paid tribute to Dolly Parton in a heartfelt statement written after her death.
story: Taylor Swift paid tribute to Dolly Parton’s “everlasting” legacy and example of “true grace and grit” following the country music legend’s death at 80 years old.
The global pop star joined a host of other music luminaries in remembering Parton after the singer’s family announced on Aug. 25 that she died after a “brief battle with cancer.”
Swift, whom Parton praised in a video at the 2023 iHeartRadio Music Awards, released a statement in the wake of her death.

“A world without Dolly doesn’t feel possible, real, or right,” she said. “But because of the eternally generous way she spent her time on this earth and the countless lives she changed for the better, her legacy will be an everlasting one.”
Swift, 36, was one of several female pop stars decades younger than Parton whom the country star befriended, including Beyoncé, Sabrina Carpenter and goddaughter Miley Cyrus.

“She was truly the gift that kept on giving,” Swift continued. “Dolly gave us someone to look up to while encouraging us to be who we are as individuals. Somehow she was able to give us her lessons about the world gently and honestly, simultaneously, and oftentimes hilariously. She managed to give the world the ultimate mystery and fantasy in some corners of her life, but to give full transparency in the ways that counted. Somehow she was true grace and true grit, all in one dazzling person. She possessed the softest heart when it came to the struggles of others, and a backbone of steel to defend her own self worth as an artist.”
Swift also noted Parton’s extensive philanthropic work, which included founding the Imagination Library. The organization has donated hundreds of millions of books to support child literacy.

“Along with her other fans, I am so grateful for all of it,” Swift said. “For the melodies and lyrics she wrote that thawed even the coldest hearts. For the millions of books she provided children all over the world so that they might fall in love with stories the way she did. For the tightropes she walked so that young girls like me could grow up dreaming of joining the circus too.
“Dolly, I’ll think of you each step of the way.”

title: Dolly Parton Visited TODAY More Than 50 Times. See Her Best Performances, Jokes and ‘Dollyisms’
summary: Dolly Parton was a frequent guest on TODAY over the years. Look back at some of her most memorable moments.
story: Dolly Parton, who died after a battle with cancer, on Aug. 25 at the age of 80, was a frequent guest on TODAY over the years, showcasing her trademark wit and big heart for viewers to see.

“I’m always happy to be on the TODAY show!” she said during a 2025 interview with Savannah Guthrie and Craig Melvin, in a spot where Savannah reminded her that she had been on the show more than 50 times.
The icon’s run of appearances began Aug. 23, 1978, and would span six decades. Her first sit-down interview was with then co-host Jane Pauley.

“I want to tell you, too, I think you’re great, and every time I’m up that early in the morning I watch you. And my husband’s watching you now,” she said, referencing her husband Carl Dean, who died in 2025.

She’s also brought her legendary pipes to the show. She took over the plaza in heels and a bright red dress for a concert in 2002 where she sang one of her trademark songs, “9 to 5,” from the movie of the same name. In 2016, she performed a dazzling rendition of “Coat of Many Colors” in a Studio 1A lit up with a rainbow.

When Dolly stopped by the show, memorable moments often followed. During a 2019 interview, everyone in the control room wore Dolly wigs, causing her to squeal in delight. That same year, she also sang “Jolene” as a duet with Hoda Kotb, with Savannah Guthrie accompanying on guitar.
“I think you girls are behind. You better stick to your hosting!” Parton joked at the time.
From the beginning, Parton also brought her unique vernacular with her.
“My momma always said that any old barn looked better with a little red paint on it,” she told Pauley with a laugh during that first 1978 interview.
“I’m out there hustling! That’s one of the reasons I’m out, I’m not going to go down on a sinking ship without looking for a dingy!” she also joked during a 1993 appearance.
Calling in to chat with Hoda and Jenna Bush Hager in 2022, she spoke frankly, joking about rumors she had certain body parts insured.
“Well, it’s not true. You can get new boobs, but you can’t get new legs,” she said.

Parton was also known for being humble. She initially declined her nomination for the Rock & Rock Hall of Fame in 2022. Her interviews showcased her modest attitude, and she often shared the secrets to her success. In 2019, she said the song “9 to 5” came to life simply because of her nails.
“I have my nails, too, my acrylic nails. That’s how I wrote ‘9 to 5’ on the set of ‘9 to 5,’” she said, confirming to Willie Geist in 2020 she actually “played” her nails on the record.
Parton, of course, was more than just music. She promoted childhood literacy with her Imagination Library, giving books to children all over the world.
“We’re trying to teach children to love books, to learn to read early,” she said during a 2000 interview.
Parton also brought a humanity with her, expressing her hopes that people be the best versions of themselves.

“Can’t we rise above? Can’t we show some love? Can’t we just lift up? And just help each other out?” she said in December 2022. “I’m going to try my best to try to bring as much joy as I can and lift people up as much as I can.”
Parton’s faith was on display during her TODAY appearances.
“I love everybody, I try to find the God light in everybody, and we all have it,” she said in May 2019.
In November 2019, she opened up about her own relationship with God.
“I just always had, with my conversations with God, I’d just ask him every day, as I still do, to lead me and guide me,” she said.
While Parton was known for her big hair and bright clothing, even in her first interview, she knew she wanted to be known for more than that.
“If they can see behind all this garbage, and if they can appreciate the music, and if they can appreciate me as a person, then that’s all I care about,” she said in 1978.

title: Tributes Pour in for Dolly Parton After Music Legend’s Death at Age 80
summary: The world is mourning the loss of country music legend Dolly Parton who died at age 82. Read tributes and reactions from Reba McEntire, Lily Tomlin and more.
story: The world is mourning the loss of beloved country music star Dolly Parton, who died Aug. 25 at a hospital in Nashville, according to her team. She was 80.

Her death comes a few weeks after she provided an update on her health in a video on Aug. 16 after she missed an event at Dollywood, telling fans, “Sometimes I get a little dizzy and I get dehydrated.”
The “Jolene” singer, who dealt with kidney stones earlier this year, also promised to keep active.
“All has gone well on the medical end of things, and I continue working away on all of our other projects,” she said.

Parton was a giant not just in country music, but entertainment as a whole, releasing her debut album, “Hello, I’m Dolly,” in 1967 before going on to win multiple Grammys and making the leap to the big screen, appearing in classics like the 1980 comedy “9 to 5” and 1989’s “Steel Magnolias.”
Here’s a look at how some famous friends are mourning her death.
Patti LaBelle
Parton used to famously use her acrylic fingernails to create rhythm for her music, and that includes a time when she and Patti LaBelle did it on her variety show, “Dolly,” in the ‘80s.
In a statement to NBC News, LaBelle remembered Parton’s “artistry” and “extraordinary life.”

“I am deeply saddened by the loss of my dear friend who was loved by all. Dolly’s artistry, brilliance, and extraordinary life inspired so many people, including me. Her light will forever shine! I send my deepest condolences to all of her loved ones and fans all over the world!”
Reba McEntire
Fellow country music legend and close friend Reba McEntire penned a tribute on X.

“Well, I just got the news that my buddy Dolly passed onto the higher and greater side,” she began. “Dolly, thank you for all the wonderful things you did for us here on earth. Your love, your music and you gave so much with your huge huge heart.”
She continued, “There will never ever be another you. We will remember and cherish every memory and every note you ever played and sang.”
McEntire said she knows Parton will be in heaven singing her favorite songs with all her loved ones.
“I’ll never forget the first time I met you and I’ll never forget our last conversation. I hold it with love in my heart. I will always love you, Reba,” she concluded.
Jenna Bush Hager

Jenna Bush Hager, who spoke with Parton on several occasions in interviews for TODAY, posted photos to Instagram on Aug. 25, along with a heartfelt message. Two of the photos show Jenna with Dolly during a conversation they had in Dollywood in 2019. At the time, Jenna said, her grandmother Jenna Welch had just passed away.

“As I write this, Dolly’s music is being played in the restaurant where I am eating,” Jenna said. “She was a legend. Her voice was unparalleled, but it was her utter originality and purity of spirit that will be sorely missed. We needed all that glitter and goodness. She gave with all that she was. In this picture of us, I had just recieved the news my grandmother, Jenna had passed away. I was already with her in Knoxville so she held me and gave me such grace. I’ll never forget that kindness. May we take just a little of her beauty and pass it on.
Dionne Warwick
Music icon Dionne Warwick uploaded a picture of her and Parton holding hands on stage together as they performed their duet “Peace Like a River.”
“I will certainly miss her laugher, jokes and her being. Rest well and in total peace my friend. My heart is heavy,” Warwick said.
Dollywood
The leader of Dollywood, the theme park near Knoxville, Tennessee, that attracts Parton’s legions of fans, issued a statement on Aug. 25 to NBC News.

The greatest privilege of my life has been helping Dolly bring her dreams to life at Dollywood,” Eugene Naughton, Dollywood Parks & Resorts President, said. “Dolly’s heart was as vast as the mountains she cherished, and her compassion knew no bounds. She inspired generations to dream boldly and love deeply. While we grieve her loss, we are honored and committed to carry her light forward. Her legacy will continue to shine in every melody sung, every smile shared and every dream kindled within these gates.”
Shirley MacLaine
Shirley MacLaine, who shared the screen with Parton in “Steel Magnolias,” said in a statement to NBC News, “God sent her to us, and she has returned home.”
Kelly Clarkson
Kelly Clarkson reflected on Parton’s legacy and why she was so beloved in her post.

“Dolly Parton had a way of making everyone feel special, and seen, and welcomed, and as if you were old friends,” she explained in her tribute. “I will miss her heart and her voice as I am sure millions will.”
She added, “What an incredible gift and talent she was and still is with an amazing catalogue of art she has left behind for all of us.”
Keith Urban
Keith Urban shared a brief message to his Instagram story that said, “Heartbroken today. Dolly Parton,” and included a broken heart. “Honestly...... I have no words right now.”
Producers of ‘Dolly: A True Original Musical’
The Broadway production inspired by the life and music of Parton said Aug. 25 after her death that the show will still go on.
“As was Dolly’s wish, the Broadway production of DOLLY: A True Original Musical will begin previews December 7 at the St. James Theatre in New York City.”
Keke Palmer
Keke Palmer, who co-starred with Parton in the 2012 musical dramedy “Joyful Noise,” shared a black-and-white photo of the icon on Instagram. She uploaded a picture of them in “Joyful Noise,” as well.
“I’m devastated. Truly,” she said in the caption.
Kacey Musgraves
Kacey Musgraves mourned Parton’s passing in a series of tweets.

“Dolly,” she wrote and included a broken heart emoji. “This one really hurts.” In a follow-up message, Musgraves said, “The world feels a lot less sparkly all of a sudden.” For her final tweet, she added, “So glad she’s with her Carl Dean,” referring to Parton’s late husband who died in 2023. “No one talk to me today.”
Lily Tomlin

Parton’s “9 to 5” co-star Lily Tomlin uploaded Jamie Lee Curtis’ tribute — which said “Thank you, Dolly. For all of it,” beneath a black-and-white snap of Parton and Dean — to her Instagram story. Tomlin added Parton’s version of “I Will Always Love You” to the post.
She then shared a few pictures of Parton on the next slide, including one of them with fellow “9 to 5” star Jane Fonda and their reunion at the 69th Emmy Awards.
She also praised Parton for being a “comedy treasure” in a third slide featuring Parton’s hit “9 to 5.”
Khloé Kardashian
Khloé Kardashian posted a photo to her Instagram story of her with Parton, writing that she was “heartbroken,” along with a longer message about her legacy.

“Some people are so so extraordinary, their existence feels almost impossible. Dolly was one of those people,” she said, in part. “A once-in-a-lifetime soul. A woman whose light, heart, talent and humanity changed this world forever.”
Parton appeared on Kardashian’s podcast, “Khloé In Wonder Land,” last July.
Paris Hilton
Paris Hilton posted a message on X alongside a photo of herself with the country legend.

“Her talent, heart and kindness touched so many lives, and she truly left this world better than she found it,” Hilton wrote. “Sending all my love to her family, friends and everyone who loved her. Rest in peace, Dolly.”
Sarah Jessica Parker
Although she never got the chance to meet her in person, Sarah Jessica Parker still felt a connection to Parton.
In her tribute on Instagram, she wrote, “No!!!!!! I never met @dollyparton but my gosh, did I love her. I don’t think any of us had to know her to love her.”
She called Parton “one of the greatest this country ever produced” and also pointed out her philanthropic efforts.
“What a loss. But aren’t we so lucky,so fortunate for the endless gifts she shared. With the world. Godspeed and RIP. You will be terribly missed,” she said.
Brandi Cyrus

Brandi Cyrus, whose younger sister Miley Cyrus was Parton’s goddaughter, posted three broken hearts on her Instagram story. She also shared a picture of Parton with her horse and added Miley Cyrus’ song “Rainbowland,” which featured Parton.
Grand Ole Opry
The Grand Ole Opry praised Parton for being “a true music icon” in a post on X.

“There is no doubt Dolly’s mark on the world, and on us here at the Grand Ole Opry, will be deeply felt for generations to come. She taught us to always lead with kindness, generosity, and compassion,” the historic music venue said. “May her legacy live on through her songs, the lives she touched, and the countless artists she inspired. There will never, ever be another one like her. We will always love you, Dolly.”
Correction (Aug. 26, 7:55 a.m.): A previous version of this story stated Dolly Parton died at her home in Nashville. The story has been updated to reflect she died at a hospital.

title: Dolly Parton’s Siblings: What to Know About Her 11 Brothers and Sisters
summary: Dolly Parton, who died on Aug. 25, was one of 12 siblings. Her death was announced by her sister Cassie’s son Bryan Seaver. Here’s what to know about Dolly Parton’s siblings.
story: Dolly Parton, country music icon and 10-time Grammy winning singer-songwriter, died “peacefully” on Aug. 25 in Nashville, Tennessee, according to a news release from True Public Relations.
Her death was announced in a video message by her nephew Bryan Seaver, the son of Dolly Parton’s sister Cassie Parton. He did not provide a cause of death.
Dolly Parton is one of 12 children. Raised by Robert and Avie Lee Parton, the kids grew up in the Appalachia region of Tennessee, according to the Country Music Hall of Fame.

Dolly Parton has six living brothers and sisters: Willadeene, Robert Jr., Stella, Cassie, Freida and Rachel. Five of her brothers have died: Larry, in 1955 when he was just a baby; Floyd, in 2018 at age 61; Randy, in 2021 at age 67; David, in 2024 at age 82; and Coy, in July 2026 at age 82, per People.
Read on for everything you need to know about Dolly Parton’s 11 siblings.
Willadeene Parton

Willadeene Parton, born March 24, 1940, is the eldest of Dolly Parton’s siblings. She “tends to act as a second mother to her younger siblings,” according to a post on Dolly Parton’s official website.

Willadeene Parton, now 86, pursued a career as an author. In 1996, she published a memoir about the Parton clan titled “Smoky Mountain Memories: Stories from the Hearts of the Parton Family.” The following year, she released “All-Day Singing & Dinner on the Ground,” a compilation of recipes from the Parton family.
David Parton

David Parton, who worked as a bridge builder superintendent, died Nov. 15, 2024, at age 82 at his home in White Pine, Tennessee, sister Stella Parton announced. A cause of death has not been revealed.
Sharing news of her brother’s death, Stella Parton posted on Threads, saying that her brother “finally got his angel wings. RIP dear soul. Love you forever.”
Before his death, David Parton largely lived his life out of the spotlight, though he had been photographed escorting Dolly Parton to events, according to Woman’s World.
Stella Parton

Stella Parton, an acclaimed musician born May 4, 1949, was 11 when she made her recording debut with sisters Dolly and Cassie Parton, singing on their uncle Bill Owens’ album, per the Smoky Mountain DNA website, which traces Dolly Parton’s family origins.
Since then, Stella Parton has released more than 30 albums, starting with “I Want to Hold You (In My Dreams Tonight),” which came out in 1975.

Stella Parton, now 77, released a memoir in 2011 titled “Tell It Sister, Tell It: Memories, Music and Miracles.” She has explored acting, too, with appearances in the film “Dolly Parton’s Coat of Many Colors” (2015) and “Dolly Parton’s Christmas of Many Colors: Circle of Love” (2016).
While promoting the 2022 Pure Flix original movie “Nothing is Impossible,” Stella Parton revealed to People that she considers herself a “loner in (her) family.”
