“Everybody knows that I’m independent,” she said. “But if they need me, if they call me out to help with something, producing, consulting or whatever, I’m always there.”
Cassie Parton
Cassie Parton, born on Feb. 12, 1951, first recorded music at age 10, singing backup vocals with sisters Dolly and Stella Parton, the Smoky Mountain DNA project revealed.
In 1970, she sang with her sisters on “The Porter Wagoner Show,” and she performed as a vocalist in the 2013 Dollywood production “My People: Dolly’s Letter Home,” according to Knox News.
She also appeared in an episode of the TV series “Dolly” and had a role in the 2022 film “Dolly Parton’s Mountain Magic Christmas,” according to IMDb. Nowadays, she leads a fairly private life.
Her son Bryan Seaver served as Dolly Parton’s head of security for two decades.
Randy Parton
Randy Parton, born Dec. 15, 1953, died in 2021 at the age of 67. On Jan. 21, 2021, Dolly shared his death on Facebook, revealing that her brother had died from cancer.

“The family and I are grieving his loss, but we know he is in a better place than we are at this time,” the country icon said in her statement. “We are a family of faith, and we believe that he is with God and that he is joined by members of the family that have gone on before and have welcomed him with joy and open arms.”

Like his older sister, Randy Parton achieved success in music and entertainment. Famous for his headline performances at Dollywood, the singer-songwriter released several hits that graced Billboard’s Hot Country Songs chart, including “Hold Me Like You Never Had Me,” “Shot Full of Love,” “Don’t Cry Baby,” “Oh, No” and “A Stranger in Her Bed,” according to the music publication.
Larry Parton
Larry Parton, Robert and Avie Lee Parton’s ninth child and fifth son, died days after his birth in July 1955. Dolly Parton was 9 years old at the time of her brother’s death.
Floyd Parton
Floyd Parton and twin sister Freida Parton were born June 1, 1957. Like many of his siblings, Floyd Parton pursued a career in the music industry, often collaborating with Dolly Parton.
He penned her 1991 duet with Ricky Van Shelton, “Rockin’ Years” and wrote “Nickels and Dimes” for her 1978 album “Heartbreaker.”
Floyd Parton died Dec. 6, 2018, at the age of 61. The Parton family paid tribute to Floyd Parton at a private memorial in Tennessee, reported Billboard.

“Dolly, and the entire Parton family, wish to thank everyone for their kindness,” the family said in a statement to People at the time. “Yesterday, we laid our sweet baby brother to rest. We all sang his lovely song, ‘Rockin’ Years,’ together as a family at the service to say goodbye to him. He lived a short life of love and beautiful songs.”
Freida Parton
Freida Parton, born June 1, 1957, is Floyd Parton’s twin sister. Freida Parton ventured into the realm of music but diverged from her family’s country origins, singing hard rock songs.

Later in life, Freida Parton became an ordained minister. She told Knoxville News Sentinel in an interview in April 2014 that she had opened Parton Family Wedding Chapel & Antiques, a wedding chapel and store, in the family’s native Sevierville, Tennessee. However, the business appears to have closed.
Rachel Parton George

Rachel Parton George was born on Aug. 31, 1959. She’s known for her portrayal of Doralee Rhodes Brooks in the ABC sitcom “9 to 5,” which was based on the 1980 comedy film of the same name that starred Dolly Parton.

In addition to acting, Rachel Parton George released a country album in 1984, per the Smoky Mountain DNA website. According to her author page for Penguin Random House, she also performed in her family’s singing group.
In September 2024, the youngest sibling of the Parton clan released a cookbook with sister Dolly Parton called “Good Lookin’ Cookin’: A Year of Meals.”
Ahead of the release, Dolly Parton shared a picture of her and her sister on social media.

“The best part of creating this cookbook is getting to spend quality time with my sister Rachel,” Dolly Parton captioned the post with a red heart emoji. “We can’t wait to share our recipes with you all, pre-order now at the link in my bio!”
Coy and Robert Lee Parton Jr.
Dolly’s other siblings — her older brother Coy Parton and younger brother Robert Lee Parton Jr. — largely led lives out of the spotlight.
Coy Parton, who worked as a crane operator, died in July 2026, according to an obituary shared by Atchley Funeral Home. A cause of death was not provided.

title: What Dolly Parton Said About Not Having Children with Husband Carl Dean
summary: Dolly Parton, the country music superstar whose career stretched from the Tennessee mountains to Hollywood, has died.
story: Dolly Parton, the country music superstar whose career stretched from the Tennessee mountains to Hollywood, has died. She was 80.
Her nephew, Bryan Seaver shared the news August 25 on Instagram, remembering Parton’s extraordinary life and legacy. Seaver, whose mother is Parton’s sister Cassie, did not share a cause of death.

Parton’s passing comes more than a year after the loss of her husband, Carl Dean, her partner of nearly six decades, who died at 82 on March 3, 2025, after the pair spent more than 60 years together. The couple did not have children, a subject Parton spoke about candidly over the years, including the way she came to understand that part of her life.
At her request, immediate family will honor Parton at a private service while fans are encouraged to pay tribute to her on social media.
Why Dolly Parton Never Had Children
The couple never had any children, and Parton, 79, has said that her journey to becoming a country music star and successful businesswoman depended on the sacrifices she’s made in her personal life.
Parton spoke with Oprah Winfrey about her career and her life with Dean during an episode of “The Oprah Conversation” on Apple TV+ in 2020.
“Since I had no kids, and my husband was pretty independent, I had freedom,” she said. “So I think a big part of my whole success is the fact that I was free to work.”
Parton also said she was OK with not having children in an interview on TODAY in 2017.
“God has a plan for everything,” she said. “I think it probably was his plan for me not to have kids so everybody’s kids could be mine. And they are now.”

But Parton had been talking about her decision — and her feelings about motherhood — for decades. In a 1984 interview with Interview Magazine, she spoke candidly about never becoming pregnant and how she eventually came to see herself as a mother figure to her extended family.

“I couldn’t have children, I tried to for years. I’ve never been pregnant in my life,” Parton said. “When I was a girl and fooling around, I was scared to death I’d get pregnant, and then when I got married and wanted to have children, I couldn’t have any. But I don’t miss it. I did for awhile, but I realize that I am everybody’s mother. I’ve raised five of my younger brothers and sisters, and now their kids call me Aunt Grannie. I’m like the grandma and the aunt.”
The couple largely lived independent lives while Parton was often off touring and performing, and Dean spent much of his life out of the spotlight after they tied the knot in 1966.
How Dolly Parton Helped Other Children
Parton has been involved in the lives of millions of kids through her Imagination Library, which has gifted hundreds of millions of books to children from birth until they enter kindergarten.

“And I didn’t have children because I believed that God didn’t mean for me to have kids so everybody’s kids could be mine, so I could do things like Imagination Library, because if I hadn’t had the freedom to work, I wouldn’t have done all the things I’ve done,” Parton told Winfrey in 2020. “I wouldn’t be in a position to do all of the things I’m doing now.”

Winfrey also asked Parton if she has had to make sacrifices in order to achieve her level of success, which includes 25 No. 1 songs on the Billboard country charts, 10 Grammy Awards, an acting career and owning the popular theme park Dollywood and several other businesses in her home state of Tennessee.

“I’ve made sacrifices, but I think, like I said, I believe what I know I’m supposed to do,” Parton said. “I’ve made the sacrifice of time ... and not having time to spend with family, and you give up family and friends, vacation, and work without end, 24/7, 365, but you got to make the sacrifice.”

title: Who Was Dolly Parton’s Husband, Carl Dean? Everything She Said About Their 60-Year Marriage
summary: Here’s what Dolly Parton said about her husband Carl Thomas Dean before she died. Here’s a story about their marriage.
story: Dolly Parton and her husband, Carl Thomas Dean, were married for nearly 60 years, and died within a year and a half of each other.
While the country music legend had been in the spotlight since the ‘50s, her relationship with the businessman mostly remained out of the limelight.

Parton, a star on the stage, television and film, died on Aug. 25, 2026, at the age of 80. Her nephew Bryan Seaver confirmed her passing in a video message shared on her Instagram page. He did not mention a cause of death.
The news of her death came about a year after Parton had to postpone multiple concerts as a she faced “health challenges.”
Her death also followed the loss of her beloved husband, who died on March 3, 2025, at the age of 82.
She penned a sweet statement at the time reflecting on their decades of marriage.

“Carl and I spent many wonderful years together. Words can’t do justice to the love we shared for over 60 years. Thank you for your prayers and sympathy,” she wrote on her Instagram, alongside the announcement of his death.
Dean, who was from Nashville, was a businessman without any industry ties. In a 2023 interview for “What Would Dolly Do? Radio,” the singer gave insight into her long-standing private relationship.
“Carl has never been in the limelight and all, never wanted to be in it. He don’t like it,” said Parton.
She shared that after one public outing, he knew that life wasn’t for him.

“He went to one thing with me early on when we first married to a BMI Song of the Year (event), and he came out there taking off his tuxedo, his tie and all that and said, ‘Don’t ever ask me to go to another one of these damn things because I ain’t going,’” she said. “I never asked him and he never did.”
The couple also never had children, though in a 1984 interview with Andy Warhol in Interview Magazine said they tried to “for years.”

Parton spoke about how independence in her marriage led to a thriving career, telling Oprah in 2020, “Since I had no kids, and my husband was pretty independent, I had freedom. I think a big part of my whole success is the fact that I was free to work.
But despite their different approaches to public life, the two had a lasting relationship, celebrating 58 years of marriage before his death.
Here’s a look back at the major events in their relationship, from their first meeting at a laundromat to his support for her music.
Parton and Dean Met in 1964

Many people can live in a city for years before going on a date, but Parton met her husband on her very first day in Nashville. She told the New York Times that she brought a lot of dirty clothes with her, and stopped at the “Wishy-Washy” laundromat.

“After I’d put my clothes in the machine, I started walkin’ down the street, just looking at my new home, and this guy hollered at me, and I waved,” Parton told the New York Times in 1976. “Bein’ from the country, I spoke to everybody. And he came over and, well, it was Carl, my husband.”
In that 1976 interview, Parton had more to say about their first meeting.

“I wouldn’t go out with him. I mean, that was somethin’ we was taught. You gotta know somebody or they may take you on a back road and kill you. But I said, ‘You’re welcome to come up to the house tomorrow because I’m baby‐sittin’ my little nephew.’”
She said he came over every day for a week, and they sat on the porch and talked. “I wouldn’t even take him in the house,” she said.
But the first day she didn’t have to babysit, she said that Dean took her to meet his parents. “Cause he said he knew right the minute he saw me that that’s the one he wanted.”
They Had a Secret 1966 Wedding

After dating for about two years, Dean proposed to her and they wed in May of that same year. While preparing for her wedding, the upcoming nuptials caused tension between her and her then-manager, Fred Foster.
“He asked me not to get married. He said it’ll make it so much harder if you’re married with all this promotion,” she said in a 2012 interview with Chattanooga, Tennessee, NBC affiliate WRCB.
“My mother-in-law had already sent out invitations,” Parton said. “It broke her heart because I said we had to call the wedding off.”

But that didn’t stop the two from getting married in a more private ceremony the following weekend. Only her mother, Avia Lee Owens, and Pastor Don Duvall and his wife were present at Ringgold Baptist Church where they tied the knot.
Parton Wrote ‘Jolene’ in 1973

One of her most famous songs, “Jolene” tells the story of a woman begging for Jolene not to “take her man.” Parton said this was inspired by a “flirtation” that her husband had with a woman working at the local bank.

“She got this terrible crush on my husband,” Parton told NPR in 2008. “And he just loved going to the bank because she paid him so much attention. It was kinda like a running joke between us — when I was saying, ‘Hell, you’re spending a lot of time at the bank. I don’t believe we’ve got that kind of money.’ So it’s really an innocent song all around, but sounds like a dreadful one.”
Parton Got Close with Her Bandleader in the 1980s

In a 1986 interview with Ladies’ Home Journal, republished in her book, “Dolly on Dolly: Interviews and Encounters with Dolly Parton,” the country icon spoke about how she had gotten “wrapped up” in an “affair of the heart” in 1982.

She told the outlet she’d faced the disloyalty of “a special friend, an affair of the heart, which just about killed me. Oh, I cried an ocean. But I ain’t gonna talk about it anymore,” she said, playfully. “I’ve got to keep some mystery.”
Parton said at the time that she and Dean were not divorcing, reiterating what she has said years earlier.

“We’ll just always be together,” she told People in 1982. “To him it’s all a joke. There ain’t a man in this world could ever live up to my husband. That’s one of the things that keeps me from going too far.”

In a 1982 interview with Barbara Walters, Parton confirmed that she’d been stuck at home in Tennessee for health issues alongside her husband. She joked that her months at home had “just about busted” their relationship.
“I’m glad to be going,” she explained. “He’s glad for me to be going and so we’re glad to get back to our abnormal.”
In the Walters interview, Parton added that she and her husband were “flirts” but were faithful “best I know how.”

“I just love people there and ... being a woman away from home, there are these good looking guys that come on to you pretty strong. And every now and then I like to come on pretty strong myself,” she said. “But I know that I’ve got something at home, that I wouldn’t threaten or take a chance on losing for anything in the world.”
Parton Said She and Dean Were Still a Team in 1997

In a 1997 interview with Out Magazine in which she promoted her latest collection of dance club remixes, Parton explained that she and her longtime companion, Judy Ogle, was “just an old maid” and not her lover.

“People think because she’s never married that she must be a lesbian, and because we’ve been together, that we must be lovers. But the fact is, I think Judy would rather be called a lesbian than an old maid,” she quipped. “If I was gay, I’d certainly never find a finer person than Judy as a mate. I’m as close to her just about as I am with (my) husband.”
She also responded to rumors about her husband being out of the picture.
“They don’t ... see my husband because he hates being in the limelight. But I see him all the time,” she told the outlet.
Parton added that the secret to her decadeslong marriage was simple.
“We just make a point to enjoy the stuff we enjoy and stay out of each other’s faces. I don’t get in his s---, and he don’t get in mine. And we get along great.”

The Out interview, along with many others, were reported in the 2017 book “Not Dumb and Not Blonde: Dolly in Conversation.” The book — which cites Parton and Randy Schmidt as authors — collected and published interviews with Parton dating as far back as 1967.
Parton and Dean Renewed Their Vows in 2016
In May 2016, Parton and Dean got the wedding they planned years ago, but never got to have. The private affair was held at their Nashville-area home, and she said they “just had fun with it.”
“I got all dressed up in the most beautiful gown you’ve ever seen and dressed that husband of mine up. He looked like a handsome dude out of Hollywood,” Parton told Rolling Stone.

“We had a few family and friends around. We didn’t plan anything big at all because we didn’t want any kind of strain, any kind of tension, any kind of commotion, so we planned it cleverly and carefully. We just had a simple little ceremony at our chapel at our place. We just had just a few people who needed to be there to make sure they got the pictures and the few things that we needed.”
Parton also said that their vow renewal inspired a large portion of her album “Plain and Simple,” which was released that August.
Parton Surprised Dean with a Playboy Look for His Birthday in 2021
In honor of her husband’s birthday, Parton donned a throwback look that she knew he would love. In July 2021, she put on a Playboy bunny costume in his honor.

“Remember sometime back I said I was going to pose on the cover of Playboy Magazine when I was 75? Well, I’m 75 and they don’t have a magazine anymore,” she said in a video at the time. “But my husband always loved the original cover of ‘Playboy’ so I was trying to think of something to do to make him happy.”

Parton was the first country star to pose for the now-defunct magazine, appearing on the cover in 1978. According to her official website, her contract at the time had “very specific parameters that did not include nudity,” but she still wore the classic bunny suit.
In her 2021 video, she said that she had a new cover made with her fresh outfit and “the new Dolly.”
“Well, the old new Dolly,” she said, good-naturedly. “In the first one, I was kind of a little butterball in that one. Well, I’m string cheese now.”
“But he’ll probably think I’m cream cheese,” Parton said with a wink. “I hope!”
Parton Released Her 2023 Rock Album with Dean’s Support
The singer released her “Rockstar” album in 2023. On “What Would Dolly Do? Radio,” she spoke more about her husband’s reaction to hearing the album.

“I played him the whole album and he said, which to me was the greatest compliment in the world, he said, ‘You know, it’s pretty good,’” she said. “That would be like anybody else saying, ‘Oh, that’s best I ever heard. That’s just so fantastic.’”
She said Dean has always been honest with her about his opinions.

“I had done a couple of things in the past, just some rock things. He said, ‘It’s OK. It’s OK,’” Parton added. “He’s very honest. We have such a great relationship. I know not to ask him if I don’t want an honest answer.”
Parton Announced Dean’s Death in 2025
On March 3, 2025, a statement was shared on Parton’s Instagram announcing the death of her husband.

“Carl Dean, husband of Dolly Parton, passed away March 3rd in Nashville at the age of 82. He will be laid to rest in a private ceremony with immediate family attending. He was survived by his siblings Sandra and Donnie,” the statement read, followed by a personal message by Parton.
“Carl and I spent many wonderful years together. Words can’t do justice to the love we shared for over 60 years,” the singer wrote. “Thank you for your prayers and sympathy.”

title: Jenna and Sheinelle React to Each Other’s Celebrity ‘Hall Passes’ with Surprise and Delight
summary: Jenna Bush Hager and Sheinelle Jones discuss their celebrity hall passes, which include Colin Firth, Brandi Carlile, Tyson Beckford and Jude Bellingham.
story: Jenna Bush Hager and Sheinelle Jones have some thoughts about their celebrity hall passes.

For those uninitiated to the concept, the hall pass is the notion that someone in a relationship can explore a romantic or physical relationship with another person without penalty from their significant other.

During the Aug. 25 episode of TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle, the co-hosts agreed a hall pass is nothing more than fun before Jenna said her hall pass “from back in the day” is Academy Award winner Colin Firth.
“He’s very handsome,” Jenna said as a picture of him appeared on the screen.
“That’s your hall pass from days of old?” Sheinelle asked.
“Days of old and days of new,” Jenna replied.
“This is all this is good. I’m getting to know your type,” Sheinelle said.
“I also think it’s a whole vibe. It’s not just aesthetic,” she continued, while Jenna outlined how Firth is British and starred in “Pride and Prejudice” and the “Bridget Jones” movies.
Jenna then mentioned her other choice would be the singer-songwriter Brandi Carlile.
“Also a vibe,” Sheinelle said.
Jenna said Carlile and her wife, Catherine Carlile, are aware that she has previously said she would leave her husband, Henry Hager, for the singer.
“Also, I’ve never kissed a woman,” Jenna told Sheinelle. “I feel like I need to say that. I have a husband, too, so there’s a lot of barriers, but it’s the vibe.”
The conversation then shifted to Sheinelle’s pick. She explained that being on a show like TODAY complicates matters because sometimes she can end up on-air with the person she fancies.
“That’s what happened to me,” she said after recalling how she had a crush on Tyson Beckford.
“The whole world knew I used to be obsessed with Tyson Beckford. I had him in my locker. It was like Tevin Campbell and Tyson Beckford,” she continued as a photo of the model splashed on the screen.
“He’s very handsome,” Jenna said.
Sheinelle said was filling in on TODAY some time ago and co-hosted with Beckford without any issue.

“I have a gear where I like turned off that gear, and then we became and we were cool,” she said before saying they were later seated together at the Victoria’s Secret fashion show, prompting Jenna said she could’ve acted on her crush.
“That’s the thing. It’s different when you have them on your locker versus like, ‘OK, so what’s coming up today?’” Sheinelle said.
Sheinelle then dished on her more current celebrity crush, saying, “I’m more of the auntie in the situation,” while Jenna said it gives off “Lolita vibes.”

“This is cougar vibes, but I’m just saying I think I like a physique, and it happens to be this one,” Sheinelle continued as a picture of British soccer star Jude Bellingham popped up on the screen. “He’s all over my Instagram feed because you can’t lie to Instagram.”
Plus, Sheinelle added, “he seems like a really nice guy.”

title: Country Music Legend Dolly Parton Dies at 80
summary: Dolly Parton, the legendary country music singer who also became a popular star of TV and movies, has died, her family announced.
story: Dolly Parton, the legendary country music singer who also became a popular star of TV and movies, has died, her family announced. She was 80 years old.

Her nephew Bryan Seaver announced her death in a video message shared to Instagram Aug. 25. Seaver, son of Parton’s sister Cassie Parton, did not provide a cause of death. The singer died “peacefully” on Aug. 25 in Nashville, Tennessee, according to a news release from True Public Relations. At her request, immediate family will honor Parton at a private service while fans are encouraged to pay tribute to her on social media.
Weeks before her death, Parton commented on her ongoing health struggles after missing the opening of a new ride at Dollywood.

“I’ve told you before, all my fans, that I’ve had a few little health issues, and sometimes I get a little dizzy and I get dehydrated,” she said in a video that played at the theme park. “So my Nashville doctor has kind of clipped my wings, saying, ‘You ain’t traveling this week.’”
Seaver shared a touching tribute to his aunt in the video announcing her death. He served as her head of security for two decades, following in the footsteps of his father.

“I have imagined the heaviness of this moment, but haven’t truly felt it until now,” Seaver said. “It is an honor, an honor that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness, but the sadness lies with us, not with Dolly. Dolly has lived in the light, and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by (her late husband) Carl, her parents and countless others who have watched her and longed for her to meet them in the heavens.”
He said Parton “opened doors” for her family as well as “generations of singers, songwriters, musicians and dreamers from every walk of life, and across every continent.”
Parton died a year after her husband of nearly 60 years, Carl Thomas Dean, had passed away at age 82. They wed in 1966 and largely kept their relationship out of the spotlight.

Born Dolly Rebecca Parton on Jan. 19, 1946, Parton, the fourth of 12 children, began life in a small log cabin in rural Pittman Center, a rural East Tennessee town near the Great Smoky Mountains. When she was a young girl, her family relocated to a nearby farm in Locust Ridge. Parton’s father, a sharecropper turned tobacco farmer, struggled with illiteracy, which inspired Parton to launch the Imagination Library, a children’s literacy program, in 1995, she told the Belfast Telegraph.
As a child, Parton sang on local television and radio. At 13, Johnny Cash introduced her for her 1959 debut at the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville.

Just a day after graduating high school in 1964, Parton moved to Nashville for a career in music. A multi-instrumentalist, she teamed up with her uncle, Bill Owens, to co-write songs that became hits for Bill Phillips and Skeeter Davis. In 1967, country star and TV personality Porter Wagoner handpicked her to be his new duet partner on “The Porter Wagoner Show.”
In 1967, Parton released her debut solo album, “Hello, I’m Dolly,” which rose to the number 11 spot on the Billboard Top Country Albums chart.

By the early 1970s, Parton had become a solo success. She mined her “dirt poor” upbringing in her homespun lyrics, recalling how her mother compensated for the family’s poverty with her ingenuity on  “Coat of Many Colors,” “My Tennessee Mountain Home,” and scored additional hits with “Travelin Man,” “Jolene” and her own recording of “I Will Always Love You,” which would later become a global hit for Whitney Houston.

Decades before Taylor Swift crossed over from country to pop, Parton, who scored 25 No. 1 singles on the Billboard country music charts, saw her 1977 album “Here You Come Again” landing in the Top 20 on the Billboard pop album chart. The album’s title track becoming Parton’s first Top 10 pop single.
As Parton’s fanbase widened in the mid- to late-1970s, her TV appearances multiplied, including a joint special with Carol Burnett on CBS, “Dolly & Carol in Nashville.”

By the 1980s, Parton had also become a box-office draw. She co-starred with Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin in the hit comedy “9 to 5” (1980), and also wrote and recorded the movie’s chart-topping theme song, earning an Academy Award nomination for best song. Her movie appearances over the years included roles in “The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas” (1982), “Steel Magnolias” (1989) and “Straight Talk” (1992).

Over the decades, Parton’s audience only broadened as she continued releasing music and appearing on television and in movies. She also made frequent in-person appearances at her Dollywood theme park in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee.
Parton gained attention early in her career for her flamboyant onstage attire and bouncy platinum blond wigs.

“My true belief with most things, you’ve got to really find out who you are, what makes you happy, what you’re comfortable in, and if you feel like you look your best, according to your rules, then you are going to do your best. I really believe that,” the singer said on the premiere episode of her 2023 podcast series, “What Would Dolly Do? Radio.”
In recent years, restless Parton showed no signs of slowing down, explaining during a 2023 interview on “Greatest Hits Radio”  that she was not “one to sit around doing nothing.”

“I would never retire. I’ll just hopefully drop dead in the middle of a song on stage someday, and hopefully one I’ve written. That’s how I hope to go,” she said during the chat. “Of course, we don’t have much of a choice in that.”

In 2020, she produced and starred in the Netflix musical film “Dolly Parton’s Christmas on the Square,” for which she won an Emmy. The following year, her 49th solo studio album, “Rockstar,” became her highest-charting Billboard 200 album, peaking in the No. 3 spot. in 2024, Parton announced she was working on an autobiographical Broadway musical scheduled to debut in 2026.
She also made it a point to collaborate with female pop stars decades younger, including Beyoncé, Sabrina Carpenter and goddaughter Miley Cyrus.
Parton and Dean never welcomed children of their own.
“God has a plan for everything,” she said during a visit TODAY in 2017. “I think it probably was his plan for me not to have kids so everybody’s kids could be mine.”
Days before her death, Parton told People that her health issues related to things “I just didn’t pay attention to when I was watching over Carl.”

She first went public about recent “health challenges” in September 2025 after she postponed a string of concerts in Las Vegas. The singer did not specify at the time what health struggles she faced but said, “my doctors tell me that I must have a few procedures.”
In May 2026, Parton said in a video message she was dealing with kidney stones and that her immune system and digestive system “got all out of whack over the past couple of three years.”

“The good news is I’m responding really well to meds and treatments, and I’m improving every day. Now, the bad news is it’s going to take me a little while before I’m up to stage-performance level, because some of the meds and treatments make me a little ‘swimmy-headed,’ as my grandma used to say,” she said at the time.

title: The ‘30 Rock’ Cast Will Reunite for the Show’s 20th Anniversary in a Live Special That Won’t Be Televised
summary: “30 Rock” stars Tina Fey, Alec Baldwin, Tracy Morgan, Jane Krakowski and Jack McBrayer will reunite for a live event in honor of the show’s 20th anniversary.
story: Liz Lemon is back!

“30 Rock” stars Tina Fey, Alec Baldwin, Tracy Morgan, Jane Krakowski and Jack McBrayer will appear at a special one-night only event in honor of the 20th anniversary of the show’s premiere. There will also be appearances by the extended “30 Rock” cast, as well as other special guests.

“Listen up tens, a five is speaking!” Fey said in a press release announcing the event. “Please join us to celebrate the 20th anniversary of the show Tom Shales once said ‘needs a better premise and funnier dialogue … and most of all a more commanding performer in the starring role.’”
All net proceeds from the reunion will benefit The Boys and Girls Club of Harlem.

“We’re honored to be named the charitable partner for this celebration,” Boys and Girls Club of Harlem President and CEO Shaba R. Keys said in the release. “All net proceeds go directly toward the after-school, academic, and career programs that help more than 2,000 Harlem young people each year chart a path to their own futures—and we’re grateful to be part of a night this special.”
When Is the ‘30 Rock’ Event?
The event, which will not be televised, will take place Oct. 11 at New York City’s Radio City Music Hall, which is located across the street from the actual 30 Rockefeller Plaza.
How Can I Get Tickets to the ‘30 Rock’ Event?
Tickets go on sale with various presales beginning Aug. 26 at 10 a.m. ET. The general ticket sale gets underway Aug. 27 at 10 a.m. ET on ticketmaster.com.
“30 Rock,” which was created by Fey, aired for seven seasons between 2006 and 2013 on NBC. The cast previously reunited during the COVID-19 pandemic.

During its run, “30 Rock” won 16 Emmy Awards, including three for outstanding comedy series. Baldwin twice won an Emmy for outstanding actor in a comedy series, while Fey took home outstanding actress in a comedy series once. She also won a pair of Emmys for her writing on the series, as well.
“30 Rock” is currently streaming on Peacock.

title: Why Is Simon Cowell Missing Weeks of ‘America’s Got Talent’?
summary: Simon Cowell’s spot on the “America’s Got Talent” judging panel will be vacant for the next few weeks. Find out why.
story: Simon Cowell’s spot on the “America’s Got Talent” judging panel will be vacant for the next few weeks as he undergoes back surgery.
“Obviously medical matters are private but it’s routine and he will be back in a few weeks,” the 66-year-old music executive’s representative said in a statement to Entertainment Weekly.
Cowell’s rep did not immediately respond to TODAY.com’s request for additional comment.

Cowell sits on the judging panel with Howie Mandel, Sofia Vergara and Mel B. The quartet are currently deciding which contestants will advance from the quarterfinals stage. The rep did not confirm when the toughest judge is expected to return to Season 21, which premiered in June.
It’s not yet confirmed if a guest will fill in for Cowell at the judge’s table.

News of Cowell’s surgery was first reported by TMZ. Sources with direct knowledge told the publication that he is undergoing a routine procedure related to his back and that there is no indication of a new major health crisis.
The television personality has had to undergo an operation to treat his back problems before.

In August 2020, he had a six-hour surgery after breaking his back in multiple places, his rep told TODAY.com at the time. The operation involved many procedures and fusions, and required a metal rod to be placed in Cowell’s back.
A spokesperson said that Cowell injured his back after falling from his electric bike at his home in Malibu.
A year later, he opened up about the severity of the situation while appearing on “The Kelly Clarkson Show.”
“I was like a millimeter away from breaking my spine, which would have been a disaster,” he revealed. “So in a weird way it was kind of meant to happen because I was really pushing my luck.”
Dowel recalled that his son Eric was with him when he was “thrown about 8 feet in the air” and landed on the ground.

“This is at the front of my house and the only thing I thought was, ‘I can’t lie here.’ And you’re not supposed to move. I knew I’d broken my back in that second, somehow managed to get back into my bedroom,” he added.
He said in addition to a large scar, he was left with a titanium rod and screws in his back following the surgery.
Cowell also addressed the accident during an interview with TODAY’s Jason Kennedy in May 2023.
“It was painful, it wasn’t great,” he said about the fall.

“However, I was so unfit before the accident. I didn’t know how unfit I was until I had to do all this stuff afterwards,” he continued. “And I’m like, ‘My God.’ Things like that, I believe, happened for a reason.”
He also shared that he planned to still ride his bike despite the injury.
“I’m obsessed with these things,” he said.

title: Oil prices dip as cautious optimism over Iran trumps new fears of Russian escalation in Ukraine
summary: Oil prices tumbled as headlines from the Middle East renewed optimism in global energy markets, and muted fears of a Russian escalation in Ukraine.
story: Crude oil prices dropped for a third day Wednesday as markets weighed a series of potentially positive developments in the Middle East against new fears of Russian escalation in Ukraine and dwindling U.S. reserves.
U.S. crude oil fell as low as $79 per barrel early Wednesday for the first time since Aug. 13. The international oil benchmark Brent dropped to around $85 a barrel.

But around midday Wednesday, oil prices made an unexpected U-turn and moved slightly higher on reports of a plan by Russian President Vladimir Putin to escalate his war with Ukraine, 4½ years after the Kremlin invaded its former Soviet satellite.
Prices ended the day slightly lower. U.S. crude oil fell to $82.23 per barrel, while Brent fell to $87.84.

NBC News has not independently verified Bloomberg News’ reporting, which was a timely reminder of the pressure global energy markets face from conflicts and supply disruptions far outside the Middle East.

Also driving oil prices was the U.S. Energy Information Administration’s announcement that oil stockpiles had risen by fewer barrels than analysts were expecting. The report also caused prices to briefly move higher, as it underscored the mammoth task ahead to replenish U.S. reserves that have been drained in recent months.

Prices were notably lower early in the day after reports from several outlets that, taken together, signaled a potential shift in how both Tehran and Washington are approaching the war after six months.
The first of those developments was a reported renewal of talks between Iran and Oman about reopening the critical Strait of Hormuz in recent days.
The State Department is also preparing to return American diplomats to their posts at embassies across the Middle East, The New York Times reported Tuesday.
And Secretary of State Marco Rubio told U.S. allies that the Trump administration does not expect to resume military strikes on Iran, according to comments reported by Axios.
Before the latest developments in Eastern Europe buffeted oil prices, President Donald Trump’s comments on social media had helped boost Iran sentiment.
“I have just been informed by the United States Navy that all mines have been removed and/or detonated from within the International Waters of the Strait of Hormuz,” Trump posted Tuesday.
The timing of the post raised eyebrows, however, because the text mirrors a Trump post on Aug. 18, when he wrote that “all water mines have been removed or detonated.”

The shipping analytics firm Kpler reported Wednesday that “Strait crossings remain subdued.” The firm assessed that just five vessels had transited the strait Tuesday, down from seven on Monday and nine on Sunday.
Those figures are just a tiny fraction of the pre-war daily average of 130 vessels.

Wednesday’s oil price action mirrored what has been a roller-coaster ride of a year for energy markets. Crude oil futures are down more than 5% since Sunday. Still, since the start of the year, oil prices overall have risen more than 40%.
After having soared to more than $110 per barrel in early April, U.S. crude oil dropped to the low $80s by the middle of that month before it rebounded again to more than $100.

By the end of May, crude oil prices had come down into the $80s. But it was the ceasefire announcement in mid-June that pushed oil prices down further, to near pre-war levels of around $70 a barrel for WTI crude.

But the low prices did not last long. Throughout July, the lack of progress in U.S.-Iran negotiations and renewed U.S. strikes on Iran pushed prices back up. By the end of the month, a barrel of U.S. crude was trading up into the low $90s.
The whipsawing energy prices helped keep inflation high in July, the Bureau of Economic Analysis reported Wednesday.

The Personal Consumption Expenditures index was unchanged from June, stuck at 3.7%. The lack of movement even extended to core PCE, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge, which excludes the more volatile categories of food and energy and came in at 3.3%.

“The United States still has an inflation problem. PCE inflation came in hotter than expected,” said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. “The impacts of the war in Iran are still apparent.”

The multiday move lower in oil prices has also dragged bond yields lower. After having traded at decades-high levels for days, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield was trading around 4.6%, down from nearly 4.75%. The 30-year yield had fallen to around 5.18%, down from its recent high of more than 5.3%.
Mortgage rates also trended lower for a second straight day. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 6.74% early Wednesday.

“When yields are falling, mortgage lenders are generally able to offer lower rates than they otherwise would have, depending on the timing and size of the move,” Matthew Graham of data provider Mortgage News Daily wrote Tuesday.
Yet even as oil prices, bond yields and mortgage rates are falling, gas prices remain high for consumers.
Since Sunday, prices have largely remained flat, and on Wednesday, the national average price per gallon ticked up to $4.10, AAA data shows.

title: Iran vows retaliation after U.S. widens sanctions, fueling fears of escalated war
summary: TEHRAN, Iran — Iran has vowed to retaliate against widened U.S. sanctions, saying Washington should “expect an attack” in response.
story: TEHRAN, Iran — Iran has vowed to retaliate against widened U.S. sanctions, saying Washington should “expect an attack” in response.

“We know how to play the game, too,” Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said in an interview televised by state media late Monday as he condemned the U.S. measures as an “economic terrorist attack.”
The U.S. has imposed sanctions on Iran since 1979, after Iranian students stormed the American Embassy in Tehran, taking U.S. diplomats hostage.

Madanizadeh said at least two countries — China and Russia — have so far given no indication that they plan to fall into line. At a news conference Tuesday, Chinese Foreign Affairs Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said Beijing was firmly opposed to “illegal unilateral sanctions,” according to Xinhua, China’s state-run news agency.
Madanizadeh warned that “they should not think that our response will be defensive and that we will only defend ourselves.” He added, “They should expect an attack from our side, as well.”
Madanizadeh did not specify what sort of attack.
He added that Tehran had been preparing for such an economic assault and that it had a two-year plan in the works to deal with the impact, which he did not expand on.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the fresh battery of measures against Iran on Monday, calling it an “economic D-Day” and warning that any country financially partnering with Tehran would be isolated. The U.S. stopped short of imposing actual penalties.

Bessent provided limited details about the measures and did not identify countries that could be targeted with secondary sanctions. He said President Donald Trump was “making phone calls to world leaders with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime.”

The Treasury Department confirmed Monday that it had launched Operation Economic Outcast. It said in a news release that it was expanding the categories of Iran-related conduct that could be subject to secondary sanctions, with determinations issued against “five critical sectors — digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping.”

It added that the Office of Foreign Assets Control had also sanctioned nearly 60 entities, people and vessels in multiple jurisdictions that it said “enable the Iranian regime’s recklessness,” in addition to other measures.
The United Arab Emirates, which has long maintained close economic ties with Iran, announced last week that it would be halting all financial transactions with Tehran.
On the ground in Tehran, some Iranians expressed resignation at the U.S. announcement, which Bessent described as “the single greatest financial offensive ever” against Iran.
“It’s nothing new,” Farzin, 27, a mechanic, told NBC News on Tuesday. “The country is already locked, and the psychological effect is worse than the actual outcome.”
Farzin said U.S. sanctions had yet to yield any significant impact on his business, with car parts still making their way into the country.
“You find a route and you find a market inside the country,” he said, adding that many parts were being imported through land borders, whether legally or illegally.
Farzin declined to give his last name. Many Iranians are wary of speaking with and identifying themselves to U.S. media.
Hamid Ebrahimi, a retired lawyer and university professor, said many Iranians felt there was little they could do to make their lives any better.

“We are just getting by day to day and can’t keep up with inflation,” said Ebrahimi, 63. “Sanctions have had an effect, and the government says it can manage them, but they have always hurt the people, and they will continue to do so.”
Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer at King’s College London’s School of Security Studies, said Washington’s latest moves were unlikely to achieve the desired results.
“Iran’s response so far suggests Washington’s ‘Economic D-Day’ is producing pain, but not the behavioral effect the administration is looking for,” he said.
Tehran appeared to be interpreting the measures as “economic warfare” aimed at its “regime survival rather than as bargaining pressure designed to produce a compromise,” Krieg added.
As a result, its response “has consequently been defiance rather than accommodation.”

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said in comments the semiofficial Tasnim news agency published Monday that the U.S. “must correct its tone and approach in dealing with Iran, because relying on force and bullying will only complicate the process.”

Krieg said the global community could expect Tehran to increase pressure on the Strait of Hormuz, the crucial trade route through which 20% of the world’s oil ran before the war, which began in late February after the U.S. and Israel launched punishing strikes on Iran.
The stated reason for waging war was to prevent Iran from building a nuclear weapon. Tehran has long denied it is seeking to build a nuclear arsenal.

Since then, the key waterway has largely been strangled by a blockade imposed by Iran, sending energy prices soaring, with the U.S. also launching its own blockade in Iranian ports in response to Iranian attacks along the strait. Hormuz was open and without tolls when the U.S. and Israel triggered the war.
“Tehran cannot prevent Washington from imposing sanctions, but it can make those sanctions expensive for everybody else,” Krieg said.
Meanwhile, Iranian media have repeatedly aired content threatening the life of Trump’s son Barron Trump, fueling fears over the escalating rhetoric surrounding the conflict.
U.S. Secret Service spokesperson Nate Herring said Monday that the agency was “aware of the video and investigates anything that can be perceived as a threat toward our protectees.”
“Out of concern for operational security, we do not discuss matters of protective intelligence,” Herring added.

title: CIA director flies unannounced to Moscow to hold talks, source says
summary: CIA Director John Ratcliffe flew to Russia to holds talks in Moscow, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.
story: WASHINGTON — CIA Director John Ratcliffe flew to Russia to hold unspecified talks in Moscow, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.
The person declined to say whom Ratcliffe was meeting with or what the focus of the talks was. The CIA declined to comment.

It’s Ratcliffe’s first known trip to Moscow as CIA director. He made headlines with a visit to Venezuela in January to meet with interim President Delcy Rodríguez about two weeks after the U.S. military seized President Nicolás Maduro in a raid in Caracas.

He also traveled to Cuba in May to meet with government leaders. He was the highest-ranking Trump administration official to visit the island, which is under severe economic pressure after the U.S. tightened sanctions.
News of Ratcliffe’s travel came as mystery swirled around a U.S. military transport aircraft that landed in Moscow, according to tracking data.
It was not known who was on board the plane and why it was in Moscow. When asked, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he did not have information about the aircraft.
Neither U.S. military officials, the White House, the U.S. Embassy in Moscow nor the Russian Embassy in Washington immediately responded to questions about the flight’s mission.
Two planes, a C-130 cargo plane and a C-40, landed in Riga, the capital of Latvia, as part of the same mission, according to a U.S. official. The C-130 then went on to Russia, the official said.
Data from FlightRadar24 tracking site showed a plane approached Vnukovo International Airport in Moscow just after 10 a.m. local time (3 a.m. ET) after taking off from Riga two hours earlier.

It had departed from the U.S. Air Force’s Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Sunday just before 5 p.m. ET, the data showed. That plane had apparently left Moscow on Tuesday afternoon, according to flight radar data.
CBS News and Axios first reported on the CIA chief’s unannounced visit.

CIA directors sometimes act as envoys for presidents in high-stakes talks with adversaries. Former President Joe Biden turned to then-CIA Director William Burns to relay stern warnings to Russia before and after President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

title: As Ukraine’s allies gather for big anniversary, one key backer is absent
summary: The lack of visible senior Trump administration participation was the latest sign of how Washington has backed off during a critical juncture for Ukraine.
story: Leaders of Ukraine’s international allies on Monday marked 35 years since the country broke away from the Soviet Union to become an independent nation.
The U.K.’s Andy Burnham flew in, while France’s Emmanuel Macron and Germany’s Friedrich Merz joined a call to reaffirm commitments to Kyiv.
But senior officials from one longtime backer were notably absent from the public show of support: the United States.
Add to Google
Add to Google

While U.S. senators and former officials visited Ukraine ahead of the commemorations, the apparent lack of senior Trump administration participation was the latest sign of how Washington has backed off during a critical juncture for Ukraine.
The message sent was especially pointed as Monday also marks 4 1/2 years since President Vladimir Putin launched his large-scale invasion of Russia’s much smaller neighbor.

Negotiations to reach a peace deal, which President Donald Trump once promised to achieve within 24 hours, have stalled as supplies of U.S. air defense missiles dwindle and the Russian leader ramps up threats to Ukraine’s allies.
Britain’s Burnham was the highest-profile Western leader to fly in and co-chair a meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing,” a group of countries backing Ukraine.

European Council President António Costa, as well as the heads of nearly a dozen European nations, was also in Kyiv, despite the country’s air force reporting Russian rocket and drone strikes overnight.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio congratulated Ukraine in a statement.
“The United States is committed to Ukraine’s sovereignty and continues to work to support a negotiated settlement to the Russia-Ukraine war that establishes a lasting and durable peace,” it said.
